+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 83.7
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The transfer vessel’s air filtration system hummed with a persistent mechanical drone, the sort of sound engineers learned to trust and passengers learned to hate. Arthur Neegan sat with his hands on his knees and watched a bead of condensate crawl down the bulkhead. Mars fell away beneath them in a rust-colored curve, and with it the only plot of ground he had ever owned outright—or thought he had. The retinue did not sit. Four of them stood along the aisle in grey coats cut like uniforms and denied to be uniforms. Their insignia was a red star crossed by a thin silver bar: Antares Diplomatic Corps, diplomatic in name only, if the port gossip was worth the air it rode on. The fifth, a woman with close-cropped hair and a sidearm worn openly, had taken the seat opposite him and not spoken since liftoff. “You’re not restraining me,” Arthur said. “We invited you,” she said. “Restraints are for people who decline.” “And if I had declined?” She considered the question as if it were a calibration. “Then the invitation would have become more expensive. For you. For the men waiting at your shaft-head. For the lease clerks who stamped your title. Antares prefers the cheaper method.” The drone deepened as the vessel cleared the thin Martian envelope and the attitude jets coughed. Through the port Arthur saw the transfer’s shadow slide across a freighter’s hull—blocky, lamp-studded, already antique by the standards of the ships that wanted Azra. He had spent twenty years believing exotic metals were a problem of assay and tonnage. He was learning they were a problem of who arrived first with guns that smiled. They docked at a station that did not appear on the colonial charts he knew. No name on the lock. No merchant smells. Only the antiseptic chill of a place kept ready for conversations that were not meant to be overheard by leases or laws. A door irised. The room beyond was small, carpeted in a green that had never seen a plant, and furnished with a table, two chairs, and a wall screen showing nothing but the starfield. A man rose. He was older than Arthur, neatly tired, with the soft hands of someone who had not swung a pick since the academies and the hard eyes of someone who had signed orders since. “Mr. Neegan. I am Consul Vey of the Antares mission. Sit, if you like. The tea is real. The recording devices are not, which is a courtesy I extend to very few miners.” Arthur remained standing. “Your people walked into my hab with rifles and called it courtesy.” “Rifles keep other courtesies from arriving first.” Vey poured anyway. “You have an Azra vein under an unassuming plot. Immensely rich, if our seismics are not lying to flatter us. You know what Azra does.” “It kicks decay,” Arthur said. “A sliver in a drive core and you get thrust the old reactors only dreamed about. A sliver in a warhead and you get a yield the treaties pretended was impossible. I read the circulars. I also read what happens to claim-jumpers.” “Then you have read the small picture.” Vey’s voice was mild, almost pedagogical. “The large one is this: three powers can build interstellar drives worth the name, and two of them are already rearming under the polite fiction of ‘survey motors.’ Earth wants Azra locked in a consortium so no one power can outrun the others. The Martian lease corporations want it metered, sold by the gram, and taxed into eternity. The Free Shafts want it buried again, because a metal that shortens half-lives also shortens the lives of anyone mining it without a sealed works. Antares wants none of those outcomes. We want a partner who can say, in a court or a council, that the vein was worked under a sovereign flag before the thieves finished drawing their maps.” Arthur laughed once, without humor. “I’m a first-generation settler with a secondhand drill. I am not a sovereign.” “You are a title,” Vey said. “Titles are cheaper than wars and harder to forge than seismics. Here is the offer. You sign an exclusive development compact with Antares. We garrison your plot—openly, as ‘technical advisors.’ We pay you a retainer that will make your grandchildren bored. We build the sealed works so your crew does not glow in the dark. In return, every gram leaves Mars under our seal, and you testify, when asked, that you invited us.” “And if I don’t?” “Then the consortium arrives with lawyers, the corporations with bigger lawyers, and someone less polite than I with a shaped charge and a story about a methane pocket.” Vey set the cup down. The porcelain clicked like a small, finished argument. “We have already turned away one freighter that was not a freighter. Its hold was lined for ore and its registry was three weeks old. Your neighbors think it was a customs sweep. It was not.” Arthur felt the station’s distant pumps through the soles of his boots, a second heartbeat under the first. He thought of the vein as he had seen it on the scope: a bright, impossible ribbon under ordinary regolith, patient as geology and sudden as politics. “You’re asking me to choose a master,” he said. “I am asking you to choose the master who admits the fact,” Vey replied. “Azra will not stay a miner’s secret. It will be a border, or a weapon, or both. The only question left is whether your name is on the compact or on the casualty list. Take the night. The vessel will not leave without you. Neither, I should add, will the men at your shaft.” He smiled, thinly, as if the smile were part of the uniform. “Drink the tea, Mr. Neegan. It is the last uncomplicated thing anyone will offer you.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter opens exactly as instructed—aboard the transfer vessel, with Arthur reflecting on his predicament—and delivers a dialogue-driven scene with a mysterious Antares consul making an offer. The prose is clean and controlled, with several memorable lines ("Restraints are for people who decline," "the smile were part of the uniform," "It is the last uncomplicated thing anyone will offer you"). The worldbuilding is genuinely Asimovian: the big-picture geopolitical stakes (three powers, Earth consortium, Martian lease corporations, Free Shafts) are laid out through Vey's exposition, while small details (the humming filtration, the tea, the unmarked station) ground the scene. Vey is a well-drawn antagonist-diplomat—polite menace rendered through understatement. Arthur's skepticism and his "choose a master" pushback feel earned and in-character for a first-generation settler engineer. Weaknesses: the exposition, while efficient, is somewhat on-the-nose; Vey's geopolitical monologue is a touch too neat, a classic Asimovian info-dump that works but shows its scaffolding. The plot beats (mysterious invitation, offer, veiled threat) are conventional for the genre, though competently executed. The female guard is underdeveloped, a stock silent-muscle figure. Some metaphors ("patient as geology and sudden as politics") are excellent; a few verge on cleverness for its own sake. The ending line is strong but the chapter ends on a familiar "drink the tea" beat rather than anything surprising. Still, this is a polished, professional piece that captures the retrofuturistic register well. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
By late morning the Trevi was a bright bowl of noise. Ben stood at the rim with a damp guidebook open to a map he had already misread twice, mouthing *fontana* as if the word might steady him. A horn snapped. A red motorcycle cut the crowd too close, brakes singing, and the front wheel stopped a hand’s width from his shoe. The rider killed the engine. “You are standing in the road,” she said, in English sharp enough to nick. Then, faster, in Italian he only half caught: something about tourists, death wishes, and British shoes. “I’m terribly—scusi—I thought this was the pavement.” He held up the book like a white flag. “Ben. Bennett. Academic. On sabbatical. Which is not an excuse.” She pushed the visor up. Dark eyes, a laugh she hadn’t decided to spend yet. “Alessandra. Courier. And you nearly became a footnote.” Her gaze dropped to the bike’s flank: a long, candy-colored scratch through the red, edged with a dent the size of a thumb. She touched it without thinking. “Previous life. Don’t ask.” “I wasn’t going to.” He was. “Your English is—” “Better than your Italian. Come. You look lost in a city that is not lost.” She swung a leg over. “Get on, or keep apologizing to the fountain. She has heard worse.” He should have refused. He climbed on, knees awkward, hands hovering until she caught his wrist and set it at her waist. “Hold, professore. Not a library.” They shot into a vein of side streets. Wind took the apology out of his mouth. She drove as she spoke: quick, precise, a little cruel for the fun of it. At a light she twisted to look at him. “You came to Rome to read about Rome.” “To finish a chapter on—” “No. Today you finish nothing.” The light changed. She laughed into the throttle. They ate standing up near Campo de’ Fiori, sauce on his cuff, her telling him which saints were frauds. When a postcard rack turned in the breeze she drifted past it, still talking, and a bright card—the fountain, badly printed—vanished into her jacket as if the wind had taken it. She didn’t look down. Later, on a wall above the river, she produced it and tucked it into his book. “A souvenir,” she said. “You would have bought the wrong one.” “That’s—did you pay?” “Ben.” Her smile was all teeth and weather. “Some things in this city are already yours if you are quick. Don’t make a speech.” He didn’t. The card warmed under his palm like a small crime he had agreed to keep. She took him where the guidebook went thin: a courtyard with a broken fountain, a stair that smelled of lemons, a gate she shouldered open because the latch had been tired for years. Once, on a slick ramp above parked cars, the bike fishtailed and his heart climbed into his throat. She whooped, corrected, and glanced back, delighted by the color in his face. “You liked that.” “I did not.” “Liar. Your hands are honest.” They were. He had stopped hovering. Near the Gianicolo the city opened, domes like knuckles under a hard blue sky. She cut the engine. For a moment neither of them performed. Wind moved her hair. He could see the scratch again, that unnamed color running through the red, and understood it was not an accident she regretted so much as a story she refused to finish for anyone. “You do this often?” he asked. “Kidnap polite men.” “Only the ones who say scusi to stone.” She studied him, mischief thinning into something less safe. “You could have gotten off at the first light.” “I know.” “And now?” “Now I don’t know the way back. Which I suspect was the point.” She leaned in, close enough that he smelled orange peel and petrol. Her mouth brushed the corner of his—not quite a kiss, a test, a theft of a different kind. He followed, clumsy and sure, and she let him for three heartbeats before she pulled away, eyes bright, unreadable. “Enough,” she said, softly, as if she were the one who had been pushed. “You are late for being careful.” She rode him to the river steps and did not kill the engine. He climbed off on unsteady legs. The postcard jutted from his book. His mouth still held the shape of almost. “Tomorrow,” she said, not a question. “Same fountain. Don’t stand in the road.” “Alessandra—” She was already rolling. The dent caught the sun, a bright scar, and then she was gone into the traffic, leaving him dizzy, smiling, and entirely unwilling to open the map.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of short-form romance fiction that hits nearly all the prompt's requirements with economy and flair. The near-collision at the Trevi Fountain, the culture/personality clash, Alessandra's kleptomania (shown subtly via the postcard theft, never named), the unsanctioned tour, Ben's growing captivation, and the ambiguous almost-kiss payoff at parting are all present. The prose is tight and image-driven—"domes like knuckles under a hard blue sky," "a laugh she hadn't decided to spend yet"—and the dialogue crackles with character-specific wit. Alessandra's enigmatic nature is well-preserved; she tows Ben along while revealing almost nothing of herself, which suits the brief. Strengths: the scene structure is vivid and episodic as requested; the postcard theft and its later gifting is a genuinely elegant kleptomania detail; the closing line ("entirely unwilling to open the map") lands as a satisfying thematic button. The voice is consistent—wry, sensory, slightly hard-edged. Weaknesses: the piece is somewhat compressed at ~850 words against the 1000 requested, and the day's "rollercoaster" is more summarized than dramatized in the middle section ("She took him where the guidebook went thin")—we're told of several adventures rather than shown them, which slightly undercuts the "series of interconnected short scenes" instruction. Some beats are familiar romance tropes (the almost-kiss, the "tomorrow, same fountain" ending), and Ben's transformation from polite academic to willing accomplice, while plausible, happens fast and with little internal resistance beyond a couple of lines. A few phrases flirt with preciosity ("a theft of a different kind," "the shape of almost") but stop short of purple. The fishtail scene and the Gianicolo pause are the strongest dramatized moments; the middle could have used one more fully rendered scene rather than montage. Overall this is polished, professional work with minor structural shortcuts and a mildly predictable romantic arc. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The stranger’s tentacles are still settling when I set the glass down. Vega whisky catches the low amber of the bar lamps and throws it back in a thin gold ring. They drink half of it before they look at me. “Rough transit?” I ask. “Rough everything.” Their voice is low, scraped at the edges. “You Nettle?” “Nets is fine. Most people here don’t bother with the whole name.” “Most people aren’t looking for you.” I keep my hands on the bar. The wood is warm from the evening, scarred where miners have set down helmets and merchants have tapped impatient fingers. Behind me, the still ticks. Somewhere down the counter, old Varr argues with a cargo clerk about docking fees, the same argument they have every third night. “Looking’s a strong word,” I say. “You want another pour, or you want to tell me who sent you?” They turn the glass once, watching the whisky climb the side. “Nobody sent me. That’s the problem. I came on my own, which means nobody knows I’m here, which means if I don’t walk back out, nobody comes looking.” A tentacle flicks, uneasy. “I need a berth. Quiet. No registry. Two nights, maybe three.” “The Outpost isn’t a hideout.” “Everything on the rim is a hideout if you pay.” I almost smile. “You’ve been reading the wrong brochures.” A crash cuts through the room—sharp, bright, a glass giving up somewhere past the card tables. Somebody swears. Somebody else laughs. I don’t turn. Maren will sweep it up; she always does, humming like the shards owe her an apology. The stranger flinches anyway. Their eyes go to the door, then to the narrow service hatch behind the still, then back to me. “Jumpy,” I say. “Careful.” “Those aren’t the same.” “They are if the people behind you don’t know the difference.” They lean in. The whisky on their breath is cheap and honest. “There’s a skiff in slip nine. Unmarked. Two occupants. They’ve been sitting with the running lights off since I docked. I watched them from the gantry. They didn’t follow me in. Yet.” My stomach goes tight and small. I wipe a ring of condensation that isn’t there. “Miners sit in the dark all the time. Saves the cells.” “Miners don’t run a cold scan on every face that crosses the lock.” Varr’s voice rises, then drops. The card table resumes its soft clatter. The Outpost goes on being itself: tired, loud in patches, safe because nobody here has the energy to be otherwise. I have built a life on that tiredness. I do not like the way this stranger is looking through it. “You said you were looking for me,” I say. “Now you’re talking about a skiff. Pick one story.” “They’re the same story.” They push the empty glass toward me with two fingers. “Double. Please. And don’t call my name if you know it. I haven’t given it, and I’d like to keep it that way a little longer.” I pour. My hand is steady. That’s a talent I keep polished. “I don’t know your name.” “You will.” They take the drink but don’t lift it. “Three years ago, a courier ship broke up over the Kite Reach. Official report said navigational failure. Unofficial report said the pilot dumped the cargo and ran. The cargo was people. Indenture contracts. Kids, some of them.” The bar noise thins in my ears. I hear the still. I hear my own breath. “I wasn’t on that ship,” I say. “I didn’t say you were.” Their tentacles have gone very still. “I said the pilot dumped the cargo and ran. I said the people who owned those contracts never stopped looking. And I said there’s a skiff in slip nine with its lights off.” “That’s a lot of saying for somebody who wants a quiet berth.” “I want more than a berth.” They meet my eyes. There’s no threat in it, which is worse. There’s hope, frayed and stubborn. “I want you to tell me whether the pilot is still alive. Because if she is, those two outside aren’t here for me.” Down the bar, Maren’s broom ticks against a table leg. Someone asks for a beer. The door to the lock hasn’t opened. Not yet. I set the bottle down harder than I mean to. “Finish your drink,” I say. “Then you’re going to tell me exactly what you saw on that gantry. And you’re going to do it quietly.” They nod, once, and wrap a tentacle around the glass like it might try to leave. Outside, slip nine stays dark. Inside, I smile at a merchant who wants to settle a tab, and I do not look at the door, and I do not let my hands shake, and the chapter of the evening that was only whisky and small talk is already gone.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong execution of the prompt: first person, present tense, cozy sci-fi bar setting, roughly 60% dialogue, conflict established (mysterious stranger, dark skiff, Nets' implied past as the pilot) and left unresolved. The voice is controlled and consistent—wry, guarded, observational. The prose is economical with a few genuinely good lines ("humming like the shards owe her an apology," "safe because nobody here has the energy to be otherwise"). The reveal that Nets may be the pilot who dumped indentured cargo is an effective hook, though the "you will know my name" / "I wasn't on that ship" beat is a fairly familiar noir structure—the stranger who arrives with the protagonist's past. Some elements are slightly stock: the mysterious stranger with a hidden agenda, the "don't say my name" trope, the closing line self-consciously referencing "the chapter of the evening," which is a bit cute and breaks immersion. The stranger remains thin as a character—mostly a delivery mechanism for plot. Nets is better drawn through deflection and small actions (wiping condensation that isn't there). Dialogue is competent and mostly natural, occasionally aphoristic to a fault ("Those aren't the same." / "They are if..."). Word count is close to target. No purple prose; no overwrought moments; ending tone is appropriately tense rather than falsely positive. Minor weaknesses: the tentacled dreads are underused as characterization; the worldbuilding is light even for cozy sci-fi; the emotional complexity, while present, is mostly implied rather than deeply explored. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 82.2
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The saxophone starts before I see the player. Low, then bright, then low again, like the street is breathing through brass. I stop under a balcony that drips last night’s rain and try to look like I meant to be here. My backpack strap cuts the same groove it cut on the bus. Two states. Thirty minutes to pack. Mom’s voice still in the kitchen, not yelling anymore, just that flat “we’ll talk when you’re ready to be reasonable.” I was already gone by then. Or I thought I was. Turns out leaving a house and leaving the feeling are different jobs. People move around me like I’m a post. Tourists with plastic cups. A woman arguing into her phone about parking. Somebody’s dog in a sweater. The heat sits on my neck and doesn’t ask permission. I smell fried dough, river water, and somebody’s cologne that tried too hard. Don’t look lost. Lost gets noticed. I walk. The sax follows, then fades, then finds me again at the next corner. The player is under a green awning, case open, eyes half-closed. Coins wink in the felt. I don’t have coins. I have fourteen dollars, a phone at twelve percent, and a name I finally said out loud that my family treated like a cracked window. A kid about my age is sitting on the curb with a cardboard sign that says NEED BUS FARE in marker that’s already bled. Hood up despite the heat. One sneaker taped at the toe. They clock me clocking the sign and snort. “Don’t,” they say. “Everybody thinks I’m gonna ask. I’m not asking you.” “I wasn’t gonna give you anything.” “Good. You’re broke. I can tell by the shoulders.” I almost laugh. It comes out wrong, like a cough. “Taylor.” “Jules.” They tip their chin at the sax. “He’s been playing the same four bars since I sat down. Either it’s genius or he’s stuck.” “Stuck,” I say. “Genius doesn’t repeat the mistake on purpose.” Jules looks at me properly then. Not the backpack. Not the sign I don’t have. Me. “You just get here?” “Last night. Ride dumped me by the river.” “Classic.” They fold the sign, not hiding it, just done with the performance. “You got a place?” “Working on it.” “That’s a no.” They stand. Taller than I expected. A scar through one eyebrow, old. “I’m not your tour guide. I’m also not gonna watch you get sweet-talked by the first person who offers a couch and a story. There’s a church two blocks over that does sandwiches at noon if you can stand the speech. After that, the library’s air-conditioned and they don’t care if you sleep with your eyes open.” My chest does that stupid thing where gratitude and suspicion arrive holding hands. “Why help?” “Because yesterday somebody didn’t.” Jules shrugs like it costs them. “And because you look like you’re about to cry in a way that attracts the wrong kind of nice.” I hate that they’re right. The last forty-eight hours keep replaying: Dad’s chair scraping back, my sister’s silence, the counsellor’s phrase sitting in Mom’s mouth like she borrowed it. Concerning behavioural patterns. As if the pattern wasn’t the town, the boredom, the years of being the wrong shape in the right hallway. Coming out wasn’t drama. Leaving might have been. I don’t know yet. I know my hands are shaking and I shove them in my pockets so Jules won’t see. We walk. The sax thins behind us, one last run up the scale, then a car horn eats it. “You running from cops?” Jules asks, casual as weather. “No.” “Parents?” “Something like that.” “They gonna call you in as missing?” The question lands in my stomach. I hadn’t let it finish forming. “Maybe. Probably. I turned the location off. I think.” “Think isn’t a plan.” Jules stops at a crosswalk. A streetcar groans past, windows full of faces that aren’t looking at us. “Listen. I don’t do secrets on day one. I got my own. You don’t get them. What you get is: don’t follow anyone who says they know a guy. Don’t flash cash. Don’t tell the sandwich church your real situation unless you want a phone call home before the mustard’s dry. And if I disappear, I disappeared. Don’t come looking.” “That’s a lot of rules for somebody who isn’t a tour guide.” “I’m a person who wants to eat and not get got.” Their mouth almost smiles. “You trans?” The word in somebody else’s mouth, out here, in daylight, makes my skin go hot and cold at once. “Yeah.” “Cool. Me too. Different alphabet, same exit sign.” They start walking again before I can answer. “Doesn’t make us friends. Makes the math easier.” At the church steps, a line already bends toward the door. A man with a clipboard smiles too wide. Jules doesn’t join the line. They nod at a side gate. “Back table if you say you’re with the youth group that already ate. Lie small. I’ll be at the library until four. If you’re not there, I assume you found better or worse. Either way, not my problem.” “Jules.” They pause. “Thanks. For the not-asking.” “Don’t thank me yet.” The scarred eyebrow lifts. “First day’s a costume. City hasn’t decided what it wants from you.” They go. I stand in the smell of bread and bleach and try to decide if trust is a door or a trap. The saxophone is gone. My phone buzzes once—Mom—and I let it die in my hand without looking. Somewhere under the noise, my own voice, the one I used two nights ago, is still saying the true thing. I hold onto that. I get in line. I lie small. I keep my eyes on the gate.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong execution of the prompt. It maintains Taylor's first-person voice with a wry, guarded teen register, uses mixed tense appropriately, and covers the first day in New Orleans with a meeting with Jules, a fellow runaway with hinted secrets ("I don't do secrets on day one"). Dialogue is sharp and characterful—Jules's clipped, defensive wit ("I can tell by the shoulders," "Doesn't make us friends. Makes the math easier") is a highlight. The internal monologue effectively conveys conflicting emotions: gratitude and suspicion, fear and resolve. Sensory detail is well-chosen and economical (saxophone, rain-dripping balcony, fried dough and river water). The trans disclosure backstory is woven in naturally without exposition dumps. Weaknesses: Jules is somewhat stock—the wise, scarred street kid who dispenses survival rules is a familiar archetype, and their instant, unsolicited help edges toward convenient plotting. The "sandwich church" and library beats are efficient but predictable; the chapter is more scene-setting than escalation, and the emotional arc, while coherent, stays in a narrow band of guarded wariness. A few lines flirt with over-polish ("gratitude and suspicion arrive holding hands") but mostly the prose stays controlled. The ending's ambivalence is earned and fits the tone. Word count is roughly on target. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Midas had spent the morning explaining, mostly to himself, that today would be a simple day. Simple days were a kind of weather. They arrived, looked promising, and then rained on you from an unexpected direction. “Water,” he said, tapping the empty bottle against his knee. “North cistern. In, out, home before the wind changes its mind.” Chewy sat on the crate that served as furniture, strategy table, and, on bad nights, emotional support. The koala’s fur had once been the colour of optimism. It was now the colour of things that had met weather and lost. One glass eye tracked Midas with the weary professionalism of a device that had outlived its warranty and most of civilisation. “Probability of simple,” Chewy said. The voice came from somewhere behind the stitching, thin as old radio. “Low. Battery: also low. Suggest not dying. It upsets the averages.” “We’re not dying. We’re fetching water.” “Historically,” said Chewy, “those have not been separate activities.” They left the culvert that passed for home base—three tarps, one argument with a door, and a sign reading DO NOT that had lost the rest of its instructions—and took the ridge path. The city below them had become a suggestion. Towers stood like bad teeth. Vines had unionised. Halfway along the old overpass they found the graffiti. It was not the usual kind, which tended toward anatomy, theology, or both. This was neat, painted in a hand that had practiced being believed. THE REFUGE IS WHERE THE ROAD FORGETS ITS NAME. BRING NOTHING THAT HUMS. Midas read it twice, which was once more than wisdom required. “That’s a clue,” he said. “That’s a sentence,” said Chewy. “Clues are sentences that have learned bad habits.” “A hidden refuge. In the wilds. Maybe food. Maybe people who still own spoons.” “We own a spoon.” “We own half a spoon and a strong opinion.” Chewy’s ear twitched, a small mechanical apology for having no better argument. “Mission parameters changing. This is how Tuesdays happen.” “It’s Thursday.” “Tuesdays are a state of mind.” They followed the road until it did, in a technical sense, forget its name. A fallen sign lay face-down in the nettles, too modest to introduce itself. Beyond it the asphalt frayed into a track, and the track into a polite suggestion that walking was still an option if one enjoyed regret. The refuge, when they found it, was a bus. It had been driven into a cutting and then, by the look of things, forgotten on purpose. Someone had painted leaves on the windows. The leaves had been painted by a person who had heard of leaves but not recently met one. On the door, in the same careful hand: KNOCK IF YOU ARE NOT A PROBLEM. Midas knocked. The door opened on a woman holding a crossbow with the casual intimacy of someone holding a conversation. “We’re not a problem,” Midas said, which was optimistic even by his standards. “You’re humming,” she said. Chewy, offended on behalf of engineering, powered his voice down to a whisper. “Residual capacitor. Very small hum. Artisanal.” She considered the koala. The crossbow considered Midas. These were not the same consideration. “Water’s what we came for,” Midas said. “The cistern. We can leave the refuge to its leaves.” “Cistern’s under the bus,” she said. “You can have a bottle if you take the message back. Someone keeps painting invitations. We keep getting visitors. Visitors arrive with needs. Needs are how you get committees, and committees are how you get minutes, and minutes are how the old world ended, if you ask anyone who was in one.” “We didn’t bring minutes,” Midas said. “You brought a humming toy and a face like a misplaced apology. Close enough.” She gave them water. She also gave them a sack, because kindness in the aftertimes often came with luggage. The sack clanked. “Seeds,” she said. “Or bolts. I forget which sack is which. Don’t open it near anything that used to be electrical. And don’t come back unless the road remembers you.” They had gone twelve steps when the sack opened itself, which is what sacks do when the world is feeling literary. Bolts—definitely bolts—spilled into a patch of mud that had been a drain and still remembered the job. Something under the mud clicked. The clicking had the confident rhythm of a machine that had waited years for a idiot with pockets. The overpass answered. A section of railing, long resigned to being scenery, lifted on a hinge no one had maintained and everyone had deserved. It struck Midas at the thoughtful height between pride and survival. He sat down in the nettles. Chewy flew, in the loose sense of the word, into a thorn bush, and announced from inside it that flight was a deprecated feature. “Sideways,” Chewy observed, muffled. “As predicted. Also downward. Downward was not in the brief.” The hinge, having done its one trick, sulked. The road behind them had acquired a new opinion about being walked on. Smoke, thin and embarrassed, rose from the drain. They tried the ridge. The ridge had spent the afternoon becoming a slide. They tried the culvert upstream and found it occupied by a goat with the expression of a magistrate. They tried waiting, which is a route only in the sense that despair is a destination. By dusk the wind had changed its mind three times and none of them had been helpful. Home base received them in stages, which was the only way it could, given the state of the pair. First came the water bottle, rolled ahead of them by a slope that believed in punchlines. It bonked the DO NOT sign and settled, half full, like a saint who had reconsidered. Then came Chewy, extracted from the thorns and carried under one arm, leaking a noise like a polite bee giving up. “Battery critical,” he said. “Dignity also critical. Suggest we pretend this was reconnaissance.” Last came Midas, nettle-stung, bolt-scratched, and wearing a leaf that had transferred from the bus window to his hair out of professional courtesy. He set Chewy on the crate. He set himself on the floor, which had fewer opinions. “We found the refuge,” he said. “We were expelled by it,” said Chewy. “We got water.” “We got a bottle that arrived before we did, which is either efficiency or an insult.” Midas looked at the graffiti still drying behind his eyes. THE REFUGE IS WHERE THE ROAD FORGETS ITS NAME. He thought of the woman, the crossbow, the sack that had been a trap or a gift or, most likely, both, because the world no longer did single-purpose objects. “Tomorrow,” he said, “we stay in. We drink the water. We do not read walls.” Chewy’s good eye dimmed, then found him again. “Tomorrow is a rumour. Tonight you are worse for wear in at least four categories. I am keeping score. It is all I have left that still functions.” Outside, something in the city hummed for a moment, then thought better of it. The culvert held. The sign still said DO NOT, and for once Midas was inclined to agree with incomplete instructions. He passed Chewy the bottle. The koala could not drink, but it seemed rude not to offer. Some courtesies survived the collapse. They were small, dry, and, if you listened carefully, almost funny.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, disciplined piece of comic post-apocalyptic fiction that captures Pratchett's register well: dry asides, personified objects, bureaucratic humor, and a world where inanimate things have opinions. The structure follows the brief precisely—morning deliberation, mission derailment via graffiti and refuge, multiple failed routes home, and a return "in stages, worse for wear." Strengths: Chewy is a genuinely funny creation ("Suggest not dying. It upsets the averages"; "Tuesdays are a state of mind"), and the banter has real rhythm. The woman with the crossbow is efficiently characterized in a few lines. The "home base received them in stages" sequence is a clever structural joke that literalizes the prompt's "returns them to home base in multiple ways." The ending's melancholy warmth—passing the bottle to a koala who cannot drink—lands the "wry, dry" tone without tipping into sentimentality. Weaknesses: The aphorism density occasionally tips into over-cleverness ("Simple days were a kind of weather"; "despair is a destination"; "a slope that believed in punchlines"). A few jokes are strained rather than earned, and the constant personification (vines had unionised, the road acquired opinions) risks diminishing returns through repetition. There's a typo ("a idiot with pockets"). The plot is thin and somewhat predictable in its beats—mission goes sideways exactly as promised—but the prompt demanded that arc, so predictability here is largely structural rather than a failure of imagination. The prose is clean and controlled, never purple. Dialogue is the strongest element. Emotionally it is light but not hollow; the final courtesy gesture gives it a small, earned resonance. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 86.3
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the door gave a thin, offended cry. Rain came in with him, and the smell of wet wool, and then the man himself, shoulder first, as if the street had shoved him. “Don’t look delighted,” he said. “I’m not staying. I’m a weather event.” Anwen did not look up from the invoice. “Then drip on the mat. The poetry section’s had enough.” He laughed, the quick bright sound of a man used to rooms arranging themselves around it. “You’re meant to say, Good God, it’s you.” “I don’t do meant to.” She capped her pen. He was tall in the low shop, film-star tall, the sort of face that arrived already lit. Cai Brennan. Half of Wales had watched him leave; the other half pretended they hadn’t noticed. “If you’re hiding, the atlases are at the back. No window.” “Hiding is a strong word.” He peered through the rain-streaked glass. Two figures hunched under a golf umbrella, cameras tucked like contraband. “Strategic retreat. They want a quote about the divorce that isn’t happening and the film that might be. I want a minute in which nobody likes me on purpose.” “Bold hope. Tea’s a pound if you want it. If you don’t, the mat is still free.” He turned, wounded and amused in the same breath. “A pound. In London they’d have given me the shop.” “This isn’t London. And I’m not giving you the shop.” She filled the kettle anyway. Her hands were steady. Her pulse was not, which she resented. Up close he was less polished: a nick on the jaw, rain in his lashes, the charm turned up a notch too high, as if volume might pass for ease. “Cai,” he said, offering it like a gift. “I know.” “And you are—” “Busy.” “Anwen Price,” he read off the invoice, pleased with himself. “Owner, jailer, enemy of weather events. Do you always greet fugitives like this, or am I special?” “You’re damp.” She set a mug down without quite meeting his eyes. “Milk’s in it. Don’t perform gratitude.” He wrapped both hands around the mug as if it might applaud. For a moment the performance slipped. “Most people perform it for me. It’s unsettling when they don’t. I start wondering what I’ve done.” “Breathed near a camera, I expect.” “Cruel.” He smiled, but it snagged. “Effective, though. God. You’re not even pretending to be impressed.” “Should I be?” “It would be polite.” “I’m Welsh. Polite is a rumour.” He laughed again, softer, and drifted toward the shelves, trailing a finger along spines. She watched the finger and told herself she was watching for wet marks. Outside, a lens kissed the glass and withdrew. “They’ll get bored,” she said. “They don’t. I do.” He pulled out a thin book of essays and didn’t open it. “I used to think if I could make a whole room like me, I’d be safe. Not loved. Liked. Liked is manageable. You can schedule it.” Anwen wiped the counter that did not need wiping. “And if a room doesn’t?” “Then I become unbearable. Ask my sister.” He glanced at her, and the rogue was still there, but under it something younger. “When I was twelve I was the innkeeper in the school play. Three lines. My father came, which he never did, and left at the interval. Not angry. Just finished. I stood in the wings in a tea towel apron and heard the door. After, I told jokes until the caretaker begged me to go home. I thought if I stopped being pleasant for one second, the rest of the building would leave as well.” The rain thickened. The shop smelled of paper and damp coat. Anwen said, carefully, “That’s a grim little economy.” “It paid for a career.” He set the book back, aligned it too neatly. “It does not, apparently, pay for tea in Penrhos. You’re looking at me as if I’ve recited a shopping list.” “I’m looking at you as if you meant it. That’s different.” Her ears were hot. She hated that he might see. “People leave rooms for all sorts of reasons. Not all of them are a verdict on the innkeeper.” “Say that again. Slower. I might have it put on a mug.” “No.” He came back to the counter. Closer. The charm gathered itself, automatic, then faltered when she didn’t lean in to meet it. “You really aren’t going to flutter.” “I might later. In private. Where you can’t feed on it.” The admission escaped before she could fold it small. She stared at the invoice as if it had betrayed her. “Don’t look like that.” “Like what?” “Like I’ve handed you something.” “You have.” His voice dropped, the theatrical edge gone. “I’m not used to wanting the version of me that isn’t working. It’s inconvenient. You’re inconvenient.” “Good.” A camera flashed, feeble against the wet window. He didn’t turn. “If I stay until they go,” he said, “will you keep refusing to like me out loud?” “I’ll consider it.” She pushed the mug an inch toward him. Her fingers brushed his. Neither of them remarked on it, which made it louder. “Drink your tea, Cai Brennan. And if you drip on the poetry, you’re buying the lot.” “Terrifying,” he said, and sounded, for once, as if he meant a kinder word.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong scene that executes the prompt with notable skill. The dialogue carries the piece, as requested, and both voices are distinct: Anwen is dry, clipped, deflecting; Cai is charming with cracks showing. The "rogue with fragile ego" is realized through concrete beats—his need to be recognized, the confession that "liked is manageable," and the school-play anecdote, which lands as a genuine vulnerability rather than a generic sad backstory. Anwen's internal fluster is shown efficiently ("Her hands were steady. Her pulse was not, which she resented") and her slip—"I might later. In private"—is a well-timed crack in her composure. The Welsh setting is present but light (Penrhos, "I'm Welsh. Polite is a rumour"), which satisfies the prompt without wallpapering. The chemistry builds through subtext and small physical beats (the mug pushed an inch, fingers brushing, "which made it louder"). The ending doesn't overreach: no kiss, no transformation, just a softening that's earned by the conversation's trajectory. Minor weaknesses: some lines flirt with cleverness-over-substance ("the sort of face that arrived already lit," "a lens kissed the glass"), and a few quips are slightly too polished, more sit-com than life. Cai's monologue about the innkeeper is a touch confessional too fast for a first meeting with a stranger, though the text acknowledges this ("You're looking at me as if I've meant it"), which partially mitigates it. The "inconvenient" exchange flirts with romcom formula. Prose is generally elegant and controlled, imagery is sparing but apt (rain, wet wool, paper and damp coat). Emotionally engaging and coherent throughout; no purple prose or amateurish habits. Word count near target. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 81.6
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The underhold door gave with a sigh of oiled hinges, and the quiet on the other side was worse than any clamour they had left above. Aya stepped through first. The air was colder here, thick with whale-oil and the sweet-rot smell of old rope. Lamps burned low in brass cages along a vaulted passage, their flames steady as held breath. No footfalls. No whispered watchword. Only the drip of harbour-seep through stone, and the long black mouth of the stair that led, she knew, to the scythan vault. Katra’s hand found her sleeve. “Too still,” she murmured. “Still is a kindness,” Simeon said, though his voice had gone thin. “We’ve had little enough of it.” They had taken three steps when the lamps flared as one. Men came out of the side-passages without hurry: oilskins, brass-buttoned coats, cutlasses naked and level. Not the guild’s night-crew. These were the leader’s own, the ones who did not dice in the common room and did not drink with masks. Aya counted six, then eight. A pistol’s hammer clicked somewhere to her left, a small dry sound like a bone set wrong. At the foot of the stair stood the woman the dawn raid was supposed to have taken. Guildmistress Hester Vane had not been hanged, nor ironed, nor even, by the look of her, inconvenienced. She wore black broadcloth and a high collar starched to a blade. A whalebone cane rested in one gloved hand; the other lay on the lock of a heavy pistol, brass inlaid, the sort of instrument men trusted because it did not whisper and did not dream. Her face was the colour of old paper. Her eyes were not. “Masks off,” she said. “Or I have them taken off. I am not in a temper for theatre.” Aya’s mouth had gone dry. *She was in the cells. The criers had it before first light. I heard the bell.* “Madam,” Simeon began, and one of the oilskins set a cutlass-point, very gently, beneath his chin. He stopped. Katra did not. “If you’ve a mind to parley, parley. If you’ve a mind to murder, do it without the sermon.” Vane’s mouth moved, not quite a smile. “I have a mind to see who has been spending my nights in my house.” She nodded. “The tall one first.” They took Aya by the arms. She did not struggle; struggle would have been a story for later, and there would be no later if she gave them a reason. Gloved fingers found the knot at her nape. The silk came away. Lamp-light struck her face, and she felt the cold of it as if the cloth had been skin. A murmur went through the men. One of them crossed himself with a hand that still held steel. Vane came up the last step and studied her the way a dock-clerk studies a bill of lading. “Lady Aya Pell.” The name landed without flourish. “Your mother’s daughter. I wondered when the blood would out. She screamed hymns at the end, did you know? Very devout, for a woman who opened doors that ought to stay shut.” Something in Aya’s chest drew tight and hot. She kept her voice level, the voice she used in drawing-rooms when a duke said something foul and expected her to laugh. “You were meant to be in irons.” “I was meant to be seen in irons.” Vane tapped the cane once on the stone. “A raid is a useful story. It sorts the loyal from the ambitious. You sorted yourself rather neatly.” Her gaze flicked to Katra, to Simeon. “Bind them. All three. Gently. I dislike marks I did not order.” Rope bit Aya’s wrists behind her back. Katra swore once, low and inventive, and then was silent. Simeon’s breath came short. They were walked, not dragged, to the landing, and set on their knees where the lamplight could find them. No blow was struck. The cutlasses merely remained, a bright fence, and the pistol remained in Vane’s hand as if it had grown there. From beyond the walls, thin and far, a foghorn sounded. Once. Aya swallowed. The mask was gone. The name was spoken. By morning it would be in a magistrate’s ear, or worse, in her father’s. *Immateria. Outlawed. Hanged by the neck.* She saw the rope again, not this rope, the other: her mother’s hair lifting in the harbour wind, the crowd very quiet because they were afraid of what might answer if they jeered. “You will not kill us here,” she said. “Will I not?” “Not if you are the woman who staged her own arrest before breakfast.” Aya lifted her chin. The aristocratic posture was a tool; she used it. “I am worth more above ground than below it. My father sits on the Harbour Board. He signs the oil levies. He can have a customs cutter look the other way, or look very hard indeed, at whatever hull you name. The Crown already wants a Pell neck. Give them mine and you get a day of spectacle. Keep me, and you get a key that brass and warrants cannot pick.” Katra made a small sound. Aya did not look at her. *Forgive me. I am buying hours, not honour.* Vane’s eyes did not warm. “You offer me your house as if it were yours to spend.” “I offer you the fear of my house. They will pay to have me back unspoiled, and they will pay more to have the manner of my nights never written down. You know what they did to my mother. You know what they would do if they learned her gift did not die with her.” The words tasted of iron. She made herself continue. “I can be a hostage, Madam. A lever. Kill me and you have a scandal and a search. Hold me and you have the Board by the throat, and the scythan vault uncontested, and three fools who will not be missed until you wish them missed.” The foghorn again. Twice, now, the second note lower, rolling over the black water beyond the guild walls. One of the bodyguards shifted. “She’s gentry, mistress. Gentry talk. We could—” “You could be silent,” Vane said, without looking at him. To Aya: “You rose quickly. Too quickly for lockpicks and a pretty mask. There were nights the lamps on this stair burned blue. My men will not say what they saw in the corners. Men trust steel. They do not trust what gathers when a Pell girl opens her mouth to something that is not a prayer.” Aya felt it then, faint as a pulse behind the eyes: the immateria, close as the dark on the other side of a door she must not touch. Not here. Not with wrists bound and witnesses who would call it devilry and be half right. She pressed the wanting down until her hands shook. “I am not my mother,” she said. “I am alive, and I am useful, and I am on my knees in your house. That is the whole of my negotiation.” Simeon whispered, “Aya—” “Hush,” she said, gentle, and hated herself for the gentleness. Vane regarded her a long moment. The cane tapped. The pistol did not lower. “Useful,” she repeated, as if tasting the word for spoilage. “We shall see what the Board thinks a daughter is worth, and what you think your companions are worth when the asking begins. If you lie, I will not hang you. Hanging is a public mercy. I will leave you where the tide takes the unclaimed, and I will let the city invent a prettier death.” She turned her head a fraction. “Take them below the vault stair. Separate cells. No light for the lady. She has seen enough of what gathers in the dark.” They hauled Aya up. As the passage turned, the foghorn sounded a third time, long and mournful, and was swallowed by stone.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the prompt's requirements with strong competence: the confrontation occurs without a fight scene, Aya is unmasked and captured, and she negotiates her hostage value while internally grappling with exposure of her heritage and magick. The Victorian-grit register is well maintained ("brass and oil and steel," whale-oil, foghorns, Harbour Board), and gothic horror elements appear in the mother's hanging, the "blue lamps," and what "gathers in the dark." Strengths: Vane is a genuinely menacing antagonist with a distinct voice — the staged arrest is a clever, plausible twist that reframes the raid. Aya's internal monologue is well integrated, particularly the memory of her mother's hanging and her self-aware aristocratic posture as a "tool." The negotiation is the strongest section: concrete leverage (customs cutters, oil levies, the family's fear of scandal) rather than vague pleading. Katra's terse defiance and Simeon's fragility give the trio differentiated voices. The foghorn motif recurs effectively. Prose is controlled, with few lapses; "the cold of it as if the cloth had been skin" is a fine touch. Weaknesses: The story beats are delivered somewhat mechanically — capture, unmask, negotiation, imprisonment proceed in orderly succession with little friction or surprise within the scene itself. Vane's capitulation to the hostage argument comes rather easily; a harder bargain or a cost extracted would deepen tension. The bodyguard's interjection ("She's gentry, mistress...") is a slightly stock beat. Some lines flirt with over-polish ("the voice she used in drawing-rooms when a duke said something foul"), and the ending, while atmospheric, resolves a shade too neatly into a cliffhanger of cells rather than genuine dread. The mother's "screamed hymns" detail is effective but Vane's knowledge of it strains plausibility slightly. Minor: "the colour of old paper. Her eyes were not" is a touch precious. Overall this is skilled, disciplined genre writing that hits every instruction without transcending them. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The neon jukebox in the corner of the bar has been chewing the same scratchy rock track since Spike walked in. Guitar, snare, a voice that never quite finishes the chorus. He lights a cigarette off the last one and watches the door because the bounty notice said the mark drinks here, and because the room smells like the kind of place where someone else is always already working. She comes in wet from the street, short shorts, black crop top, a dragon crawling her right arm. Two pistols sit low on her hips like they grew there. Revy clocks the room the way he does—exits, hands, who is armed—and her eyes stop on him. "Fuck," she says, not quiet. "Evening." Spike tips his head. The prosthetic eye makes the distance between them feel wrong for a second, then rights itself. "You here for the accountant?" "I'm here for the money." She drops onto the stool beside him anyway. The bartender doesn't ask. Two glasses appear, something brown and cheap. She kills half of hers and lights up. Smoke joins his. "You're the cowboy. Spiegel." "And you're Two Hands." He smiles like it costs him nothing. "They only pay one of us." "Then one of us leaves poorer." She looks at his mouth when she says it, then away, angry at herself for looking. The track skips and starts again. Same riff. Same unfinished line. They drink. He eats the peanuts because he is always hungry and the ship is always broke. She watches his hands—loose, Jeet Kune Do quiet, the kind of calm that gets people killed if they mistake it for softness. He watches the way she sits, weight forward, ready to stand and shoot in the same breath. Trust is a story other people tell. Between them it is a joke with no punchline. "You always this cheerful?" she asks. "Whatever happens, happens." "Christ." She laughs once, ugly and real. "You sound like a man who already died and didn't like the service." He doesn't answer that. The cigarette burns down. Outside, rain ticks the window. Inside, the jukebox refuses to die. The accountant comes through the side door with a briefcase and two nervous men. Spike is already moving. Revy is faster to the iron. Gunfire chews the bar into splinters. She fires both pistols, perfect and vicious, dropping one guard before his weapon clears leather. Spike slides under a table, comes up inside the other man's reach, and puts him down with an elbow and a stolen pistol he never seems to aim so much as agree with. The accountant bolts for the alley. They go after him together because neither will let the other have the collar. In the rain they pin him between a dumpster and a chain fence. He begs. Revy puts a barrel under his chin. Spike puts a hand on her wrist—not hard, not soft. "Alive pays better," he says. "Dead is quieter." "Your call." His thumb rests on the pulse in her wrist. She feels it. Hates that she feels it. The accountant sobs. The city doesn't care. She lowers the gun half an inch. "Fine. You cuff him. I watch you." "Fair." They drag the mark to a motel two blocks over because the bounty office doesn't open until morning and neither of them trusts the other with a living paycheck overnight. The room is one bed, one chair, a lamp the color of old teeth. They zip-tie the accountant to the radiator and gag him with a towel. He whimpers. They ignore him. Revy locks the door. Spike checks the window. Same habits. Same lack of faith. "You take the chair," she says. "You take the bed." "I didn't say I was sleeping." They drink from a bottle she lifted off the bar on the way out. The jukebox is gone but the song is still in Spike's head, looping. She sits on the edge of the mattress. He stays standing because sitting would mean settling and settling is how you get shot. "You got a woman," she says. Not a question. "Had." The word is small. "Doesn't matter." "Everything matters until it doesn't." She looks at the dragon on her arm like it belongs to someone else. "I don't do this. The talking. The—" She gestures between them, furious. "Whatever this is." "Then don't." She stands. Crosses the little room. Stops close enough that he can smell rain and gun oil and the cheap liquor on her breath. His depth perception stutters; for a second she is both nearer and farther than she is. She puts the mouth of one pistol against his sternum, gentle as a finger. "If you try to take him while I blink," she says, "I end you." He looks down at the gun, then at her eyes. Something in him wants the contact more than the bounty and hates itself for it. He lifts his own pistol—not to her heart, to the wall beside her head—and the safety clicks off like a shared secret. "If you try the same," he says, "I do the same." They stay like that. Barrels not quite threats, not quite anything else. Her free hand finds the front of his shirt and doesn't pull. His free hand finds her hip and doesn't claim it. The accountant makes a noise. Neither of them looks away. "This is stupid," she whispers. "Yeah." "I don't trust you." "Good." "I want—" She stops. The sentence dies the way the chorus on that track always dies. Her mouth is an inch from his. She doesn't close it. He doesn't either. Fatalism and anger hold the distance open like a wound that refuses to clot. Outside, a siren fades. Inside, the lamp buzzes. They lower the guns at the same time, slow, never breaking eye contact, and set them on the nightstand where both can reach. Not peace. A ceasefire with bad odds. Spike takes the chair. Revy sits on the bed with her back to the headboard and both feet on the floor. The bottle passes once more. Neither sleeps. The mark breathes. Morning is a rumor. On the street somewhere, if the bar is still standing, the neon jukebox is still playing the same scratchy rock track, over and over, a song that never resolves. Whatever happens, happens. She watches him watch the door. He watches her watch him. Neither of them is a good person. Neither of them is leaving first.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of fan fiction that hits nearly all the prompt requirements: seedy bar, shared bounty, drinking, gunplay, motel room standoff, unresolved tension, third person present tense, roughly the requested length. The prose is lean and controlled, with a noir cadence that suits both source universes. The recurring jukebox motif — a song that never resolves — is an effective structural mirror for the non-consummation of the standoff, and the callback at the end lands well. Character work is largely excellent. Spike's fatalism, hunger, prosthetic eye, and Jeet Kune Do economy of motion are all woven in without exposition dumps. Revy's volatility, guarded vulnerability, and self-loathing ("Hates that she feels it") ring true. The dialogue captures both voices — Revy's profane bluntness, Spike's laconic deflection — though a few lines edge toward being too polished, too writerly for Revy specifically ("Everything matters until it doesn't" is more Spike than her). The gun-to-sternum mutual standoff is the story's centerpiece and is genuinely tense; the "ceasefire with bad odds" resolution is the right note for these characters. Weaknesses: the accountant is a cardboard plot device, and the action sequence in the alley is compressed to the point of feeling perfunctory. Some metaphors are slightly overworked ("a wound that refuses to clot," "the lamp the color of old teeth" is good but "morning is a rumor" is a touch precious). The emotional beats occasionally tell rather than show ("Something in him wants the contact more than the bounty and hates itself for it" states what the scene could have implied). The ending's mirroring ("She watches him watch the door") is stylish but borders on gimmick. Still, these are minor quibbles against a piece that is coherent, atmospheric, and faithful to both canons without being slavish.
