+ Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The church bell found us before we were ready. One stroke, thin and exact, and then nothing—no second, no service, no reason for it to ring at all. I remember looking at Astrid as if she might laugh and admit she’d timed it. She didn’t. She only tilted her head, listening the way you listen when you already know what you’ll hear. We had left the village on the gravel track that ran past the last lit windows. Mid-nineties, northern Sweden, late enough in the year that the dark felt like a substance. My father’s new job had put us in a house that still smelled of someone else’s coffee. Stockholm was a train ride and a different accent away. Astrid had met me at the edge of the sports field with a plastic bag from the Konsum and said we were going to sit out. Útiseta. She said it the way she said everything her grandmother had taught her: flat, practical, a little bored, as if the old words were tools you kept in a drawer. “Don’t look back until we’re on the mound,” she said. “And don’t say anyone’s name. Not even yours, if you can help it.” I almost asked whose name she meant. The classmates, I supposed—the ones whose secrets she claimed we could pull loose if we did this right. She had been feeding me that for weeks. Midnight games. A pin in a windowsill. A question asked three times into a cup of water. I had gone along because the alternative was another evening of my parents speaking in the careful voices of people who had moved a child against her will. Also because Astrid made rebellion sound like competence. She knew which fences you could climb. She knew the mound. It rose beyond the last birches, a low swell in the pasture, stones showing through the grass like knuckles. The fence wire sang when we ducked under it. My boots were already wet. Astrid set the bag down and unpacked it without ceremony: a wool blanket that smelled of mothballs, a thermos, a candle stub, a handful of coins, a knife that was only a kitchen knife, the kind with a black handle. She laid the blanket on the highest part of the mound and told me to sit with my back to the village. “Shoes off,” she said. “Feet on the ground. If something asks you a question, you don’t answer the first time. Grandmother was clear about that.” “Something,” I said. “Or nothing. That’s the point. You sit until you know which.” I took my shoes off. The grass was cold enough to hurt. Astrid lit the candle and set it between us, then placed the coins in a small arc, heads up, as if paying a fare she expected to be collected. She cut a lock of her own hair with the kitchen knife—quick, no drama—and pressed it into the earth with her thumb. Then she looked at me until I understood I was meant to do the same. The knife was warmer than the air. A few pale strands. My hands shook, which I told myself was the cold. “We’re not calling anyone,” she said. “We’re only sitting where they sat. If they want to show us something, they will. If they don’t, we’ll freeze and go home and tell no one, because if you tell, it doesn’t work next time.” Next time. She already had a next time. I remember that more clearly than the wind. We sat. The candle guttered and held. Far off, a dog barked twice and stopped. I tried to keep my eyes on the dark line of the forest and not on the thought of what was under us—bones, or only the idea of bones, which in that hour amounted to the same thing. Astrid’s instructions kept coming in a murmur, teenage and ceremonial at once. Don’t cross your ankles. Don’t whistle. If you hear your mother, it isn’t your mother. If you hear your name from the village side, don’t turn; that’s only habit trying to pull you back. Count your breaths but don’t count past nine. I counted. At seven I was sure I heard footsteps on the gravel we had left behind. At eight they stopped. At nine the candle leaned though I felt no change in the air, and the flame drew itself thin and blue at the base. “Linnea,” Astrid said, very quietly, which broke her own rule, or maybe proved she had never meant the rules for herself. “Don’t answer that.” “Answer what?” She didn’t look at me. Her face in the candlelight was ordinary—chapped lip, a smear of ink on her thumb from school—and that ordinariness was worse than any mask. “The second time. There was a second time.” I had heard nothing that was my name. Or I had, and my mind had filed it under wind. The ambiguity sat between us like a third person who had not been invited and would not leave. I wanted to stand. My feet had gone numb against the mound, and the numbness felt less like cold than like the ground agreeing to hold me. A coin at the end of the arc had turned. I was certain I had seen heads. It showed tails now, dew on the metal. I had not seen a hand. “Ask,” Astrid said. “Not a name. A thing you want to know. Quietly. Then we wait until the candle dies or something answers. Whichever comes first.” I thought of a girl in our class who had stopped eating lunch. I thought of my father, and the job, and whether he had lied about how long we would stay. I thought of Astrid’s grandmother, dead two winters, and whether Astrid was repeating her or inventing her, and whether the difference mattered once you had cut your hair and put your skin against a burial mound at the stroke of a bell that should not have rung. I asked nothing. That was the only sense I managed. Astrid asked something I didn’t catch—a classmate’s name after all, I think, or a question shaped like one. The candle hissed. From the forest side, not the village, there was a sound like cloth dragged over stone, then like breath held and released by someone who had been sitting longer than we had. Astrid’s hand found my wrist. Her grip was steady. “Don’t get up,” she said, matter-of-fact, the way she told me not to look back. “If we leave before it finishes, it follows the one who stood first.” I don’t know how long we stayed after that. Long enough for the candle to drown in its own wax. Long enough for me to understand that we had stopped playing, if we had ever been playing, and that the line we had crossed was not marked on the ground. It was the moment we treated the mound as a dare and the dark as an audience. Whether anything stood in that dark besides our nerve, I still won’t say. I only know that when we finally walked back, shoes in our hands, neither of us turned around, and the bell did not ring again—and that in the morning Astrid knew something about a girl at school she should not have known, and smiled at me across the classroom as if we had won. I smiled back. That is the part I have had the most years to regret.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, controlled piece of folk horror that hits nearly every requirement of the brief. The setting (mid-90s rural northern Sweden) is economically established through concrete period details: the Konsum plastic bag, the gravel track, the house smelling of someone else's coffee. The first-person past-tense recollection frame is handled with a light touch, surfacing only occasionally ("I remember that more clearly than the wind") and closing with the retrospective regret the prompt requested. Astrid is the piece's best creation. Her matter-of-fact instructions—shoes off, don't cross your ankles, don't count past nine, "if you hear your mother, it isn't your mother"—perfectly blend teenage swagger with eerily specific traditional elements, exactly as the prompt demanded. The ritual details (coins as fare, hair cut and pressed into earth, the candle) feel researched and lived-in rather than invented. The ambiguity is maintained skillfully: the turned coin, the bell that rings once, the name Astrid claims to have heard—none are resolved, and the narrator explicitly refuses resolution ("Whether anything stood in that dark besides our nerve, I still won't say"). The ending is the strongest move: Astrid knowing something she shouldn't by morning validates nothing supernatural definitively but confirms the dangerous line crossed, and the final line about regret lands with earned weight. The prose is elegant without being purple—lines like "the dark felt like a substance" and "the numbness felt less like cold than like the ground agreeing to hold me" are precise and unsettling. Dialogue is sparse but characterful. Minor criticisms: the word count is somewhat under 1000 (roughly 950, acceptable). The middle section's list of Astrid's rules, while atmospheric, slightly delays momentum. The "third person who had not been invited" metaphor is a touch self-conscious. Linnea's interiority occasionally tips toward essayistic summary ("the ambiguity sat between us") rather than pure experience. But these are quibbles against a piece that is coherent, chilling, and thematically exact. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The diagram on the wall has every muscle I used to own drawn in red, labeled like a parts list. I keep my eyes on the vastus medialis while Drew’s hand finds the back of my left knee. “Supine. Both legs long. I’m taking the left one.” His voice is the same one that used to count reps beside me in a weight room that smelled like chalk and tape. He is a clinician now. I am a file. The table paper crackles under my shoulders. I hate the sound. I hate that my career ended in a pop I can still hear, and that recovery is a room I am required to enter twice a week so an insurance form can say compliant. He cups the calcaneus in his left palm and slides his right hand under the distal thigh, just proximal to the joint line, so the knee is supported and not hanging. “Hip to ninety.” He lifts. My femur rises. The lumbar spine wants to follow; I press it down because I know he will tell me to if I don’t. At ninety degrees of hip flexion he pauses, thumb along the lateral hamstring, fingers in the popliteal fossa, checking that I haven’t locked or rotated. “Straighten the knee. Slow. Stop where it grabs.” He extends my tibia. The heel travels toward the ceiling. Posterior thigh lights up first—semitendinosus and semimembranosus, a broad, honest pull—then a thinner line along the biceps femoris. Not nerve. I know nerve; nerve is electric and distant, into the calf. This stays in the muscle. My toes curl without my permission. He feels the hamstring bunch under his fingers and eases two degrees off the end range. “There. Breathe into it. Don’t chase it.” I breathe because he said to, not because I want the tissue longer. Length is a betrayal. The body that failed me does not get to be improved while I watch. His forearm is warm against my calf. He is close enough that I can see the pulse in his throat and the place where his collar sits wrong, the way it used to after intervals. I look at the diagram. Rectus femoris. Sartorius. A red cable I refuse to name as desire. “Down.” He lowers the leg, keeps the knee slightly flexed over a half-bolster so the joint isn’t forced into extension. His web space settles over the patella. “Mobilization. Medial, then lateral. Small. Tell me if it’s sharp under the tendon.” The kneecap shifts under his hand, a dull glide, not a grind. Scar tissue along the patellar tendon tugs. I flinch—not from pain exactly, from the anticipation of it—and the quadriceps fires, a hard involuntary set that lifts the patella into his palm. “Guarding,” he says, quiet. “Let it go.” I try. The muscle obeys late, in a twitch, then settles. He glides again, medial, a centimeter, hold, back to center. Lateral. His other hand stabilizes the distal femur so the force stays at the patella and doesn’t torque the joint. Each pass is precise. Each pass is also his skin on mine, clinical pressure that my nervous system refuses to file correctly. Heat gathers under my ribs. I keep my face still. He keeps his eyes on the knee, not on me. We are both bad at it. “Flexion next. I’m supporting the thigh. You don’t lift. I bring the heel toward you until the capsule stops me.” He slides one forearm under the posterior thigh, proximal to the knee, and takes the ankle with the other hand. Hip stays near forty degrees so this is knee motion, not hamstring. He guides the tibia into flexion. Heel approaches glute. At about one hundred ten degrees the anterior knee tightens—capsular, deep, a pressure behind the patellar tendon that is not muscular. My breath catches. The VMO flickers. Toes curl again. A sound almost leaves my throat and doesn’t. He stops at the firm end-feel, not past it. “Scale.” “Six. Anterior. Not sharp.” “Hold.” Five seconds. His grip doesn’t wander. The inside of his wrist rests against my shin. I can feel his pulse there, or I invent it; either way I hate that I am counting it. On the wall the diagram’s hip flexors point at nothing. He returns me to the bolster, slow, so the joint doesn’t rebound into extension and spark. “Prone for rectus. Roll toward your right. I’ll keep the left leg.” I turn. Paper sticks to my shoulder. He tracks the limb so the knee doesn’t twist in the air—hand still at the ankle, other hand guiding the thigh—until I am face-down, forehead on my stacked hands, pelvis level. The table edge is cold against my iliac crest. “Pelvis stays down. If your lumbar extends, I’m stopping.” His left hand spreads over the sacrum and the near PSIS, a broad stabilizer, weight enough to pin the pelvis without grinding bone. His right hand flexes the knee, drawing the heel toward the same-side glute. Because the hip is extended on the table, the rectus femoris takes it first: a line of fire from the anterior inferior iliac spine down the thigh, sharper than the hamstring stretch, meaner. At the same time the femoral nerve complains in a faint anterior tingle. He feels my pelvis try to lift into anterior tilt and adds pressure through the sacrum. “Down. You’re substituting.” I press my hip bones into the vinyl. The stretch narrows to something I can survive. Pain sits at a five, then a six when he adds five more degrees of knee flexion. My fingers crush each other. A tremor runs through the quad and dies. His hand on my sacrum is steady and impersonal and entirely too much. I am furious that my skin knows the difference between a stretch and a touch, and that he is giving me only the first while my pulse answers the second. “Breathe out. Three more seconds.” I do. The muscle yields a fraction. He does not take the extra range. He returns the knee to ninety, then to rest, and lifts his hand from my pelvis last, as if the order matters. Maybe it does. The skin there stays warm after the pressure leaves. “That’s the session,” he says. His voice has gone careful again, the way it used to go careful before a final attempt we both knew I might miss. “Extension bias at home. No forcing flexion in the morning. You’re done.” I stay prone a second longer than necessary, staring at the scuffed floor, because if I roll over now I will have to look at him, and the diagram will not be between us. The resentment is still there—at the knee, at the protocol, at the life that kept moving after mine locked. Under it, worse, is the simple fact of his hands: exact, withheld, and gone.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is technically accomplished: anatomically precise, physically coherent, and disciplined in its restraint. The physical therapy sequence is genuinely coherent—each manipulation (supine hip flexion, SLR, patellar mobilization, knee flexion end-feel, prone rectus femoris stretch with sacral stabilization) is anatomically accurate and spatially consistent. The tension between clinical touch and desire is handled with admirable economy ("my nervous system refuses to file correctly"). The muscle-diagram motif works as both setting and metaphor, and the ending's "exact, withheld, and gone" lands well. Notable flaw: the prompt specifies a female physiotherapist and male protagonist ("her body," "she is attracted to him"). The response genders the therapist male ("Drew," "his hand"), inverting the specified dynamic. This is a clear instruction deviation, though the emotional content is intact. Also, the piece is ~750 words against a 1000-word seed—slightly under, though not egregiously. The prose is controlled, mostly show-don't-tell, with strong sensory detail (table paper crackle, popliteal fossa, pulse counting). Occasionally the anatomical naming becomes a crutch—listing muscles risks reading like a textbook—but it's justified by the character's athletic background. The resentment is well-drawn without melodrama. Dialogue is sparse but functional and in-voice. No purple prose; no unearned transformation; the ending stays appropriately bitter-tender. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 56.3
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The sampan bumped the stone steps below the Thirteen Factories before the sun had cleared the river mist. I paid the boatman in copper and kept my face turned from the water, where the Navy’s boats would already be counting hulls. “Lieutenant,” said a voice from the shadow of a godown. Ah Fook, sleeves rolled, ledger under his arm. “Your captain sent a boy at dawn. He wanted the tide report.” “Tell him the tide is late,” I said. My tongue felt thick. “And that I am with the compradors.” Ah Fook looked at my hands. I had already found the jade in my pocket: a little seated figure, worn smooth at the knees. I rubbed it until the tremor eased enough to pass for cold. “You owe me for last week,” he said. “Not coin. A name. Which of your ships will not search the outer anchorage on Thursday.” “I don’t sell the Navy.” “You sold it on Tuesday.” He did not raise his voice. A coolie passed with a shoulder-pole of tea chests that smelled, falsely, of tea. “Thursday, or I send your chit to the superintendent’s clerk. He reads English when it concerns silver.” The jade bit my palm. Sweat started under my collar though the morning was still damp and grey. “The sloop at the second buoy,” I said. “Her lieutenant drinks. He will not board anything that does not fly a flag he recognises.” Ah Fook made a mark. “Go to the lane behind the plasterer’s. Ask for the widow who sells thread. Do not use my name.” I went because the alternative was the deck, and the deck meant hours before I could lie down. Canton at that hour was wet stone, charcoal, fish guts, and the sweet rot of sugar from a split bag. I kept to the walls. A Portuguese clerk I knew from the hongs stepped out of a doorway and caught my sleeve. “Merrick. You look like death’s clerk.” He smiled without warmth. “Still hiding from your own gunroom?” “Running an errand.” “For whom?” He leaned in. Cassia on his breath, and under it the same sweet smoke I was hunting. “If it’s the same widow, she watered the last pipe. Half the foreigners on Hog Lane are cursing her.” “Then why are you here?” “Because half is still more than none.” He let go. “If you see my boy, tell him I am not at the factory. Tell him anything. Just not where.” I nodded and did not promise. Promises had started to feel like ropes. The lane narrowed until two men could not pass without turning sideways. Lime flaked from the plasterer’s wall onto my coat. A woman sat on a stool with reels of undyed thread, her face plain, her eyes not. “Thread,” I said. “What weight?” “The heavy. The one that does not snap.” She studied the shake in my fingers, then the cut of my coat. “Navy cloth. Navy debt. Show me you can pay before you waste my morning.” I set down the last of the advance Ah Fook had not yet clawed back: Spanish dollars, warm from my pocket, stacked beside the jade because I would not put the figurine down. She did not touch the jade. She touched the coins, bit one, and jerked her chin at a bead curtain. Inside, the room was small enough that the brazier’s heat met me at the chest. No silk. No lacquer fantasies. A mat, a tray, a lamp with a dirty glass, and a boy who did not look at my uniform. “How many?” the widow said from the curtain. “Enough for the day. And something I can carry if I am called back aboard.” “Aboard men spill it,” she said. “Then they come weeping. I do not sell weeping.” “I won’t spill it.” She named a price that was an insult. I laughed once, dry. “I can give you a manifest copy. Indian cotton. The hongs will pay you more for knowing which chop is short than I can pay you in silver.” The boy glanced up then. The widow was quiet long enough for a dog to bark twice in the lane. “Whose manifest?” “Mine to copy. Not yours to keep. You read it here. You remember. You forget my face.” “Faces like yours are hard to forget,” she said. “White, sweating, rubbing a toy.” But she nodded. “Sit. The heavy. You talk after, not before. Men lie better when they are still hungry.” I sat. The lamp smelled of cheap oil. My hands would not stay still, so I closed them on the jade and listened to the street: a mallet, a woman scolding, the distant creak of a yardarm I should have been standing under. The boy worked without ceremony. I watched the flame and not his fingers. When the pipe came, I took it because the day had already narrowed to that, and the rest of me could be court-martialled later. The smoke was harsh, not the perfumed lie the factory clerks described in their letters home. It hit the back of my throat like hot wire, then loosened. The plaster cracks in the wall stopped crawling. The jade went quiet in my fist. “The cotton,” the widow said. I told her the chop mark, the shorted bales, the hour the lighter would leave the ship I had just betrayed by silence if not by flag. She repeated it once. She did not write it down. That frightened me more than a ledger would have. “Out,” she said. “If your captain’s boy comes down this lane, I have never seen a lieutenant. I have seen a drunk who bought thread for a whore.” “A plausible story,” I said. On the way back toward the river I met the captain’s boy after all. He was red in the face, hat crooked, brave with errand. “Sir, Captain says the survey can’t wait. He says if you’re in a hong, drag yourself out. There’s a junk standing off Lintin he wants eyed before noon.” “Tell him I eyed it at first light,” I said. The lie came easy, smoothed by the smoke. “Fishing junk. No guns. No smell of anything but nets.” The boy hesitated. He was young enough to still believe ranks meant truth. “He’ll ask why you didn’t write it.” “Because my pencil was wet.” I put a hand on his shoulder and felt him flinch at the sweat. “Go. I’ll follow.” He ran. I did not follow. I stood at the end of the lane where the mist was burning off the Pearl, rubbed the little jade figure until my thumb hurt, and counted how many hours the heavy thread would hold before the dragon woke and asked, again, to be fed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of historical fiction that largely delivers on the prompt's demands. The writer establishes 1830s Canton with convincing specificity — the Thirteen Factories, Hog Lane, Lintin, chop marks, Spanish dollars, compradors — without descending into travelogue. The "thread" euphemism and the widow's code-speak give the drug transactions a plausible underworld texture. The structure works: a single day, sliced into encounters, driven forward by escalating debts of information rather than money. Merrick's corruption is rendered incrementally and believably — first the sloop's search schedule, then the manifest, betrayals that feel like small, rationalized surrenders rather than grand villainy. The jade figurine is an effective recurring object, a talisman of respectability he cannot put down even while paying with everything else. Dialogue is the piece's chief strength, as the prompt requested. Ah Fook's "You sold it on Tuesday," the widow's "I do not sell weeping," and "Men lie better when they are still hungry" are sharp, characterful, and avoid period-pastiche stiffness. The exchange with the captain's boy lands the moral cost economically — "young enough to still believe ranks meant truth." Weaknesses: the Portuguese clerk interlude is the flattest beat, functioning mostly as exposition about the widow's watered opium and adding a stranger whose purpose feels underdeveloped. The prose occasionally leans on aphoristic narration ("Promises had started to feel like ropes"; "the rest of me could be court-martialled later") — effective once, but the mode recurs enough to feel like a tic. The metaphor of "the dragon" in the final line is slightly clichéd given the prompt's own phrasing. Sensory detail, while present and good (charcoal, fish guts, hot-wire smoke), is deployed sparingly rather than richly — the prompt asked for lush sensory writing, and the piece is more austere than sumptuous. The ending is coherent and earns its darkness without melodrama; no unearned redemption occurs. Overall: confident, controlled, professional-grade work with minor flat spots and a slight overreliance on epigrammatic narration. + Humour: Sisyphus Gives Advice — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The boulder had reached the point on the slope where it always paused, as if considering its options. Sisyphus leaned a shoulder into it and nodded at the bird. “Next.” Crow, who had appointed himself both amanuensis and postmaster on the grounds that he already stole things and could fly, flipped a letter over with one claw. “From a woman in Ephesus. She says her husband has taken up philosophy and now explains her feelings to her before she’s had them.” “Ah.” Sisyphus found a better purchase with his heel. “Tell her: he is not listening ahead of you. He is afraid of the gap. Most people would rather be wrong quickly than quiet long enough to find out. Next time he begins a sentence with ‘What you’re really feeling is,’ ask him what he had for lunch. If he cannot remember, he is not qualified to inventory your heart. If he can, ask him to describe the lunch in the same detail he uses on you. He will hear himself. People usually do, once the sound is outside their head.” Crow scratched. “I’m adding, ‘Also he sounds exhausting.’” “You may add that he sounds tired,” Sisyphus said. “Exhaustion is a diagnosis. Tired is a kindness.” The stone moved. It always did, eventually, in the way weather does: not because anyone had won an argument with it. The next letter smelled faintly of lamp oil and resentment. A clerk in a counting-house wanted to know how to stop working after the lamps were lit, “as the work is never finished and my wife has begun addressing remarks to the chair.” Sisyphus walked. The hill did not become less of a hill. “Write this. Work that cannot be finished is not a task. It is a climate. You do not defeat weather by staying out in it. Choose one thing each day that, when done, lets you say *done* without lying. Put the pen down after that thing even if the rest of the desk looks like a small war. Your wife is not angry at the chair. She is angry at being made to compete with a pile of paper that does not love her back and never will. Paper is very consistent that way.” “Snappier if I say the paper is winning,” Crow muttered. “The paper is not winning. It isn’t playing.” Sisyphus wiped grit from his palm onto his thigh. “That’s the part she needs him to notice.” A cart creaked somewhere on the road below. Someone laughed. The sound arrived late, thinned by distance, and Sisyphus smiled at it without looking down. Crow pretended not to see this, which was his version of tact. “This one’s from a man whose brother-in-law corrects him at dinner. Pronunciation. Facts. The way he holds a cup. He wants a cutting remark that will end it.” “He wants a cutting remark that will make him feel like the sort of man who owns cutting remarks,” Sisyphus said. “Those rarely survive contact with a Tuesday. Tell him: thank the brother-in-law, once, in front of everyone, for caring so much about cups. Then ask him to pass the bread. Do not explain the joke. Men like that can survive being hated. They go faint if they suspect they have become a small entertainment. And sit where you can see your wife’s face. If she is trying not to laugh, you have already won the only contest in the room.” Crow’s quill—technically a feather he had disagreed with another crow about—paused. “I’m noting in the margin that this advice is suspiciously non-violent.” “Violence is a loud way of admitting you brought nothing else.” They climbed. The letter after that had been folded and refolded until the creases had opinions. A young woman wrote that she could not tell whether she loved the man she was marrying or merely the relief of having decided. The wedding was in a month. Her mother had already hired the flautist. Sisyphus was quiet long enough that Crow looked up, which he hated doing; it ruined the silhouette. “Say this,” Sisyphus said. “Relief is not nothing. People marry for less, and some of them are happy later, which is an argument for time rather than for certainty. But relief that depends on not asking a question will send you a bill. Before the flautist is paid in full, spend one afternoon with this man in which nothing is being planned. No linens. No aunts. If, by the end of it, you are interested in what he will say next, that is love or its near neighbor, and neighbors can be lived with. If you are only interested in getting to the end of the afternoon so the decision can go back to being decided, write to your mother. Flautists can be unrehearsed. Lives are harder.” “I’m adding,” Crow said, “that flautists hold grudges.” “You’re not.” “I’m adding it smaller.” The boulder slipped a hand’s breadth. Sisyphus caught it with the easy irritation of a man retrieving a cup he had set too near an edge. He reset his feet. From this height the plain was a mild gold, and the road was a thread someone had failed to pull. The last letter of the morning was short. A boy—Crow insisted on “boy” after inspecting the handwriting, which leaned as if hoping to be believed—asked what he was supposed to do with his life. He was seventeen. He was not good at the things his father was good at. He was afraid this meant he was a waste of a person. Sisyphus breathed out. The breath fogged and went. “Tell him the waste is not in being unlike his father. The waste is in spending the next forty years apologizing for the difference. He does not need a destiny this week. Destiny is what people call a direction after it has already worked. He needs a direction he can stand for a month: a craft, a study, a road, a kitchen, a ship. Something with Tuesdays in it. If it is wrong, it will teach him the shape of wrong, which is useful and cannot be inherited. If it is right, he will not have to announce it. The people who love him will start setting a place as if they had always known. Fathers come around or they don’t. That is information about fathers.” Crow wrote. His side note, this time, was only a small star, which meant he agreed and refused to say so. “And Crow.” “Hm.” “At the end. One line. Tell him that a life is not a stone. It does not have to be pushed uphill simply because uphill is available. It can be carried level, and set down when his arms are done, and picked up again in the morning if he still wants it.” Crow’s head tilted. “That’s one.” “That’s one,” Sisyphus said. The boulder nudged his shoulder, patient as a habit. He put his hands to it. Below them, a woman on the road shaded her eyes, watching a bird drop a sealed letter into a passing cart. She would not know, later, why the advice felt as if someone had sat with her rather than above her. She would only know that she read it twice, and that the second time she laughed, quietly, at herself, which is the only laughter that changes a room. Sisyphus pushed. The hill accepted this, as it always had. He was already thinking of the afternoon post, and of whether Crow could be persuaded not to illustrate the replies.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an accomplished piece that fulfills nearly every constraint of a demanding prompt. The epistolary-with-interjections format is respected; Sisyphus is warm, zen without being preachy, and genuinely enjoys the work; Crow is a deadpan comic foil with his own personality (adding side notes, refusing to look up "because it ruined the silhouette"); the advice is practical and specific; exactly one boulder metaphor appears and it's flagged wittily ("That's one"); stoicism is never lectured about; the fish-out-of-water trope is avoided — Sisyphus is a natural. Strengths: the prose is Pratchett-adjacent in its understated wit ("the creases had opinions," "weather does not... win an argument," "a feather he had disagreed with another crow about"). The advice letters are genuinely insightful — the wife-made-to-compete-with-paper observation, "exhaustion is a diagnosis, tired is a kindness," "violence is a loud way of admitting you brought nothing else" — and the humor stays understated. The final image of the woman on the road reading her letter twice is a graceful, earned emotional landing. Weaknesses: a few lines flirt with aphorism-overload; nearly every Sisyphus utterance lands as polished epigram, which can feel slightly written rather than spoken, a mild over-polish rather than Pratchett's looser conversational rhythm. The risqué/mundane spectrum of letters is underused — no genuinely risque letter appears despite the prompt inviting it. The closing paragraph's omniscient shift to the woman on the road is lovely but slightly narrator-heavy, edging toward telling us how she felt. The relief/marriage letter, while good, is the weakest of the four responses. Word count is near target. Overall: a very strong execution with only minor reservations about relentless aphoristic polish and a slightly soft epistolary variety. Prompt:
Lost & Found in Osaka Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The last chord rang off the arcade glass and died under the pachinko clatter. Mio had stopped three shops back, headphones crooked over one ear, and only now realized she was standing in the busker’s sightline. “You gonna clap,” the girl said, grinning around her pick, “or just audit me?” Mio’s mouth opened. Closed. “It was— the bridge. You changed the voicing.” “On purpose.” The busker—maybe a year or two older, denim jacket open, a sticker-scabbed guitar—tilted her head. “Most people just yell the title. You caught the chord. Dangerous.” “I didn’t mean—” Mio’s headphones slid. She shoved them up. They slid again when she nodded. “Sorry. I was listening. Not— auditing.” “Relax. I’m Rina.” She flicked a coin in her case with her toe, like she was proving the hat wasn’t empty. “You from around here, or did Den Den Town swallow you?” “Mio. I live— not far. Nipponbashi. I come for parts.” She gestured vaguely at a synth shop, then at her own chest, as if the explanation lived there. “Filters. A broken envelope. It’s stupid.” “Not stupid.” Rina unslung the strap and sat on the amp. “You play?” “Keys. Mostly. Alone. In my room. The neighbors—” A small, helpless shrug. The headphones betrayed it. Rina laughed, not unkind. “So you heard me murder a thirty-year-old anime theme and decided to risk social interaction. I’m honored.” “You didn’t murder it.” Mio stared at the fretboard. “The original has that square-wave lead. You played the harmony under it. People skip that. They just— shred the melody.” “Okay, nerd.” Rina said it like a compliment. “What’s your poison? Juno? A cheap Volca you pretend is ironic?” Mio’s ears went hot. “A Juno. Used. The sliders stick. I like that they stick. It makes you commit.” “Commit,” Rina repeated, delighted. “She has opinions. I was starting to think you only came in monosyllables.” “I don’t— I’m not good at this.” “At talking?” “At people who are… on.” Mio waved at the street, the neon, Rina’s whole posture. “You look like you belong in the noise.” “I look like I haven’t eaten since noon.” Rina snapped the case shut. “There’s a kaiten two blocks toward Namba. Plates, no eye contact required, soy sauce crimes encouraged. Come with me.” Mio blinked. “Now?” “Unless your envelope is dying in real time.” “It’s already dead.” A beat. “I can come. If— if you want. I might be quiet.” “Quiet’s fine. Weird music opinions are mandatory.” Rina stood, guitar on her back, and waited until Mio fell in beside her. “Headphones.” “What?” “They’re winning. Again.” Mio caught them at her collarbone. “They do that when I nod.” “Then stop agreeing with everything,” Rina said, and bumped her shoulder, light. “Or keep agreeing. I like being right.” The restaurant was bright and loud in a softer way: plates clicking, a radio under the chatter, vinegar in the air. They took the end of the counter. Mio set her headphones in her lap like a nervous animal. “Tuna,” Rina told the belt, already reaching. “And whatever looks like it lost a bet. You?” “Salmon. And— tamago. I always get tamago. It’s predictable. Sorry.” “Stop apologizing to eggs.” Rina slid a plate over. “So. You knew the harmony. You play keys in a room where the neighbors hate joy. What else?” Mio turned a teacup so the handle faced away from her. “I make little loops. Bass, a pad, something that sounds like rain on a vending machine. I don’t show anyone.” “Show me sometime.” “They’re not—” “Good? Finished? Cool enough for Den Den Town?” Rina popped ginger into her mouth. “I busk covers outside an arcade. My standards are a public health hazard.” Mio almost smiled. “The square wave. In the theme. I could do that part. If you ever— I mean, not that you’d—” “Want a shy synth goblin on a track?” Rina leaned in, playful, not unkind. “Mio. That’s the whole invitation.” “I don’t perform.” “You just critiqued my voicing in front of a claw machine. That’s a performance.” A plate of cucumber rolled by. Rina let it go. “You don’t have to sing. You don’t have to look at the crowd. You can stand behind me and make the sky beep.” Mio nodded. The headphones jumped. She caught them, ears red, and this time she laughed—small, surprised at itself. “See,” Rina said. “There you are.” “I’m still here,” Mio said. “Just— slower.” “Slower’s allowed.” Rina nudged a salmon plate toward her. “Eat. Then tell me which cheap pedal lies the least. I’ve got fifty minutes before the arcade security remembers I exist.” Mio picked up her chopsticks. They clicked once against the plate, steady. “The modulation one,” she said. “Not the yellow. The one with the scratch on the knob. It sounds broken in a way that isn’t lying.” Rina’s grin went wide. “God. Okay. Eat faster. I need the rest of that sentence before you remember to be shy.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-crafted scene that fulfills the prompt's core requirements with notable skill. The piece is written primarily in dialogue, as instructed, and the two voices are sharply differentiated: Mio's fragmented, self-interrupting speech ("Keys. Mostly. Alone. In my room.") versus Rina's playful, rapid-fire banter ("or just audit me?"). The dialogue does heavy lifting, revealing character through rhythm and word choice rather than exposition. The setting details are economical and evocative: Den Den Town, the arcade glass, pachinko clatter, the kaitenzushi with its "soy sauce crimes." The recurring headphone gag is a nice physical motif that externalizes Mio's awkwardness without narrating it — strong show-don't-show work. The synth-nerd specificity (Juno sliders, square-wave lead, envelope, Volca) grounds Mio's character authentically and earns Rina's intrigue. The transition from awkwardness to ease is gradual and believable; Mio doesn't transform, she thaws slightly ("I'm still here. Just— slower."), which is the right instinct and avoids an unearned transformation. The ending's warmth is earned through the accumulating rapport. Minor criticisms: the word count falls somewhat short of 1000 (roughly 750-800). Rina's wit occasionally tips into overly polished quip-machine territory ("My standards are a public health hazard"), which flirts with the manic-pixie-busker archetype. Some lines strain slightly for cleverness ("sounds like rain on a vending machine" is charming but borders on writerly showing-off). The scenario itself — shy nerd meets cool confident musician — is a familiar trope, though the execution elevates it. The prose is clean and rhythmic, with no purple tendencies, and the scene never meanders. Overall this is a polished, engaging piece with authentic dialogue and well-observed character dynamics, held back only by its brevity relative to the instruction and some slight archetypal familiarity. + Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The watch buzzed at 3:07, same as always, right when the last bell dumped the hallway into noise. Maya tapped the screen to kill the reminder for band practice and felt the glass give under her thumb—soft, like warm wax. The hallway snapped backward. Lockers unslammed. A paper airplane flew into somebody’s hand. The bell sucked itself silent. Maya was standing at her locker again, heart hammering, the watch face glowing a sick green she had never set. She did it twice more before she believed it. Once to un-spill chocolate milk down her shirt. Once to take back the thing she’d said to Jordan in front of everybody: that his science-fair volcano looked like a diaper. Both times the world rewound clean, and both times the watch left a faint heat on her wrist, like a fever that belonged only to her. By Thursday she was using it the way other kids used erasers. Wrong answer on the quiz—rewind. Almost walked into the wrong bathroom—rewind. The cat by the bike rack watched her each time she came back out into the afternoon that had already happened. It was orange, one ear torn, and it never blinked when the light stuttered. After the third rewind it tilted its head like it was checking a name tag only it could read. “Don’t,” Maya told it, which was stupid. Cats didn’t keep score. Friday she rewound the pop quiz, the spilled milk, Jordan’s volcano, a missed bus, a cracked phone screen she hadn’t even paid for yet, and the moment Mr. Ellison called on her and her mind went blank. Six jumps. Maybe seven. She lost count somewhere between the cafeteria line and the moment the cat was suddenly closer to the doors, tail straight up, eyes fixed on her wrist. In the bathroom mirror the changes didn’t look like magic. They looked like a month that had happened while she was looking away. Her sleeves stopped at the knobs of her wrists. Her shoes pinched. A shadow of something—not a mustache, not really, just the idea of one—sat on her upper lip when she turned her face into the fluorescent light. Her voice cracked on the word “here” during attendance, and two boys in the back row laughed like she’d told a joke she didn’t know she was in. People made room for her in the hallway. Not the polite kind. The kind you make for someone who might shove. Jordan wouldn’t meet her eyes. At lunch, Priya slid down the bench and said, too carefully, “You good? You look… taller. Did you, like, hit a growth spurt overnight?” “Maybe,” Maya said. The word came out lower than she meant. The watch pulsed. Green. Hungry. She told herself one more rewind would put it back. She pressed the glass. The cafeteria rewound—trays rising, milk unspilling, laughter reversing into mouths—but when the world settled, Priya wasn’t on the bench. Priya was at the far table with the eighth graders, and she looked at Maya like Maya was a substitute teacher who’d wandered in by mistake. The clock on the wall said 12:14. It had said 12:14 before. It also said October, and Maya was sure, sick-sure, that yesterday had still been September. Outside, the orange cat sat on the low wall. It opened its mouth in a silent meow, the way you call a name you aren’t allowed to say out loud. Maya ran to the office. The secretary frowned at the screen, then at her. “You’re not on the sixth-grade roster,” she said. “You’re on the eighth. Have been since August. Are you feeling all right, hon? You look flushed.” August. Maya’s hands were too big on the counter. A scar she didn’t remember crossed her knuckle. In the glass of the office window her reflection had cheekbones that weren’t hers yet, or had been hers too soon, and eyes that looked tired in a way twelve wasn’t supposed to look. She found Jordan by the gym. He was shorter than she remembered. Or she was taller. He flinched when she said his name. “I didn’t mean the diaper thing,” she said. “I took it back.” “What diaper thing?” Jordan’s voice shook. “You shoved me into the lockers last week. Everybody saw. Coach benched you. Why are you—why do you keep looking at me like we’re friends?” The watch burned. Maya saw it then, the way you see a stain after you’ve already sat in it: every rewind hadn’t erased the push of time. It had spent her. Minutes, weeks, a season. And the world had stitched itself around the person those spent minutes made. A taller Maya. A meaner one, maybe, in the hours she hadn’t lived but everyone else had. A timeline where Priya had stopped sitting with her. Where the cat had learned her face because the cat had watched her age in jumps, like a bad cartoon. She could feel another jump waiting under the glass. One more press might drag her backward far enough to undo the shove, the roster, the wrong October. Or it might spend another year. Or it might land her in a hallway where nobody knew the name on her backpack, and the only creature that did was the one with the torn ear, already turning as if it knew which door she would come out of. The bell rang. For a second it rang backward, a thin metallic inhale, and every head in the gym hallway lifted at once. Maya’s thumb hovered over the watch. In the window of the trophy case, her reflection was still changing—jaw, shoulders, the frightened eyes of somebody who had run out of childhood faster than the clock would admit. The orange cat appeared in the glass behind her, though the hallway behind her was empty. It blinked, slow. Once for yes. Or once for don’t. The watch face cracked, hairline, green light leaking through like a vein. Maya didn’t know if the next rewind would fix the world or finish eating her. She only knew the cat was waiting, and that somewhere in a September she could no longer find, a smaller girl was still trying to take back a sentence about a volcano, and the clock was no longer on her side.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong execution of the prompt. The piece hits all required beats: the smart watch discovery, escalating casual use, physical aging (accelerated puberty shown through sleeves, shoes, voice cracking, facial hair shadow), social consequences (people treating her differently, fear rather than admiration), a timeline shift (the roster change, the shove she never made, Priya's estrangement), and an ambiguous ending hovering over one more rewind. The Goosebumps tone is well captured—middle-school texture, the uncanny orange cat as a horror-tale witness, the "clock is no longer on her side" closer. Strengths: The prose is controlled and image-driven ("a fever that belonged only to her," "the idea of a mustache," "the way you see a stain after you've already sat in it"). The cat is an excellent recurring device—understated, eerie, and thematically apt. The reveal that rewinds "spend" her time and the world stitches itself around the person those minutes made is a clever, coherent mechanic. The dialogue is functional and believable, especially Jordan's frightened confusion and the secretary's bureaucratic wrongness. Weaknesses: The middle section compresses the escalation quickly; the Friday montage of six or seven jumps is efficient but slightly rushed, and the emotional interiority of Maya aging is more observed than felt at times. The ending's ambiguity is appropriate to the genre, though the final image of "a smaller girl still trying to take back a sentence" is a touch ornamental. Some metaphors flirt with cleverness ("laughed like she'd told a joke she didn't know she was in" works; "hungry" for the watch is a bit stock). The cat's "once for yes, or once for don't" is a nice beat but borders on cute. Overall these are minor; the piece is coherent, well-paced at ~1000 words, and tonally consistent. + Noir romance: Carnival of Dangerous Intentions — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
She had almost turned back at the ramp. The boardwalk smelled of salt and burnt sugar, and the shooting gallery’s tin targets chimed under a boy’s careless aim. Near dusk the bulbs along the rail stuttered—bright, then a sickly amber, then dark—so that the crowd seemed to appear and vanish in pieces. She stopped short of the counter and pressed her gloved fingers together until the leather creaked. His locks. The phrase came again, absurd and old, as if she had borrowed it from a book she ought not to have finished. She had promised nothing except to be here. That was the trouble. A promise made to a man whose name she did not know felt, in the failing light, like a promise made against herself. “You came.” He was already beside the rail, not in front of the gallery as she had pictured, but half in its shadow. Obsidian curls, yes; the darker eyes she remembered only when the bulb overhead held. In the next flicker his face broke into bars of light and shade, and she could not tell whether he was smiling. “I said I might,” she answered. “You said you would.” His voice was low enough that the barkers did not steal it. “There’s a difference. I prefer the second.” She looked past him at the prizes strung on wire: celluloid dolls, a brass compass, a knife with a cheap pearl handle. “Preference isn’t the same as a claim.” “No.” He didn’t move closer. That restraint unsettled her more than a hand at her elbow would have. “But you walked the length of the board to argue the point. That tells me something.” A bulb popped and died. For a moment his mouth was only a line. She thought of the room she had left—the lamp she had not switched off, the note she had not written—and of how easily a woman could be mislaid between one light and the next. I should ask his name, she told herself. I should ask what he wants and then leave before the wanting answers for me. “What do you want?” she said. “To walk you past the lights before they decide for us.” He tipped his head toward the stretch where the bulbs were worst, stuttering over wet planks. “And to hear you say, out loud, that you knew it was unwise and came anyway.” “That’s a cruel thing to ask.” “It’s an honest one.” The light returned and caught the edge of his cheek. He looked younger than his manner, and that was its own kind of danger. “Cruelty would be pretending this is a game you can win without stakes.” She laughed once, short. “You talk as if you’ve already won.” “I talk as if I know what losing costs.” He glanced at the gallery, where the boy had missed again and was being consoled with a whistle. “Your friend with the rifle doesn’t. You do. That’s why you’re still standing there instead of buying a ticket home.” Home. The word landed wrong. She had a key, a street, a woman who would notice if she were late for supper. None of it felt like armor. “I don’t know you,” she said. “You know enough to be afraid of the right things.” His eyes held hers through another flicker; the pattern slid across both their faces like water. “Not of me snatching your purse. Of what you’ll permit if I ask nicely and don’t touch you until you ask me to.” Heat rose under her collar. She hated that he had named it cleanly, and hated more that the naming did not make her step back. “You assume a great deal.” “I assume you returned.” He offered his arm, not quite extended—an invitation balanced on the air between them. “If I’m wrong, say so and I’ll walk you to the train and not follow. If I’m not, take it, and we’ll go where the lights misbehave. You can change your mind at any plank. I won’t argue with a no. I will remember a yes.” Internal caution rose, precise and late. A stranger. A meeting she had arranged and then tried to forget. The old phrase again—his locks—as if desire were a door she had already unlatched in some other hour. “And if I take your arm and then decide I was a fool?” “Then you were a fool who kept her word to herself,” he said. “Not to me. I’m only the occasion.” The gallery bell rang. Someone won a doll. She watched the prize swing on its wire and thought how easily bright things were given to people who aimed badly. “Your name,” she said. “Before anything else.” “Julian.” No surname. The light died, returned, died. In the dark interval she heard him breathe. “And yours, if you mean to use it.” “Margaret.” It felt like handing over a key she could not get back. “Not Maggie.” “Margaret.” He said it without softening it. The arm waited. “Well?” She looked down the boardwalk. Sodium and carnival glass threw broken ladders across the wet wood. Beyond them the ocean kept its own counsel. She could still turn. The train would smell of coal and other people’s coats. Supper would be cold and safe. “If you touch me before I say,” she told him, “I will leave you on this rail and not look back.” “Agreed.” “And if you lie about what this is—” “I won’t dress it up.” His voice dropped with the next flicker. “It isn’t proper. It may not be kind. It is wanted. By me. I think by you. That’s the whole of my honesty tonight.” She set her gloved hand on his sleeve. The wool was warm from his body. Under the stuttering light his face came apart and reassembled—beautiful, then severe, then only a man who had waited. “Then walk,” Margaret said. “And don’t mistake my coming for surrender.” “I wouldn’t dare,” Julian answered, and did not smile until the next bulb held long enough for her to see that he almost had.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong period romance scene with restrained menace. The flickering boardwalk lights function as both atmosphere and metaphor—faces appearing and vanishing, desire glimpsed in intervals—which is a genuinely effective device. The dialogue is the standout: Julian's lines ("I talk as if I know what losing costs," "I'm only the occasion") carry the requested edge without tipping into melodrama, and Margaret's guarded replies establish agency and self-awareness. The internal monologue is economical and well-integrated ("a promise made against herself"). The ratio of dialogue/monologue/exposition roughly matches the requested proportions, and the ~1000 word target is met. Weaknesses: Julian risks becoming a type—the omniscient, articulate stranger who reads her perfectly is a familiar romance archetype, and his dialogue occasionally edges toward aphorism ("Cruelty would be pretending this is a game you can win without stakes"). The "I will remember a yes" consent-negotiation exchange is slightly modern in sensibility for 1937, though the period voice mostly holds. Some metaphors are near-misses ("broken ladders across the wet wood" works; "how easily bright things were given to people who aimed badly" is a touch on-the-nose). The ending lands well—her taking his arm with conditions preserves tension rather than resolving it, which suits the brief. Prose is polished, controlled, and mostly avoids purple excess. The scene is coherent, purposeful, and never meanders. + Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 85.9
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The wind shifted after noon and carried a smell JT couldn't place—wet wool, maybe, or the sweet rot that got into old apples if you left them in a cellar too long. He kept his eyes on the trail and didn't mention it. Mike was talking about the Patriots, the way he did when the woods went quiet, filling the space so nobody had to hear what the trees were doing. Their father walked ahead with the rifle across his arms, not slung, the way a man carries something he might need in a hurry and doesn't want to admit. "You hear that?" Mike said. "Hear what?" their father asked, without turning. "Nothing. That's the point. No birds. No squirrels. Like somebody turned the volume down." "It's hunting season," their father said. "Things get quiet." JT didn't think that was true. He'd hunted these woods since he was twelve and the quiet had never felt this complete, like a hand laid over a mouth. He adjusted the strap of his pack and felt the canvas-wrapped weight of his own rifle knock against his hip. The metal was cold through the cloth. He kept thinking about the buck in the clearing, the way his father's hand had gone out as if to a dog he knew by name. He hadn't told them he'd seen it. He wasn't sure, anymore, that he had. They came over a rise and the land dropped into a bowl of spruce. Down in the middle of it, half swallowed by alder, was the old cabin. JT stopped. He knew the place the way you know a story you've heard too many times to trust. Hunters called it the Ward place, though nobody could say which Ward, or when. The roof had gone in on one side. The door hung open on a single hinge, black as a throat. People said a man had wintered there in the seventies and walked out in April talking to somebody who wasn't with him. People said a lot of things. JT's uncle had once claimed the cabin answered if you knocked. Their father had told him to shut his mouth and pass the salt. "We don't need to go down there," JT said. His voice came out smaller than he wanted. Mike glanced back, eyebrows up. "Nobody said we were." "Good." Their father had already started down the slope. Not fast. Just the steady, unthinking walk of a man following a track he could see and the rest of them couldn't. JT looked at the ground. There were no prints he could make out in the frost-stiff moss, only a darker line where something heavy might have passed, or where the shadow of the trees lay wrong. "Dad," Mike called. "Trail's east. We're burning light." Their father didn't answer. He stopped ten yards from the cabin and stood with his head cocked, the way the caribou had stood that morning, listening to a frequency the others weren't on. The rifle hung at his side again. Forgotten. JT felt the crawl start low in his stomach and work up toward his throat. "He's just looking," Mike said, but he didn't sound sure. "Place gives everybody the creeps. Remember when Uncle Ray—" "Don't," JT said. They watched their father lift a hand. Not a wave. A greeting, almost. His lips moved. From where JT stood he couldn't hear the words, only the shape of them, soft and private, the way you talk to someone in a hospital room when you don't want the nurses to hear. The open door didn't move. Nothing moved. And yet JT had the sudden, stupid certainty that the dark inside the cabin had leaned forward to listen. "Dad!" Mike shouted. Their father flinched as if struck. He turned, blinking, and for a second his face was a stranger's—too bright around the eyes, mouth wet, confused in a way that made JT want to look at his boots. Then the man JT knew slid back into place, embarrassed and angry at once. "What are you two yelling about?" "You were talking to the cabin," Mike said. He tried to laugh. It didn't take. "Like it was gonna invite you in for coffee." "I was checking the wind." Their father shouldered the rifle properly this time, hard enough that the sling snapped. "And I don't need my boys telling me how to hunt. We go east. Now." He walked past them without meeting JT's eyes. Mike followed, shaking his head, already rebuilding the moment into something he could live with—old man spacing out, long drive, no big deal. JT stayed where he was a moment longer. The smell was stronger here. Apples. Wool. Something under it like copper pennies held too long in a sweating fist. From inside the cabin came a sound so small he might have imagined it: the dry click of a tongue against teeth. Or a hoof on bare board. Or his own pulse, knocking. He looked at the doorway and saw, or thought he saw, a shape standing just past the light—tall, still, antlers raking the ruined ceiling, eyes flat and dark and patient. Not a buck. Not quite. The face under the rack was wrong in a way he couldn't hold onto, human and not, his father's mouth maybe, or his own, parted as if about to share a secret. JT blinked. The doorway was empty. Of course it was empty. He was tired. The woods were getting into his head. That was all. He turned to follow the others and found he had taken three steps toward the cabin without deciding to. His hand was lifted, palm out, the way you reach for an animal you don't want to spook. He snatched it back. His fingers tingled as if he'd touched something cold and alive. "JT!" Mike's voice, already distant. "You coming or what?" "Yeah," JT called. His throat felt packed with cotton. "Yeah, I'm coming." He didn't look back. He told himself that if he looked back the door would still be open and nothing would be standing in it, and that would prove he was fine. He also told himself that if he looked back he might see his father there instead, or Mike, or all three of them, waiting with that bright, borrowed calm, glad at last to be found. Ahead, his father and brother moved through the spruce like men who had already forgotten the bowl, the cabin, the minute they'd lost. JT walked in their tracks and listened to the woods not making a sound, and kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Behind him, very softly, something knocked. Once. As if answering.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The continuation is a strong piece of King-style rural horror. It maintains JT's limited, unreliable perspective, builds dread through sensory detail (the smell of wet wool and rotting apples, the unnatural silence), and escalates the pattern established in the prompt—the father's trance-like attraction to the entity—via the abandoned Ward cabin. The dialogue is naturalistic and character-revealing: Mike's deflection through humor, the father's defensive anger, JT's small voice. The imagery is precise and unsettling ("black as a throat," "the dark inside the cabin had leaned forward to listen"). The ending knock answering JT's earlier uncle's claim is a well-earned payoff that ties back to planted detail. Weaknesses are minor: some phrases flirt with familiarity ("the woods were getting into his head" repeats the prompt verbatim, though this reads as intentional echo), and the antlered figure in the doorway is a fairly conventional image for this subgenre. The pacing is tight, no meandering. Prose is controlled, not purple. Emotionally it conveys dread and shame effectively, though the emotional range is somewhat narrow (fear/dread dominates). Character actions are believable and consistent with the established family dynamic.
