+ Fantasy-humour: Hell is Other Demons — Score: 87.5
Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. 1000 words.
Model Output:
By the third hour of the morning audience, the iron throne had developed a wobble. Lucifer noticed it the way one notices a loose tooth: with his tongue, in this case the heel of one bare foot, testing the give while a minor duke of avarice explained, at length, why his quota of whispered temptations had fallen short. The duke blamed the weather. Hell did not have weather. Lucifer let him continue. It was easier than interrupting, and the chewing sound from beneath the dais was doing most of the interrupting anyway. The hound had a name, though Lucifer had stopped using it after the third sofa. It lay on its side under the throne, enormous, smoke-colored, and occupied with the left front leg of the seat of all damnation. Iron shrieked in a small, domestic way. A flake of rust fell onto the duke’s polished shoe. The duke pretended not to see it. Everyone pretended not to see the hound. This was policy. “Forty-seven souls,” Lucifer said, when the weather had been exhausted. “You promised me forty-seven. You delivered eleven, and one of those was already halfway to despair without your help. I’m not paying a commission on gravity.” The duke bowed. The throne rocked. From somewhere in the vaulted dark, a clerk coughed the cough of a man who has been holding a ledger too long and has begun to suspect the ledger is holding him back. Lilith arrived without being announced, which was either a privilege or a failure of security, depending on the week. She wore something that had once been a coat and was now mostly intention. Ash clung to the hem. She looked as if she had walked through a fire and found it disappointing. “You’re listing,” she said. “The throne is listing. I am composed.” “Mm.” She circled the dais, not quite looking at him. The hound thumped its tail once, a sound like a door slamming in a distant wing of the palace, and returned to the iron. “He’s worse.” “He has preferences. Currently, furniture.” “You could kennel him.” “I could kennel a great many things. It rarely improves them.” Lucifer dismissed the duke with two fingers. The man fled with the relief of the moderately condemned. “You’re early. Or late. I lose track of which offense we’re practicing.” “I was in the second circle,” Lilith said. “A scheduling error. Someone put lust next to bureaucracy again. The lines were obscene in the wrong way.” She stopped at the foot of the throne. Up close, the wobble was worse; the whole seat leaned toward her as if eavesdropping. “You look tired.” “I look like a man whose dog is eating his office.” “You look like a man who hasn’t slept since the Renaissance. The dog is incidental.” He almost smiled. The almost was the problem. It had been the problem for centuries: the way the air changed when she was in it, the way Hell’s ordinary cruelties became slightly embarrassed, as if they had been caught rehearsing. They were off. They had been off since the incident with the mirror, or the treaty, or the Tuesday—accounts differed, including their own. Off meant she did not stay. Off meant he did not ask. Off meant she kept finding reasons to be in the throne room that were not, strictly, violent. Today’s reason presented itself in the form of a sealed slip, dropped onto his knee. “A petition,” she said. “From the river wardens. They want the hound banned from the banks. He drank half the Styx and then was sick on a barge of the newly dead. They’re unionizing about it.” “Hell doesn’t have unions.” “It does now. I may have suggested the phrasing.” Lucifer turned the slip over. The wax was her color, which was to say no color that stayed still. “You came all this way to deliver a complaint you inspired.” “I came because the wardens are right, and because your breakfast is still on the sideboard from yesterday, and because—” She glanced at the leg of the throne, now visibly grooved. “—that noise is going to drive you into one of your moods, and your moods reorganize the geography. I have appointments in the geography.” “How considerate.” “I’m not.” She sat on the step, not the throne. The distinction mattered to both of them and to no one else. “I’m practical. You’re lonely, and lonely makes you inventive, and your inventions tend to have weather. Actual weather. Last time it rained nails for a week. The glovers were thrilled. Everyone else filed claims.” He said nothing. The audience hall breathed: distant screams arranged, by long custom, into something almost like ventilation. A clerk approached with the day’s remaining petitions and, seeing Lilith, developed a sudden interest in the far wall. “I am not lonely,” Lucifer said. “I am understaffed.” “You have legions.” “Legions don’t argue with me about the throne.” “I don’t argue with you about the throne. I argue with you about everything the throne pretends to solve.” She reached down without looking and scratched the hound behind one ear. The chewing paused. In the pause, the hall seemed to lean in. Then the teeth found iron again, thoughtful, as if the hound were editing a text. “He misses the hunt. You used to take him out.” “I used to do a number of things.” “Yes.” They let that sit. It was a small word and it covered a great deal of scorched ground: palaces, bargains, a garden that had not been a garden, mornings when the off had been on and the on had felt, dangerously, like a plan. Lucifer watched her hand on the hound’s skull. Domestic. Absurd. The King of Hell, a woman who had walked out of the first story and declined the moral, and a dog reducing the symbol of his office to iron filings. If there was a joke, it was not on them so much as through them, like a draft. “Stay for the afternoon session,” he said. It came out flatter than he intended, which was perhaps why it landed. “The pride contingent is disputing seating. They’ll perform. You like it when they perform.” “I like it when you pretend not to.” “That isn’t a yes.” “It isn’t a no.” Lilith stood. Ash drifted from her coat and did not reach the floor; it had somewhere else to be. “I’ll stay until the throne gives up or you do. Whichever is funnier.” “The throne doesn’t give up. It sulks.” “Then we have something in common.” He should have answered. Instead he shifted his weight, and the weakened leg answered for him: a bright, indecent crack, not quite a break. The hound emerged from underneath with a mouthful of metaphysical iron and the expression of a craftsman satisfied with the morning’s work. The throne settled two inches to the left. From the queue beyond the doors, someone applauded, assuming it was policy. Lucifer closed his eyes. When he opened them, Lilith was still there, not smiling, which was closer to mercy than smiling would have been. “Lunch,” she said. “Before the pride contingent. And you’re feeding him something that isn’t a political institution.” “Demanding.” “Off again,” she said lightly, already walking toward the sideboard, where yesterday’s breakfast had achieved the status of a relic. “For now.” He followed, because the throne could wait, and the wardens could wait, and the lonely inventive weather could, with any luck, be postponed by the ordinary business of finding a plate. Behind them the hound dropped its prize, considered the other three legs, and began, with professional calm, on the right.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an accomplished piece of understated dark fantasy comedy that hits nearly every note the prompt requested. The central conceit—Hell's bureaucracy as workplace drudgery, the Lucifer/Lilith relationship as a familiar on-again/off-again domestic drama—is executed with wit and restraint. The hound eating the throne is an excellent running absurdity, and the image of the throne "listing" toward Lilith as if eavesdropping is a standout detail. Strengths: The prose is elegant and controlled, with a Gaiman-like dry irony ("a coat that was once a coat and was now mostly intention," "the moderately condemned," "screams arranged, by long custom, into something almost like ventilation"). Dialogue is sharp and character-revealing; the sparring carries real subtext about loneliness and history without ever stating it directly. The emotional complexity is genuinely earned—the "off again" dynamic is shown through small gestures (sitting on the step, not the throne; the "almost" smile) rather than exposition. The ending lands with appropriate lightness that feels consistent with the piece's tone rather than falsely redemptive. Weaknesses: The piece is a single scene rather than a full "day in the life" as requested—the afternoon session and lunch are deferred, not shown, which slightly undercuts the structural brief. Some of the aphoristic exchanges ("It isn't a no") flirt with cleverness for its own sake. The duke of avarice opening is a touch conventional for this genre. The word count is somewhat under the 1000-word seed. These are minor quibbles against an otherwise polished piece. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
The oil had gone sharp in the jar, but I worked it into my shoulders anyway, until the skin shone like wet stone. The yard smelled of that oil, of straw, and of beans left too long on the brazier. Over the wall Rome was already spending its morning. A cart groaned on the stones. A woman called the price of figs and then called it lower. Somewhere a smith answered with a thin, bright clang. The city always sounded richer than it smelled. What reached us was smoke, dung, and the sweet rot of fruit in the gutter. I was not to fight that day. The lanista had said so at first light, tapping my name on his wax tablet as if he were striking a bargain with heaven. Tomorrow, perhaps, when the Emperor’s games went on and the sand would be raked clean of what yesterday had left in it. I did not ask. In that house a question cost more than silence. Hercules watched from the niche beside the door. Someone had painted him badly: the club too thin, the lion’s skin the color of old wine. Still I touched two fingers to my brow. My mother, in a village the legions had since renamed, had prayed to other gods. Rome had given me this one, and I had kept him because he had been a man before he was divine, and because his labors never seemed to finish. I did not ask him for victory. Victory belonged to the crowd and to the man who paid for the day. I asked for a straight spine, and for an hour in which no one owned my thoughts. The cook’s boy brought barley boiled to a grey patience, slicked with oil and a scatter of salt. I ate standing, as we were made to, so the body would not learn the softness of a chair. Across the yard the new men were learning the shield. One of them was Dacian, taken in the last war, and he moved as if the ground itself meant him harm. I knew the look. I had worn it when they brought me south after the river fighting, while Trajan’s columns were still singing and the Senate was still pretending the Emperor asked its leave before he spent its sons. They said the Forum had been dressed that year in Dacian gold. I had not seen the triumph. I had seen the cages. When the gate opened, a secretary came in with the day’s orders, his toga edged just enough to show he belonged to someone who mattered. He did not look at us. We were infames: famous and filthy at once, painted on walls and shut out of the law’s clean courtesies. We could not sit where decent men sat, nor give testimony, nor marry as free men married. I had heard a senator’s wife sigh my name at the games as if it were a spice. I had also heard how little a senator’s hand mattered once the Emperor’s men had counted the hands that did. Bread and games, the old joke went, and the people forget the rest. I did not laugh. I was part of the rest. By midmorning the heat had climbed the wall and sat on the training sand. I walked the shade along the eastern side because walking was permitted and because the stone there still held a memory of night. A kitchen boy scraped a hide. Flies stitched the air. From the street came garum, that salt-rot of fish Romans poured over everything, and under it the warmer smell of bread from a bakery I could not see. My stomach, already full, tightened anyway. Hunger is a habit the body keeps after the bowl is empty. I thought of the tablet in the lanista’s office, where my price was written, and of the years left on the contract I had signed with a hand that still remembered a plow. Some of us were slaves. Some had volunteered, which the law called a kind of civil death, so a man might climb out of debt across the bodies of other men. I had been both: taken, then offered the stylus, as if choice could be poured back into a cup already broken. The stories said Hercules chose his labors. They were quieter about the madness that came first. At the gate two guards talked of the grain ships. One said the wind had held them at Ostia and the dole would run thin if the warehouses stayed shut. The other spat and said the Emperor would open them, because an empty belly made a louder citizen than a full one, and because the old families were already whispering that the provinces bled for Rome while Rome forgot how to bleed. I listened without turning my head. Politics arrived in the ludus the way weather did: over the wall, unasked, and usually late. A trainer called me then, not for the sword but for the physician. My shoulder had been stiff since the exhibition they held for a guild of fullers who wanted to look rich. The Greek prodded the muscle, muttered about humors, and rubbed in a salve that stank of resin and vinegar. “You will be wanted,” he said, which was his way of being kind. He did not say by whom. By the Emperor, perhaps, sitting above us like a god who still ate. By the crowd, which was a god with worse manners. By the lanista, who counted my breaths as coin. When he finished I sat on the bench beneath the niche and shut my eyes. The city roared softly, a beast turning in its sleep. I pictured the sand and then put the picture away. The doctores said a man who fought the fight in his head before the gate opened had already spent his strength. Instead I thought of the village, of a river that did not yet have a Roman name, and of the thin painted club above me. If I lived long enough they might give me the wooden sword and call me free. Free to do what, I did not know. The empire was wide, and every road in it seemed to lead back to a gate where a guard knew your price. A horn sounded toward the amphitheater, not for us: a procession, a sacrifice, some cleaner ceremony of the morning. Incense drifted over the wall, cut with burning fat, and for a moment the yard smelled like a temple. I opened my eyes. The Dacian boy had dropped his shield. No one struck him. It was not that kind of day. He looked at me as if I might tell him how to survive the city. I had no such sentence. I only nodded, the way I imagined Hercules nodding at a man still carrying his first labor, and the sun kept climbing, and Rome kept spending itself, loudly, in the street beyond the stone.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, controlled piece of historical fiction that fulfills nearly every instruction. It is first person, past tense, roughly the requested length, non-combat, and rich in sensory detail: the rancid oil, garum, burning fat and incense, the "grey patience" of barley. The voice is consistent — weary, wry, observant — and the prose is economical rather than ornate, with a few genuinely excellent lines ("Rome was already spending its morning," "an empty belly made a louder citizen than a full one," "a god with worse manners"). The political and social context is woven in organically: the infames legal status, the grain dole and Ostia shipping, Trajan's Dacian wars and the triumph the narrator saw only as cages, the tension between Emperor and Senate. These arrive "over the wall, unasked," which the narrator explicitly notes — a self-aware structural device that mostly works, though occasionally the exposition leans slightly toward lecture (the paragraph on infames and volunteering is the most tell-heavy passage). Character work is nuanced: the narrator's fatalism, his Hercules devotion framed as a man-made god whose labors never finish, his complicated status as both slave and volunteer ("choice poured back into a cup already broken"), and the quiet closing nod to the Dacian boy, which earns its small warmth without sentimentality. The ending is appropriately unresolved — a slice of a larger story, as requested. Minor criticisms: a couple of aphorisms strain slightly ("Hunger is a habit the body keeps after the bowl is empty" is good; "the city always sounded richer than it smelled" is a bit pat). Dialogue is minimal and functional. Some metaphors are near-misses rather than misses. Nothing is purple or overwrought; the piece shows admirable restraint. It is not quite a masterpiece — the Dacian boy thread and the physician scene are somewhat conventional beats in gladiator fiction — but it is confident, coherent, and engaging throughout. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 87.5
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Stoer Head Light 18 March 1964 Mother, I have the western room. The glass is up sixteen steps and then another iron flight, and the wind gets in at the collar of it no matter the door. Mr Lean, the principal, is a Harris man and does not talk at his meals. That suits me. The relief put me ashore in a swell and was glad to be gone. You can see the Old Man of Stoer from the gallery if the rain is off it. A stack, not a man. Grey, with a dirty white ring where the birds sit. I walked the cliff yesterday until the path stopped being a path. There is nothing past it but the Minch. The money will come to you as we said. Do not send it back if it is more than the coal. I am eating. Tinned soup and the bread they left, which is not your bread. Callum Lochinver 29 March 1964 Callum, The order came. I paid the coal and the electric and put ten shillings in the tin for Andy’s boots, which are through at the toe. Do not tell him I said so. Mrs MacKay asked was it true you were out at the light and I said it was, and she said it was a lonely job for a young man. I told her lonely is not the worst thing a job can be. She did not like that. It has rained here since Tuesday. The step at the back door is green and I nearly went on it with the bucket. Nothing torn. Ishbel at the hotel said to tell you the tea is still sixpence if you are ever in on the boat, which was her idea of a joke. Eat something that is not from a tin. I have posted socks. If they are too short say so. I am not minding the quiet in the house. The wireless fills it. Your mother Stoer Head 22 April 1964 Mother, The socks are right. Thank you. The relief did not make it this turn. Mr Lean says the landing is a bad one when the swell is from the west, and it has been from the west for nine days. We are not short. There is paraffin and tea and a side of bacon that is more salt than pig. I have spoken to him and to the wireless and that is the whole of the company. I went down again toward the Old Man. You cannot get onto it. The gap is wider than it looks from the gallery. Kittiwakes in the cracks, and the water at the foot a pale green, like bottle glass. I stood longer than I needed. When I came up I had to say my own name out loud in the lantern room to hear it. That is a foolish thing and I will not do it again. Do not worry at Mrs MacKay. If the boat is late next month the money may be late with it. I will send two months when it comes. How is the step. You said nothing torn. That is not the same as nothing wrong. Callum Lochinver 3 May 1964 Callum, The step is a step. I put ashes on it. Andy was in for a night between the boats. Thin in the face. The shares were poor and he pretended they were not, so I pretended I believed him. He asked if you were managing. I said you were, because you write as if the weather is the only thing that happens to you, and men do that when they are managing and also when they are not. Write one true sentence to me that is not about the light or the food. Ishbel was not joking, for what it is worth. I am not sending her your address. I am only telling you a person asked. The house is fine. My chest is the damp. It will go when the wind goes. Mother Stoer Head 19 June 1964 Mother, One true sentence, then. I do not like the hour between finishing the lamps and going to my bed, because there is nothing left in it that needs me. The rest you can have as weather if you want it. A boat came too close on the Thursday fog, a small one, the Harvest Moon out of Lochinver, I think, though I could not read her in the murk. I had the horn going and the light burning though it was not quite the hour. A man on her deck lifted his hand. I lifted mine too late. They cleared the point. Mr Lean said I had done what the Board pays for. It did not feel like enough and it did not feel like too much. It felt like a job. I am not wanting Ishbel’s address either. Tell her the tea is sixpence here as well, if you must tell her anything, and that I am not in. You did not answer me about the step, not really. And “the damp” is what you called your knee the winter father died, and it was not the damp. Callum Lochinver 28 June 1964 Callum, I spent the last order. The electric had gone up and Andy’s boots would not take a patch. I am sorry. There is a pound in the tin still. I will not touch it. The doctor came to the house because I would not go to him, and you can be angry about that if you like. He says rest, and less of the sheds, and he has written to Inverness for a look at my chest. He did not say heart in so many words. He said we will see. I was going to wait until after they had seen, so as not to have you staring at the sea thinking of me staring at the ceiling. The step is mended. A man from the pier did it for a packet of tea. Do not do anything sudden. The light is your wage and your wage is this house until I am back on my feet. I am not frightened. I am annoyed. There is a difference, and I will thank you to remember I know it. Mother Stoer Head 2 August 1964 Mother, I have written to the superintendent for relief off this rock before my turn is up. If he refuses I will still come, but I will not leave Mr Lean alone with it. He has said he will cover two nights if the boat can be got. That is the most I can do without putting out the light, and I will not put out the light. Not for you and not for me. You taught me better than that, even if you are now telling me to stay for the sake of the electric. You should have told me at the first. I have been counting days out here as if they were mine. They are not. I walked to the cliff this morning. The Old Man was clear, every ledge of him, and the gap as wide as ever. I do not need to stand and look at it again. Callum TELEGRAM Lochinver 11 August 1964 CALUM REID STOER HEAD LIGHT DO NOT LEAVE THE LIGHT STOP APPOINTMENT RAIGMORE TWELVE SEPTEMBER STOP I WILL TAKE THE BUS STOP ANDY COMING TO THE HOUSE STOP I AM ANNOYED NOT FRIGHTENED STOP MOTHER Stoer Head 29 August 1964 Mother, Relief is granted. The boat is Thursday if the landing allows, Friday if it does not. Mr Lean has the nights. The lamp is trimmed and the horn tested and the log written up to the hour I mean to leave, so the next man will not have to guess at me. I am not coming to drag you out of the sheds or to sit in the kitchen looking like a funeral. I am coming to go to Inverness with you on the twelfth. Andy can have the house for those days. The pound in the tin stays in the tin. You asked once for a true sentence. Here is another. I can stand the quiet. I could not stand hearing about your chest from a telegram that was trying not to say heart. I will see the Old Man from the deck on the way in. He will still be there in September, and after that. So will the light. Callum Post Office, Lochinver 4 September 1964 Mother, I am ashore. The landing was wet and ordinary. Mr Lean shook my hand, which is more than he has done in four months, and said the bacon would last him. I have been to the house. The step is sound. I aired the back room and left Andy’s boots by the stove with a note that he is not to thank you where I can hear it. There is soup that is not from a tin, because Mrs MacKay put her head in and would not be refused, and I am eating it out of your blue bowl so you cannot say I didn’t. The bus is the morning one. I will be at the hospital before you, if the road is kind. If you are annoyed, be annoyed to my face. I would rather that than another month of letters that walk round the thing. The Old Man was in cloud when we passed. I did not mind not seeing him. Callum
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a disciplined, well-crafted epistolary piece that fulfills nearly every instruction. The correspondence spans roughly six months (March–September 1964), uses letters and one telegram, and builds a coherent plot: a young Scottish lighthouse keeper's isolation, his mother's concealed illness, and his eventual relief and return. The voices are distinct — Callum is clipped, observational, self-protective; the mother is brisk, deflecting, dryly funny ("lonely is not the worst thing a job can be"). The telegram is a nice formal variation, and its stilted compression ("I AM ANNOYED NOT FRIGHTENED STOP") carries real emotional weight. Strengths: the "one true sentence" device is an elegant engine for the emotional arc, and Callum's answer ("nothing left in it that needs me") is a genuinely fine line. The recurring motifs — the Old Man of Stoer, the step, the tin, the blue bowl, tinned soup vs. bread — are deployed with restraint and pay off without being signposted. The mother's withholding of her illness and Callum's rebuke ("You should have told me at the first") is earned conflict. The prose is spare and idiomatic, avoiding cliché almost entirely. The ending resolves without false sentiment: the illness is unresolved, but the relationship has been corrected, and "I did not mind not seeing him" is a quiet, earned closing note. Weaknesses: the plot is modest and somewhat predictable in its trajectory (isolation → family crisis → return); a reader familiar with the genre will see the mother's illness coming from the "damp" chest mention. The mother's character risks being a familiar type (stoic Highland widow). Some of the middle letters slightly restate the same emotional beats (the step, the tin) without advancing much. The Harvest Moon boat incident is a nice texture but doesn't integrate fully into the arc. The word count is somewhat under the 1000-word seed, though not egregiously. Still, the piece shows strong craft: showing over telling, subtext in every exchange, no purple prose, no overwrought moments, and an emotionally complex, believable resolution. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 59.3
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The candle is doing that restaurant thing where it pretends to be intimacy. Across from me, Jordan is mid-sentence about a commander deck that somehow runs both graveyard recursion and a straight-faced tax package, and I am trying, I am actually trying, to stay on the person and not the board state of the room. Exit by the kitchen. Camera over the bar with a dead IR bloom, so it’s either fake or aimed at the liquor and not the till. Server’s PIN pad is the old kind that sulks if you cover it. None of that is mine to fix tonight. I came here to be a person who can hear a story about a janky Enchantress list and not immediately rank the teller by how easy they would be to spoof. Jordan laughs at their own bad mana base and it lands. Real laugh, not the date laugh. Shared religion: cardboard, bad decisions, the specific shame of keeping a pet card that has never once performed. I feel the part of me that inventories people go quiet for a second. It is a good second. Then the phone lights up face-down beside the bread plate, and they flip it without thinking. Muscle memory. Four swipes. I don’t even decide to watch. The shape is a house. Start bottom-left, roof, back down the other side, little porch. A child’s drawing. On a glass screen, in a room full of reflective surfaces, with me sitting where the ceiling light makes a second copy of the gesture in the butter knife. “That’s a really guessable pattern,” I say. The sentence is out before the reformed part of me gets a vote. Jordan’s hand stops over the phone. The laugh is gone. I can hear the kitchen door slap. “Sorry,” I say, which is the correct word and also useless. “Occupational hazard. I don’t— I’m not trying to—” “You memorized it.” Not a question. Fair. I did. Not on purpose, which is the same as on purpose if you’ve spent a decade being paid to notice what people give away for free. The pattern is already in the place where I keep things I wish I didn’t keep. I could describe the house. I will not describe the house. I will not be helpful to the worst version of me, not even in my own head, not as a party trick. “I saw the shape,” I say. “I shouldn’t have said it like that. Or at all. You can change it later if you want. Or not. It’s your phone.” Jordan sets it face-down again, slower. Thumb along the edge, a small private calculation: how much of the evening was a person, how much was a scan. I know that calculation. I have been the variable in it. They were telling me, before the cards, about growing up on Maple, about a golden retriever named Biscuit who died the year they started college, about a mother who still uses her maiden name on the rare family email because she never updated the account. Breadcrumbs. I clocked them the way you clock a loose window. Security questions are just autobiography with a submit button. I have the answers sitting in the recent tray of my attention, labeled, disgusting, ready. I push the tray shut. I do not repeat them back, not even silently in a list. Listing is how it becomes a tool. “Most people don’t say it,” Jordan says. “They just… know things about you by dessert and call it chemistry.” “I call it a bad habit I’m trying to quit.” The candle pops. “I used to get paid to find the unlocked door and walk through it before somebody worse did. The problem is the looking doesn’t clock out. You said Enchantress and I thought about your deck. You moved your hand and I thought about your lock screen. Both of those were me. Only one of them was a reason to be here.” Jordan studies the bread. I let the silence be bad. Salvage, if it happens, shouldn’t be a social engineer’s close. No mirroring. No strategic disclosure calibrated to rebuild trust. If I perform vulnerability, it’s still a performance, and they will feel the seam. What I actually want is smaller and harder. I want to hear the rest of the tax package. I want to know whether they keep the pet card in the deck or in a binder where it can’t disappoint them. I want to be someone who can sit across from a readable person and choose not to read them for sport. “You can leave,” I say. “I’d get it. I killed the bit where this was just two nerds and a candle.” “You did.” A pause. “You also warned me instead of using it. That’s… not nothing. It’s also not a personality.” “No.” “Change of subject, then. Real one. Not a redirect.” They tap the table, not the phone. “If I tell you about the deck, are you going to grade my threat model the whole time, or can you just lose to a bad include like a normal person?” Something in my chest unclenches that isn’t strategy. “I can lose. I’m good at losing. The pet card thing—I have a foil that has never resolved and I will defend it with my life.” “That’s worse than the pattern comment.” “It’s close.” They almost smile. The phone stays down. I do not look at the knife. Maple, Biscuit, the maiden name: I let them blur into the ordinary mess of a first date, facts I am not entitled to keep sharp. If I wanted to be dangerous tonight I already have enough. I don’t want to be dangerous tonight. I want another turn of the conversation where the only exploit is a greedy draw and the only thing I take is a chance to stay.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece executes the prompt with notable skill. The internal monologue voice is consistent and distinctive: clipped, self-aware, technical vocabulary bleeding into personal reflection ("the board state of the room," "autobiography with a submit button"). The hacker mindset is rendered through observation rather than exposition—the dead IR camera, the PIN pad, the butter knife reflecting the unlock pattern. The MTG fandom is integrated organically (commander deck, tax package, pet card) and even becomes the vehicle for the ending's emotional resolution. The phone-pattern incident lands well because the protagonist's slip ("That's a really guessable pattern") is involuntary and in-character. The fallout negotiation is the strongest section: Jordan's "You memorized it" is a sharp, believable beat, and the protagonist's refusal to perform vulnerability ("If I perform vulnerability, it's still a performance, and they will feel the seam") is genuinely nuanced—it resists the easy redemption arc. Jordan's "It's also not a personality" is excellent dialogue: forgiving without absolving. Minor weaknesses: the ending is slightly tidy—Jordan's pivot back to warmth comes a touch quickly, though the "not a personality" line and the pet-card exchange earn enough of it. A few metaphors strain slightly ("the candle is doing that restaurant thing where it pretends to be intimacy" is good; "the place where I keep things I wish I didn't keep" is a bit vague). The word count is somewhat under the 1000-word seed (~850), a mild adherence issue. Some aphoristic constructions ("Not on purpose, which is the same as on purpose") flirt with cleverness over substance, but mostly land. The prose is controlled, the emotional complexity real (shame, restraint, desire to not-read someone), and the lightness at the end is earned through the protagonist's demonstrated discipline rather than granted by the narrative. + First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 60.5
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The projector squeaks again, that thin rubbery sound, and I have already decided three different ways to say hi and thrown all of them out. He is two chairs over, unzipping his backpack like it is a normal thing a person does with their hands. I know his name. I have known his name since September. Saying it out loud would still feel like I borrowed it without asking. Okay. If I wait until Mrs. Ellison assigns the groups, then I can just look up and say, “Hey.” One word. Nobody has ever died from one word. Except I would say it too quietly and then he would say “What?” and I would have to say it again, louder, and the second time it would sound like I had been practicing, which I have, which is the whole problem. The slide changes. Squeak. Cell diagrams. I am not looking at the cells. Maybe I don’t say hey. Maybe I just pull my chair over when she calls our names and start on the worksheet like a person who has never thought about another person in her life. That could work. That is what normal people do. They exist next to each other without narrating it. I could be that. I could be a worksheet person. Except if I don’t say anything at all, then the whole period is just the sound of my pencil and his pencil and I will spend forty minutes trying to figure out whether silence means I hate him or I don’t know he exists or I am weird, and he will not be thinking any of those things because he will be thinking about mitochondria, probably, or lunch, and I will have done all that work for an audience of one. My face feels hot already. I haven’t even moved. Mrs. Ellison says our names together. Of course she does. I knew she would. I also somehow didn’t believe it until it happened, which is a stupid way to be surprised by something you predicted. I stand up. My chair leg catches on the tile and makes a sound that is too loud for how small it is. I want to apologize to the chair. I do not apologize to the chair. That is growth. “Hey,” I say, and it comes out fine. It comes out like a person. I almost ruin it by smiling too much at the fact that it came out fine, so I look down at the handout instead, like the handout has just said something fascinating. He says hey back. Two letters. I replay them twice before I sit down, checking for tone, and there is no tone. It was just hey. I need to let it be hey. The projector squeaks. Somebody in the back laughs at something that is not us. Good. The room is busy. We are not the room. I should say something about the project. I have a sentence ready: “Do you want to split the questions or just go in order?” It is a good sentence. It is practical. It does not say I notice the way you tap your pencil when you’re thinking, which I do, which I will not say, which I am already embarrassed for thinking in a sentence this long while he is waiting for me to look up from the paper. “We could, um.” I stop. Um is not part of the sentence. I hate um. Um is the sound of me watching myself talk. “Split them? Or go in order. Either way.” Either way. Now I’ve given him nothing to answer. Excellent. A multiple choice question with no wrong option and also no point. “In order is fine,” he says. Fine. Fine is good. Fine is not “why are you like this.” I write our names at the top because writing is something my hands can do without a committee meeting. My handwriting looks too careful. I make the second letter of his name a little messier on purpose so it doesn’t look like I was trying. Then I worry the messy letter looks like I don’t care. I cannot win against a letter. Question one is about organelles. I know this. I know this cold. Inside my head the answer is already in paragraphs, with the examples from the video and the thing about how the membrane is picky, not just a wall. Out loud I say, “The mitochondria one is, like, the energy.” Like. I said like. I had a better sentence and I sanded it down until it was small enough to escape. He nods and writes energy, which is not wrong, and I want to add the rest and I don’t, because if I add the rest it might sound like I’m showing off, or like I think he doesn’t know, or like I’ve been sitting here constructing a speech, which I have. He reads question two out loud. His voice is ordinary. I am grateful for ordinary. I am also listening so hard that I miss the last three words and have to pretend I didn’t. “Sorry, the last part?” “Just which structure does the filtering.” “Right. Yeah. The—membrane. Selectively permeable.” There. That one landed. I feel the tiny click of a sentence that matches the one I meant. It lasts about a second before I start checking his face for whether “selectively permeable” was too much, too textbook, the kind of thing a girl says when she wants to be impressive. He is just writing it down. He is not compiling evidence. I am the only one compiling evidence. I am so tired of being the only one. The projector squeaks through three more slides. Mrs. Ellison is talking about the quiz on Friday. I should mention the quiz. A shared enemy. People bond over shared enemies. I almost say, “I am going to fail that,” which is a lie, I am not going to fail it, I say things like that so nobody thinks I care too much about being right. If I say it he might think I’m fishing. If I don’t say it and then I do well, he might think I was hiding it. There is no version where I am just a person taking a quiz. I stay quiet. My knee bounces. I stop it. Starting it was unconscious and stopping it is loud in my own body, a whole production: notice, judge, correct, hope he didn’t see the correction. He didn’t. He is drawing a tiny arrow on the diagram. The arrow is slightly crooked. I like the crooked arrow more than I should, and then I am annoyed at myself for liking an arrow, and then I am annoyed at being annoyed, and the stack of that is so stupid I almost laugh. Don’t laugh at nothing. That is rule one of not being weird. “You can do the next one if you want,” I say, which is fine, which is collaborative, which also might sound like I’m dumping the work. “Or I can. I don’t mind.” Stop offering options. Stop building him little exit ramps from a conversation he is already in. “I’ll do this one,” he says. “You want the one after?” “Sure.” Sure. I can live with sure. Sure is a word that does not shake. We work. The pencil sounds line up for a minute and it is almost easy, the way group projects are easy when you forget there is another person attached to the other pencil. Then he shifts his chair and his sleeve is close to my arm and my whole side of the table becomes a map I have to navigate. I move my elbow a half inch. Not away like I’m disgusted. Not closer like I’m anything. A half inch of nothing. I monitor the half inch like it might testify later. I think of something true I could say. Not a speech. Just: this question is worded badly. It is worded badly. I could say that. It would be normal. It would be us against the worksheet instead of me against the air. I open my mouth. The projector squeaks, and the sound knocks the sentence off its track, and what comes out is, “Yeah.” He glances over, mild, waiting for the rest. “The question,” I say. My ears are hot. “It’s kind of confusing. The way it’s written.” “Oh. Yeah, it is.” He frowns at it, not at me. “Like, do they want the name or the function?” “Both, maybe. To be safe.” “Okay.” He writes both. He doesn’t look relieved to escape me. He doesn’t look trapped. He looks like a person doing a science worksheet with another person. I let that be the whole fact for a second. It doesn’t stay. Already I’m drafting the next thing, and crossing it out, and drafting a smaller one, and wondering if my face is doing too much, and whether I laughed at the right time earlier even though I didn’t laugh, and how long until the bell, and whether I’ll replay this period tonight until the words go smooth and meaningless. But the sentence happened. The confusing-question sentence. It made it out of my head and into the room, and the room did not break. He slides the paper back toward the middle. “Your turn.” “Okay,” I say, and this time okay is almost the size of what I mean. I pick up the pencil. The projector squeaks. I don’t rehearse the next word before I need it. I just start reading the question, quietly, on purpose, like somebody who might finish it out loud if she decides to.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally strong execution of the prompt. The narrative is almost entirely internal monologue, as instructed, and captures the exhausting recursive self-monitoring of social anxiety with precision and wit. The gap between the articulate inner voice ("the answer is already in paragraphs") and the diminished spoken output ("The mitochondria one is, like, the energy") is dramatized rather than stated—perfect show-don't-tell. The humor is character-true ("I want to apologize to the chair. I do not apologize to the chair. That is growth."), and the details land with authenticity: deliberately mussing the letter of his name, "um is the sound of me watching myself talk," the half inch of elbow movement "like it might testify later." The structure cycles through rehearsal, execution, post-mortem, and small victories without repeating itself mechanically; each beat escalates or varies the anxiety pattern. The prose is clean, rhythmic, and controlled; sentences like "I replay them twice before I sit down, checking for tone, and there is no tone" achieve genuine elegance without ornament. The recurring projector squeak functions as an effective ambient motif and pacing device. Minor criticisms: the boy is thinly sketched (though arguably appropriate given the POV's limited perception—she's watching herself, not him). The "metacognitive aphorism" style ("I am the only one compiling evidence") occasionally edges toward over-cleverness for an 8th grader, though the prompt specified an intelligent narrator, so this is defensible. The ending's small victory—the confusing-question sentence surviving into the room—feels earned rather than saccharine, and the closing line resists over-resolution ("I don't rehearse the next word before I need it") while still being honest that she's only partially changed. The dialogue itself is sparse and appropriately awkward, mirroring the narrator's halting speech. Word count is near 1000, format adhered to, all prompt requirements hit. + First-person unique perspective: Rehearsing Rejection — Score: 81.8
Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The mirror is too honest and not honest enough. I look fine. I look like someone who tried. If I look like I tried, they’ll know I needed this to go well, and needing it is the thing that makes people leave. Battery at four percent. Of course. I should have charged it. I didn’t, because some part of me wanted the excuse: if they don’t text, it’s the phone. If I don’t text, it’s the phone. Four percent is a story I can tell later that doesn’t include the part where I refreshed the thread eleven times in the cab. They said seven. It’s 6:52. Early is desperate. On time is fine. Late is a test I don’t mean to run and will run anyway. I practice the face. Not the smile—the smaller one, the one that says I noticed you were quiet this week and I’m not going to make it a thing. Except I am going to make it a thing. I already made it a thing in the kitchen, out loud, to no one. You don’t have to do this, I tell the version of them in my head. They answer before I finish. That’s the problem with rehearsals. They always know their lines. I just needed space, they say, which is what people say when the space is permanent and they want you to help them pack it. So this is the goodbye dinner. It’s not a goodbye dinner. Then why did you take two days to answer about Thursday? Because I was tired. Because work. Because not everything is about you. There it is. The cleanest cut. I feel it land and I haven’t even left the apartment. I put on the jacket they said they liked. Then I take it off. Then I put it back on, because changing again would mean I believed the first choice was wrong, and if the first choice was wrong then so was asking them to come over last month, and so was telling them I loved them on a Tuesday like it was allowed. Three percent. Outside, the air is ordinary. People are walking like the evening has already decided to be kind. I hate that. I want weather that matches. They text: here, window table, got you the thing with the chili. I read it twice. Got you the thing. They remembered. Remembering is a kind of staying. My chest does something stupid and warm, and I immediately tax it. They ordered before I arrived so they wouldn’t have to sit with me longer than necessary. They picked the window so they can watch the door and leave if I walk in looking like this. I walk in looking like this. They stand. That’s worse, somehow. Standing means effort. Their hand finds the back of my arm, brief, and I feel the whole week rearrange around that second of contact. I needed it so badly I almost say so. I don’t. Need said out loud becomes a bill. “You look—” they start. “Tired,” I finish, so they don’t have to lie. “I was going to say good.” They smile like they mean it. The smile is not a performance I can catch them in. That’s the dissonance: the evidence is kind, and kindness feels like a trap with better lighting. We sit. The drink is the one I order when I want to seem easy. They got it right. I take a sip so I have something to do with my mouth besides ask why they went quiet. “Sorry I’ve been weird,” they say, before I can build the courtroom. “Work’s been a mess, and I didn’t want to dump it on you and make it sound like I was pulling away. I wasn’t. I just go quiet when I’m overloaded. I should’ve said that.” There. The explanation I rehearsed them refusing to give. It arrives whole, unforced, a little clumsy. I feel it in my throat, the stupid relief, the way my body believes faster than I do. Loved. Chosen. Not tonight’s casualty. Then the other voice, quick as a flinch: They practiced that. They know what you need to hear. Quiet is what people do before they practice leaving in smaller rooms. “It’s fine,” I say, which is a lie wearing a soft coat. “It’s not fine if it scared you.” They look at me like they’re allowed to know that. “Did it?” Yes. Obviously. I built three endings and a speech for each. I resented you for crimes you hadn’t committed so it would hurt less if you committed them. I almost canceled so I could be the one who left. “A little,” I say. They nod, not victorious, not clinical. Their knee touches mine under the table and stays. I press back before I can decide whether pressing back is too much. The contact is simple. I am so hungry for simple that I mistrust it on principle. Two percent. The phone dies between us like a small accusation. “Shit.” “Use mine if you need to,” they say, already unlocking it, already trusting me with the rectangle that holds their life. They set it by my hand. No performance. No pause. I stare at the screen and feel the pattern snag, briefly, on something true. This is the moment. They are not leaving. They ordered my drink. They named the fear without making me beg for the name. The story in my head is louder than the table, but it is not the table. I know this, I think. I know I do this. I know the rehearsal is a shelter that becomes a room I can’t get out of. I know if I say the whole thing—I already hated you a little so you couldn’t surprise me—they might stay anyway, and the staying would ruin the rehearsal, and I don’t know who I am without it. “I had this whole thing ready,” I hear myself say. “Where you were done, and I was dignified, and nobody had to watch me need anything.” They don’t laugh. That’s good. Laughing would have proved the speech. “I’m not done,” they say. “I’m here. I’m sorry I made it noisy in your head. Can we just eat, and you can tell me the noisy parts if you want, and I’ll tell you which ones aren’t true?” The chili thing arrives. Steam. Ordinary mercy. My eyes sting and I hate that they sting, and I let them, a little, because looking away would be another rehearsal. I believe them for three breaths. On the fourth, the question arrives anyway, small and vicious and familiar: how long until here isn’t enough? I pick up the fork. Battery dead. No exit text. Their knee still against mine. I stay in the chair, which is not the same as being sure, but it is the only interrupt I can manage tonight, and I do it with my hands, not my arguments, while the other voice keeps talking and I try, badly, not to answer it out loud.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece executes the prompt's demanding brief with considerable skill. It is almost entirely internal monologue, cycling convincingly between imagined confrontations (the imagined dialogue with the friend who "always knows their lines"), preemptive resentments ("I resented you for crimes you hadn't committed"), and desperate-but-questioned validation. The actual interactions are warm and non-rejecting, exactly as specified, and the narrator's reinterpretations ("They ordered before I arrived so they wouldn't have to sit with me") are sharply rendered. The limited self-awareness is captured well: "I know this, I think. I know I do this" — recognition that fails to interrupt the pattern, ending with a partial, unheroic step ("I stay in the chair, which is not the same as being sure"). The battery-percent device is a clever, unifying thread — the dead phone as "small accusation," the refusal of an exit. The prose is controlled, aphoristic without tipping into overwrought ("Need said out loud becomes a bill," "kindness feels like a trap with better lighting"). A few lines flirt with preciousness ("Steam. Ordinary mercy"), and some of the epigrammatic density is slightly mannered, but it largely suits a hypervigilant BPD interiority. Dialogue is minimal but effective — the friend's lines are natural, kind, and notably un-perfect, which grounds the piece. Length is near the 1000-word target. Cognitive dissonance is the engine of the piece and it works. Weaknesses: the friend's self-awareness ("I'm sorry I made it noisy in your head") is slightly too articulate, bordering on therapeutic idealization; the relentlessly polished cleverness of every sentence occasionally flattens into a stylistic tic rather than raw thought; and the ending's small hopeful turn, while earned and heavily qualified, is almost tidy given the friend's near-perfect responsiveness. + Physical-spatial: Blood Debt — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The torch burned in a cracked sconce on the eastern pillar, the only light in the ruined hall. Its flame leaned and recovered with every draft, throwing the fighters’ shadows long across broken flagstones and then snatching them back. Around the edges of the open floor, men and women pressed shoulder to shoulder against leaning walls, coins clenched in fists, voices low. No one crossed the cracked ring of stone that marked the fighting ground. Kaito stood with the torch on his left, feet set wide, shoulders squared to Lin Wei. The light cut the hard line of his jaw and left his right side in black. He wore a short practice jacket, sleeves bound tight, and he did not bow. Across from him Lin kept a narrower stance, weight on the ball of his rear foot, hands loose and low. His shadow climbed the western wall and broke where plaster had fallen away. “Begin,” someone said from the dark. Kaito moved first. Two explosive steps closed the gap before the word had finished dying. His lead fist shot for Lin’s face, hip turning through it, the second fist already chambered behind his ear. Lin did not meet it. He slid his lead foot to his own left—Kaito’s right—and the punch tore air where his cheek had been. The follow-up came anyway, a short, heavy cross. Lin’s forearm rose late and only partly, and the blow skidded off bone into his shoulder. The impact spun him half a step toward the western wall. Kaito was already on him. He drove a front kick at the floating ribs, then a rising elbow as Lin folded. The kick landed. Lin’s breath left him in a sharp sound, and he gave ground toward the fallen beam that lay along the north edge of the ring, three paces from the crowd’s toes. Kaito pursued in a straight line, cutting the angle, fists pumping, each strike meant to end it before the other school could claim a story. Lin’s feet found the beam without looking. His heel kissed the wood, and he used it. Instead of retreating farther into the corner where the north wall met the dark, he whipped his rear hand in a wide, rising arc as he pivoted off the beam, circling to Kaito’s outside. The palm did not crash; it snapped, the arm uncoiling from the shoulder like a lash. It caught Kaito across the ear as he committed to another straight punch. The sound was thin and wet. Kaito’s head jerked sideways. Blood threaded from the ear down his neck. He did not retreat. He reset low and exploded again, this time not at the head but through the center, a short stamp and a thrusting forearm meant to smash Lin’s guard and pin him against the beam. Lin was no longer there. The pivot had carried him past Kaito’s right shoulder, into the open middle of the floor, torchlight now on his back, Kaito between him and the eastern pillar. The crowd on the west surged and was shoved back by the men holding the line. Kaito turned. Too fast, too square. Lin was already inside the turn, not in a clinch but at a bad angle, his lead shoulder pointed at Kaito’s ribs. A whipping backfist came from the blind side, circling over Kaito’s extended arm, and cracked the cheekbone. Kaito tasted iron. He answered with a knee that rose through the space Lin had just left; Lin had dropped his level and stepped to the torch side, so the knee found only cloth and then air. For a heartbeat Kaito was extended, weight forward, the flame flaring at the edge of his vision. Lin took it. He fired a low, circular kick at the lead ankle, not to break it but to steal the base, then followed with a palm that traveled up from his hip in a tight spiral and burst against Kaito’s jaw from underneath. Kaito’s head snapped back. He staggered two steps toward the eastern pillar, toward the torch, one hand out for balance and not finding the stone. The sconce’s light jumped. His shadow leaped across Lin and the western crowd like something trying to flee the body that cast it. He caught himself on the third step, short of the pillar, and the arrogance came back hotter than the pain. He spat blood onto the flagstones between them and smiled with red teeth. “Commoner’s tricks.” Lin did not answer. He was breathing through his mouth, left arm tucked where the kick had landed, circling again—always to Kaito’s right, always making the Jigen man turn toward the darker half of the hall. The raised lip of a broken stone sat just left of center. Lin had stepped over it twice. Kaito, driving, had not marked it. Kaito charged a third time, and this was the best of him: no wind-up, no tell, the floor exploding under his feet, a straight lead into a short hook into an elbow, all of it on one line, all of it meant to overwhelm. The first fist got through. It split Lin’s brow. Blood sheeted into the left eye at once, and the crowd made a sound like cloth tearing. The hook grazed the guard. The elbow was the finisher, and it would have been, except Lin’s rear foot had already cleared the broken lip and his hips had turned. He was not where the elbow was aimed. He was half a body to the outside, close enough that Kaito’s forearm scraped his chest, close enough to smell the iron. Lin’s hands did not stop. The injured arm whipped across Kaito’s extended elbow, not a block so much as a redirection, and the free hand came the long way around—from behind his own hip, up, over, and down in a tight circle that ended at the side of Kaito’s neck, just below the ear he had already cut. The palm landed with the whole turn of the waist behind it. Kaito’s legs went loose. He took one more step because the charge still owned him, and that step found the raised lip of stone. His ankle turned. He went down on his side at Lin’s feet, facing the torch, one arm still trying to rise into a guard that no longer had a stance under it. Lin did not follow him to the ground. He stood over the space Kaito had occupied, chest heaving, blood in his eye, the torch painting one half of him gold and leaving the other in the crawling dark. Kaito pushed up onto an elbow. His hand slipped in his own blood on the flagstone. He got a knee under him. Lin’s whipping hand was already drawn back, the circle loaded, and every man who had wagered on the old school saw where it would land. Kaito lifted his chin. He would not yield. The hand came down anyway—not a killing stroke, a short, final snap across the same cheek, precise as a rebuke. Kaito’s head struck the stone. He stayed down, blinking at the flame, breath sawing, alive and beaten. No one cheered at first. Coins changed hands in the shadows. The torch guttered, steadied, and threw both their blood in small dark coins across the floor between the pillar and the fallen beam. Lin wiped his brow with the back of his wrist and did not look at the men of either school. The debt was on the stones now, and the stones did not care which art had written it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a disciplined, tightly choreographed fight narrative that fulfills the prompt's core demands with notable skill. The physical coherence is the standout: positions are tracked meticulously (torch on the eastern pillar, fallen beam on the north edge, the raised lip of broken stone planted early and paid off late), and every strike, pivot, and momentum shift is spatially legible. The choreography reflects the two styles accurately—Jigen-ryū's linear, explosive first-strike aggression versus Piguaquan's whipping, circular redirection and angular evasion—so the martial-arts characterization is embedded in the mechanics rather than asserted. The prose is lean and controlled, mostly "show" rather than "tell," with a few well-chosen images (the shadow "like something trying to flee the body that cast it," blood as "small dark coins"). The dialogue is minimal but functional; "Commoner's tricks" efficiently conveys the class animosity. The ending is appropriately somber and unsentimental—the refusal to cheer, the ambiguous "debt" on the stones—avoiding both false triumph and melodrama. Weaknesses: the characters are archetypes more than people. Kaito's "arrogance came back hotter than the pain" is a rare tell; the crowd and schools remain undifferentiated background. The emotional register is somewhat narrow—tension and violence without much interiority or complexity beyond pride. The narrative arc (aggressor dominates early, evasive fighter turns the tide) is a familiar underdog structure, though executed well. Some phrasing flirts with repetition ("whipping" used often). Length is close to target. Overall this is a strong, professional piece of combat writing whose main limitation is emotional and characterological depth rather than craft. Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The clock on the far wall reads 00:47:12 in red digits that don’t blink so much as accuse. I plant my left foot on the tape mark—third row, second from the left—and the rubber of my worn sole sticks, then releases with a sound too soft for this room. Mirrors triple us. Sixteen bodies, one grid. Instructor Han stands downstage center, back to the glass, so we see his face only in reflection: calm, almost bored, which is worse than anger. “From the top,” he says. “Eight-count. No ornaments.” The track hits. Four clicks of a metronome buried under a synth stab, then the vocal. I know the counts. I do not know how to live inside them. One: right arm shoots to shoulder height, palm flat, fingers glued. Two: left follows, a half-beat late in my bones even when my eyes swear I’m on it. Three-four: weight drops through the right hip into a sharp plié, knees tracking over toes, torso upright like someone nailed a rod along my spine. On the street I’d fold here—chest cave, shoulder roll, let the bass pull my ribs sideways. Here the fold is a crime. My obliques seize trying to keep the line. Sweat already maps the small of my back. Five-six: we travel. Two steps right, heel-toe, heel-toe, shoulders square to the mirror. The dancer on my left—Minjae, scholarship like me but from a hagwon that actually taught this—clips my elbow because I drift an inch off the lane. The formation breathes wrong for a second. Han’s eyes find me in the glass and stay. Seven-eight: hit. Chest pop on the snare, but not a pop. A lock. Muscles fire and freeze: pecs, traps, the little muscles under the jaw. Hold. I feel the old impulse climb my arms—the wave that wants to ripple from fingertip to shoulder and die in a grin. I kill it at the wrist. The kill costs me. My right hand trembles in the freeze, a street tell, a glitch in their machine. 00:46:01. “Again,” Han says, before the track ends. “You.” He doesn’t use my name. He points at my reflection. “Your downbeat is honest. Your transitions are lies. Street habits. You decorate the space between counts as if the song owes you something.” Heat climbs my neck. Back home the cypher rewarded the lie—the unexpected, the flavor, the way you could steal a beat and give it back prettier. Here the space between counts is empty on purpose. Empty is the point. Empty is how twenty people become one logo. We reset. I slide my left foot back to the tape. The floor is scuffed pale where thousands of shoes have worried the same marks. My mark is already darker than the others; I keep missing it and correcting, grinding rubber into wood. Track. One-two: arms. This time I nail the height. Three-four: plié, and I let my chest stay high even though my lungs want to drop. Five: step right—then muscle memory fires a cross-step I used in a battle last winter, left foot cutting behind, hips switching, the kind of move that opens your silhouette and dares someone to answer. In this grid it throws my shoulder into Minjae’s path. He stumbles. The whole second row ripples. Someone in the front gasps, small and professional, like a mistake is a personal insult. Han stops the music with a tap on his phone. Silence except for our breathing and the clock’s tiny electronic tick, which I might be imagining. 00:44:38. “Out,” he says. I step off the mark. The formation closes without me, bodies sliding into the hole as if I’d never been a coordinate. They run the phrase clean: arms level, plié identical, travel lanes straight as ruler lines, locks arriving on the same fraction of the snare. It looks like violence done politely. It looks like money. Han walks to me. Up close he smells like menthol and starch. “You have a center,” he says quietly, so the others keep drilling. “Most of them are learning where theirs is. Yours already knows. That is why you are here. It is also why you will fail if you keep negotiating with the choreography.” Negotiation. That’s what he calls it. I call it not disappearing. “The phrase is not a suggestion,” he continues. “Five-six is lateral. Not a cross. Not a groove. Lateral. Show me the arm path without the music. Slow.” I lift. Right, then left. He adjusts my elbow with two fingers, a centimeter. The difference is nothing and everything: the line from shoulder to wrist suddenly matches the mirror line of the front row, who are still running full-out behind him, a metronome made of people. “Again. With weight.” I plié. He watches my knees. “Track. Don’t sit into your heels. You are not catching a beat. You are arriving at a picture.” Picture. Not feeling. My quads burn in a way freestyle never asked for—sustained, identical, no rest inside the flourish because there is no flourish. On the hold, my fingers want to flare. I press them flat until the tendons sing. 00:42:10. “Back in,” he says. Minjae makes a sliver of space. I take the mark. Left foot. Tape. The clock has eaten five minutes and I have not yet completed eight clean counts in company. My scholarship letter is in my bag by the door, cheap paper already soft from being folded too much. If I wash out, the letter becomes a story I tell bitter. If I stay, I might become someone whose hands don’t know how to talk unless a choreographer gives them a script. The track starts again. I don’t look at Han. I look at the tape, then the mirror, then the red numbers bleeding at the edge of the glass. One. Two. Arms true. Three. Four. Plié, chest up, the rod in my spine imaginary and cruel and, for these two counts, obeyed. Five. The cross-step rises in my hip like a dare—old alley, old bass, the version of me who never asked permission. I feel the choice in the joint: cut behind and break the lane, or send the foot straight lateral, heel-toe, inside the picture. Six. I send it straight. The impact is small. My shoulder clears Minjae by a finger’s width. The second row holds. The lock on seven arrives and my hand still wants to wave, still wants to prove I wasn’t built in this room—but I freeze the wrist, flat palm, empty space between counts left empty on purpose. Eight. We hit together. Sixteen chests. One picture. It doesn’t feel like winning. It feels like setting down a weapon I might need later and not knowing if I’ll be allowed to pick it up. Han doesn’t smile. He nods once, the way you nod at a tool that finally fits the hand. “Hold the shape,” he says. “Do not decorate the silence.” We hold. My arms shake. In the mirror I look like them, and also not: jaw too tight, eyes too loud, a street kid wearing a grid. The clock drops to 00:41:02. Somewhere under the perfect freeze, my pulse keeps a rhythm nobody counted, and I don’t know yet whether that rhythm is the thing that will save me or the thing this room is paid to erase. I keep my palms flat. I do not wave. Not this count. The next eight is already coming, and the tape under my foot is warm, and I am still here—inside the formation, and not entirely gone.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of controlled, kinetic writing. The narrative tracks spatial and physical detail with genuine precision: tape marks, row positions, the cross-step collision with Minjae, the elbow adjustment of a centimeter, the lateral travel lanes. The eight-count structure gives the prose its own choreography, and the countdown clock is an effective recurring device that externalizes pressure without stating it. The central conflict—improvisational street instinct versus militaristic precision—is dramatized through the body rather than explained. "The space between counts is empty on purpose" is a sharp thematic articulation of commercial K-pop's aesthetic. The muscle-memory betrayal (the cross-step rising "in the joint") is exactly the kind of embodied decision point the prompt requested, and the narrator's choice to conform is rendered with appropriate ambivalence—"setting down a weapon I might need later"—rather than false triumph. Weaknesses: Han's dialogue occasionally tips into aphorism ("You are arriving at a picture"), and the mentor's recognition of raw talent is somewhat stock in the genre. The ending's "not entirely gone" is a slightly tidy note of preserved selfhood, though it avoids full incongruence. Some metaphors ("a metronome made of people," "violence done politely") are excellent; a few ("eyes too loud") strain slightly. The piece is compact and purposeful, with no meandering. Class anxiety and culture shock are present but somewhat lighter than the prompt demanded—the scholarship letter detail carries most of that weight. Overall, this is disciplined, vivid, and coherent work that fulfills nearly all prompt requirements with craft.
