Model Output:
The gallery was mostly empty. Dreams, when summoned as evidence, preferred not to attend their own trials. Dream sat the bench as if the marble had grown him. His robe did not so much fall as refuse to be elsewhere. A fly circled the empty witness stand, thought better of it, and became a footnote. “First Love,” he said. “State the injury.” The plaintiff rose, rosy to the ears, clutching a sheaf of wildflowers that kept trying to be a bouquet and failing out of nerves. “My lord. A recurring dream. A field. A boy named Max. A girl he has not yet found the courage to name aloud. They lie among the flowers. They nearly kiss. They do not. He wakes fond, and slightly stupid, which is the correct outcome. I have tended this for eleven nights.” “Eleven,” Dream said, in the tone of a man counting grains of sand he had already counted. “Mora entered on the twelfth.” From the dock came a sound like dry twigs agreeing with each other. Mora was small in the way a closed fist is small. Her cackle did not stay with her. It went up into the vaults and came back wearing someone else’s voice. “A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” First Love flushed harder, which was unfortunate, as it made him look guilty of something gentler. “She waits until the girl leans over him. Playful. Then the dream bends. Weight. No air. The almost-kiss becomes a mouth that is not kissing. He cannot move. She takes the breath he was going to use on a sentence he would have regretted.” “Feeding,” Mora said, reasonably. “On a sleeper’s spare air. He has plenty. He was going to waste it on poetry.” “It was not poetry,” First Love said. “It was going to be her name, wrong.” Dream’s mouth did almost nothing. An observer who had watched him since the first court might have called it irritation. The fly, now a marginal note, underlined itself. “The dreamscape is claimed by craft,” First Love said, finding his footing and immediately losing it. “I built the field. I placed the hour. I allowed the muddle. Ownership follows work.” “Ownership follows hunger,” Mora said. “He was already on his back. I improved the posture.” A clerk, who was also a moth, read the charge into the record: trespass, subversion of a recurring dream, unlicensed terror, and one count of confusing attractiveness, which the clerk declined to define. Dream turned his head a fraction. The vaults pretended not to echo. “Show it.” The field arrived without asking. Knee-high flowers. Late light. Max, school-thin, staring at a girl as if she were a difficult sum. Their faces drew near. The kiss failed, as commissioned. Pleasant confusion rose off him like heat. Then the girl settled across his chest with the unhurried certainty of weather. Her smile stayed. The rest of her remembered older work. Max’s arms did not answer him. His breath left in small, polite amounts. Somewhere under the terror, embarrassingly, he still wanted to know her name. First Love looked at his shoes. Mora’s cackle toured the ceiling and sat down again, satisfied. “Your defense,” Dream said. “Practical,” Mora said. “First loves are rich. All that held breath. I don’t take the dream. I take the tax. He still wakes thinking of her. I only make sure he wakes.” “He wakes afraid.” “Afraid is a kind of awake.” She tilted her head. “And he liked the weight. A little. That’s not my fault. That’s his.” First Love made a wounded noise. “The muddle was meant to be kind.” “Kind is a seasoning,” Mora said. “Not a meal.” Dream was silent long enough for the flowers in evidence to consider wilting and decide against it. He disliked this sort of docket. Borders. Appetites. Entities who spoke as if the Dreaming were a market stall. He disliked, more, the neatness of both arguments. Work against hunger. Neither was false. Both were rude. Mischief arrived the way it always did with him: not as a grin, but as a correction no one had requested. “The field remains the work of First Love,” he said. “The hour, the flowers, the failed kiss. Mora will not unmake them.” First Love brightened, doomed. “However,” Dream went on, “a sleeper who offers his breath to a sentence he cannot finish has created a vacancy. Vacancies may be tenanted. Mora may attend on the twelfth night, and only the twelfth, and only after the kiss has failed. She may take one breath. Not the name. Not the waking. One breath, no heavier than the sentence he did not say.” Mora’s cackle started, then snagged. “And,” Dream said, “she will wear the form of the field while she does it. Flowers. Light. The girl’s face, unaltered. If the boy is to be confused, let him be confused by what was already his. Terror that borrows another’s craft is theft. Terror that must sit inside a kindness and still feed—that is a craft of its own. We will see if she is equal to it.” First Love opened his mouth. Closed it. The rosy had gone somewhere more complicated. Mora stared at the bench. “That’s not eating. That’s dining with the family.” “Yes,” Dream said. “He’ll think it was still her.” “He already does.” The evidence-field folded itself away, taking the almost-kiss with it, and the small unpaid breath. In the vaults, Mora’s cackle tried the old route, found the stone newly uninterested, and came back thinner, as if it had been asked to mind its manners. “Court is adjourned,” Dream said. The fly finished its footnote and died of completion. First Love left still holding flowers that had finally become a bouquet, and hated that this felt like a victory. Mora remained a moment in the dock, weighing one permitted breath against an infinite appetite, and discovering, with faint professional disgust, that she was already planning the twelfth night’s table manners. Dream did not watch them go. Irritation settled back into the marble, where it kept better than mercy, and almost as long.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of understated dark comedy. The prose is economical and controlled, with a distinctive voice that captures Gaiman-esque dryness well ("His robe did not so much fall as refuse to be elsewhere"). The courtroom farce works: charges like "confusing attractiveness, which the clerk declined to define" land well. Dream's irritation is conveyed through restraint rather than statement, and the resolution—forcing Mora to feed while wearing the field's kindness—is a genuinely clever piece of mischief that satisfies the prompt's requirement. Dialogue is sharp and character-revealing, especially Mora's "Afraid is a kind of awake." The ending's ambivalence (First Love's "hated that this felt like a victory," Mora's "professional disgust") avoids incongruent positivity. Minor flaws: a few aphorisms strain slightly ("Kind is a seasoning. Not a meal"), and the fly/footnote conceit is a touch precious. The word count is under the 1000-word seed but the piece feels complete. Character nuance is high for a short comedic scene; emotional complexity is present but bounded by the piece's brevity and comic register. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 78.2
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The moon hangs low and red, bloating the sky above the empty village until the rooftops look drowned in old blood. Alucard walks the street as if the silence belongs to him. His coat drags the dust. Orange glass hides his eyes. Somewhere a shutter knocks, once, and then thinks better of it. He smells her before he sees her: lilac cut with something green and sharp, wrong for this place, wrong for the century. Magic. Not the thin, church-scented kind. Older. Hungrier. Yennefer stands in the square where the well has gone dry. Violet eyes take him in without flinching—the hat, the guns, the way the moonlight refuses to sit properly on his shoulders. “You’re late,” she says. He laughs, low. “I wasn’t invited.” “Everything that feeds comes when the moon looks like that.” She doesn’t step back. Her hands stay loose at her sides, but the air around them has already gone thin, ready. “I felt you from the ridge. You don’t bother hiding.” “Hiding is for things that can die badly.” He tips his head, studying the line of her throat, the careful architecture of a face that was not always this face. “You rebuilt yourself. I can taste the seams.” Her mouth tightens. “And you wear yours like jewelry. How original.” They circle. Boots on packed earth. His shadow stretches wrong, too many limbs for a moment, then obedient again. She tracks it without comment. A crow startles from a chimney and doesn’t return. “Sorceress,” he says, almost pleased. “You could burn this village to glass and still look bored. I respect that.” “I don’t need your respect.” Lilac and gooseberries, closer now as the wind shifts. She hates that she notices the cold rolling off him—not winter, not night, something that has forgotten what warmth is and enjoys the forgetting. “You’re a corpse that learned manners. Barely.” “Manners?” The guns gleam when he shifts his coat. Silver in the cylinders, blessed and useless against what she is, which only makes him happier. “I eat what disappoints me. That’s a kind of honesty.” “Honesty.” She almost smiles. It doesn’t reach her eyes. “You want someone who can hurt you. I can hear it. All that power, and you’re still begging the dark for a door.” The red moon paints her cheekbones the color of a wound. Alucard’s grin shows too many teeth, then remembers itself. “And you want a child the magic took,” he says, soft as a knife laid down. “Centuries of bending the world, and one small mercy stays shut. Don’t look so offended. Monsters recognize the empty places.” For a heartbeat the square goes white-hot at the edges—her power, insulted, rising. Windows shiver in their frames. He doesn’t raise a hand. He wants to see if she’ll spend it. She doesn’t. The light dies back into crimson. Control, vicious and exact. He exhales like a man who’s been offered wine. “There,” he murmurs. “That’s better than screaming.” “I don’t scream for audiences.” Yennefer steps in until the brim of his hat shadows her face. Up close he is wrong in every proportion that matters: beautiful the way a blade is beautiful, interested the way a cat is interested in a bird that might still have a trick. Revulsion moves through her, clean and honest. Under it, fascination, which she trusts less. “If you came to feed, choose something that won’t unmake you for the attempt.” “If I came to feed, you’d already be quiet.” His voice drops. “I came because the night tasted like a challenge. You reek of one.” “Flattery from a leech.” She lifts two fingers. A sigil ghosts in the air between them, violet as her eyes, then folds away before he can read it. Not an attack. A measurement. His regeneration prickles under it like skin remembering fire. “You’re not local. You’re not even properly of this age. Something dragged you across the years the way a storm drags ships.” “Hellsing will scold me,” he says, delighted. “Let them. I was bored.” “Bored monsters burn villages.” She glances at the dead windows, the doors barred from inside by people who knew enough to hide and not enough to run. “These ones are hiding from both of us. Try not to disappoint them by being ordinary.” He laughs again, and this time it sounds almost human, which is worse. “Ordinary. From you. Careful, witch. I’ll start to like you.” “Don’t.” The word is flat. She means it, and she doesn’t, and she hates the second truth more. His nature repels her—the casual sadism, the joy in being the thing in the dark—but the power does not. Power never has. It recognizes itself across species, across sins. “Liking me has a cost. So does underestimating me.” “I don’t underestimate anything that smells like it could end me.” He leans in, sunglasses reflecting her own uncompromising face. “The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame. You understand that, don’t you? The hunger that chews its own escape.” Yennefer holds his gaze. The moon throbs overhead, a crimson harvest with no one left in the fields to fear it. “I’m not sweet,” she says, quiet, precise, “and I’m not a maiden in distress in need of saving. If you want a game, vampire, play it standing up. The moment you treat me like prey, I stop being curious.” “Curious.” He tastes the word. Approval, dangerous and bright, moves behind the glass. “Then we understand each other.” They stand in the square, neither yielding the last step, the deserted street stretching away under a moon the color of an open vein. Somewhere a dog refuses to bark. The night waits to see which of them blinks. Neither does.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a taut, atmospheric standoff that fulfills the prompt's central dynamic: two predators circling, neither yielding. Present tense, third person is maintained throughout, and the ~1000 word length is respected. Both characters are recognizable—Alucard's sadistic playfulness and death-wish ("begging the dark for a door") and Yennefer's control, vanity, and hidden grief over her infertility are used as levers against each other. The famous quotes are integrated naturally rather than pasted in, which is a mark of craft. The prose is controlled and image-rich: "moonlight refuses to sit properly on his shoulders," "a moon the color of an open vein." Dialogue crackles with mutual probing and threat. Weaknesses: the piece is essentially one scene of verbal sparring with no escalation or resolution—the ending is a static tableau ("Neither does"), which feels slightly like a shrug rather than a payoff. Some metaphors strain ("beautiful the way a blade is beautiful" is stock; "a knife laid down" is fine but "soft as a knife laid down" muddles). The rhythm of short declarative sentences ("She tracks it without comment.") becomes a tic. Yennefer's interiority is occasionally told rather than shown ("Revulsion moves through her... Under it, fascination"). Alucard instantly diagnosing her infertility is a convenient omniscience that short-circuits how he'd know. The "measurement" sigil is a nice beat but the piece flirts with repetitive exchanges in the middle third. Overall, however, this is skilled, disciplined fan-fiction-level writing with genuine tension and character fidelity—engaging, coherent, and largely avoiding melodrama. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The overhead light stutters, dies, and returns in a thin yellow wash. Jolyne stops beneath it. The corridor smells of bleach and something older, like iron left in rain. Her butterfly tattoo itches under the sleeve. She has been walking this wing for twenty minutes and the numbers on the doors do not change. A woman stands at the far end, hands folded, as if she has been waiting for the light to settle. “You must be lost,” the woman says. Soft. Almost kind. Auburn hair, eyes the color of old coins. “This block isn’t for visitors.” “I’m not a visitor.” Jolyne’s voice comes out rougher than she means. “And you’re not a guard. Guards don’t smile like they’re selling something.” Makima tilts her head. The smile does not move. “You’re observant. Most people here stop looking after the first week. They decide the walls are the only story left.” “Yeah, well, the walls here are lying.” Jolyne takes one step closer and feels the air tighten, not with Stand pressure exactly—something thinner, like a leash drawn taut just out of sight. Stone Free stirs under her skin, string ready at the fingertips. “Who are you?” “Makima.” She says it the way other people say please. “I work with difficult cases. People who refuse to be improved.” “Improved.” Jolyne laughs once, ugly. “That’s a cute word for whatever you’re doing. I’ve met types like you. Sweet voice, dirty hands. You want something. Spit it out.” Makima’s gaze drops to Jolyne’s wrist, where a single green thread has already slipped free and curled like a question. Interest lights behind the rings in her eyes—not warmth. Appetite. “Your ability,” she says. “It isn’t a devil. It isn’t a contract. It comes from you, and it answers only you. I find that… inconvenient. And rare.” “Stone Free isn’t for sale.” “I didn’t say I wanted to buy it.” Makima steps forward. The flickering light steadies, as if embarrassed to interrupt. “I want to understand the terms. Everyone has terms. Fear. Loyalty. A name they can’t stand to hear broken. Yours is louder than most. You shout so no one can hear you ask to be believed.” Jolyne’s jaw locks. The string at her wrist thickens, splits, becomes a net between her fingers. “You don’t know me.” “I know the shape of people who have been framed,” Makima says gently. “They grip the truth so hard their hands bleed, and then they thank anyone who pretends to see the blood. I could be that person. I could also be the reason the blood was there. Both are useful.” The corridor seems longer now. Doors Jolyne passed are gone. In their place are hooks, empty, waiting. She feels the first real cold of it: not a threat of pain, a rearrangement. Makima is not raising her voice because she does not need to. The prison is already listening. “Cute trick,” Jolyne says. She unravels her left arm to the elbow in a hiss of thread and lashes it around a pipe, anchoring herself to something that still feels solid. “You talk like the building’s yours. News flash—I’ve broken out of worse with less. You want a contract? I don’t do leashes. I don’t do owners. And if you think you can put me under you because I swear and throw punches, you’re reading the wrong girl.” Makima’s smile thins by a degree. “Dogs don’t have to like the leash. They only have to stop running when I say stop.” “I’m not your dog.” “Not yet.” Jolyne moves. Stone Free punches through the string of her own arm and drives at Makima’s throat—not to kill, to test, to make the sweetness crack. The fist meets nothing that yields. Makima is simply not where the blow arrives. She is one step to the left, unruffled, as if the attack were a courtesy she had already accepted. “There,” Makima murmurs. “That impulse. You would die for the people you choose, and you would kill to keep the choice yours. That is a beautiful chain. I don’t even have to forge it. I only have to hold the end.” Jolyne yanks herself sideways on the pipe-line, boots skidding, and the net of string snaps shut around the space Makima occupied. It closes on air and a single fallen hair, auburn, which the threads refuse to cut. The hair lies in the web like a signature. Makima watches it with something like fondness. “You see? Even your power wants to keep pieces of me. That’s how it starts. Curiosity. Then a favor. Then a name you say when you’re afraid, because saying it feels like being held.” “Keep talking,” Jolyne says, breathing hard, string reeling back into skin with a burn she welcomes. “Every word tells me where not to stand.” “And every refusal tells me where you will.” Makima lifts a hand. Down the corridor, something answers—a shuffle, a collar’s faint ring, too many footsteps for the doors that remain. “This facility keeps what cannot be corrected by ordinary means. You were sent here because someone needed you contained. I can offer a cleaner story than the one that put you in a cell. All I ask is that you look at me and admit you are tired of being the only one who fights clean.” Jolyne stares at the ringed eyes and feels the pull, soft as a hand on the back of the neck. For a second the light stops flickering. For a second she wants the quiet Makima is selling: no frame-up, no blood on a steering wheel that wasn’t hers, no father on the other side of a silence she can’t punch through. She spits on the concrete between them. “If there’s no Mickey,” she says, voice low and bright with fury, “this shit ain’t Disney. You don’t get to dress up a cage and call it mercy. You don’t get my Stand, my friends, or my name on your little list of pets. You want a war of words? Fine. I’ll unravel every pretty sentence until there’s nothing left but the hook.” Makima’s pleasantness does not break. It settles, colder, more precise. “Then we’ll continue,” she says. “Prisons are patient. So am I. And you—” her gaze flicks to the butterfly, to the string still trembling at Jolyne’s knuckles, “—you are exactly the kind of trouble that makes control worth perfecting.” The light dies again. When it returns, Makima is closer, and the hooks along the wall are no longer empty. Jolyne plants her feet, Stone Free singing in her bones, and does not look away. Neither of them blinks first.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong crossover piece that captures both characters effectively. Jolyne's suspicion, foul-mouthed defiance, and Stone Free usage feel authentic, and Makima's soft menace and control-oriented dialogue ring true to her character. The famous quote is integrated naturally rather than shoehorned. The prose is controlled, atmospheric, and largely shows rather than tells—Makima's menace comes through imagery (hooks, leashes, the light steadying) rather than exposition. The battle of wits escalates credibly, and the ending's standoff is appropriately unresolved without being falsely positive. Minor weaknesses: some metaphors flirt with overwrought territory ("a beautiful chain. I don't even have to forge it. I only have to hold the end"—though this is actually effective). A few lines lean slightly literary for Jolyne's POV. The piece is somewhat predictable in structure (suspicion → probing → attack → stalemate), but the execution elevates it. Length is roughly on target. Third person present tense is maintained throughout. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 57.8
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
I found the first note on a Tuesday, under the blotter in my office at Site-19. It was standard Foundation memo paper, the pale stock with the watermark in the corner, and the handwriting was mine. "Do not open the secondary airlock on Sublevel 4 after 03:17. The seals fail from the inside. I am you. You will not believe this. Believe it anyway." I had not written it. My pen was capped. The pad in my drawer was blank. I logged the page and turned it over to Temporal Anomalies. Fiber analysis matched our current pulp lot. The ink was Foundation issue. My fingerprints were on the margins. No one else's. Dr. Lang from Psychology asked whether I had been sleeping. I said I had. She wrote something down and did not show me. The second note was inside a locked drawer I had not opened since Monday. Same paper. Same hand, leaning harder. "Lang will say it is a contained entity. She is wrong. The entity does not write. I write. The breach starts with a smell like hot copper. Burn the secondary seals before Thursday." Thursday was three days off. When I showed her the page, a black bar covered a designation I was sure had not been there. She said the bar had always been there. I was sure it had not. They sealed my office and moved me to observation. I locked the room's memo pad in the wall safe and gave Security the combination. I did not touch a pen. On Wednesday night the safe stood open. One sheet lay on the floor. My handwriting had worsened; some letters doubled, and the pen had torn the paper. "THEY WILL SAY YOU WROTE THESE IN YOUR SLEEP. YOU DID NOT. I AM PAST THE BREACH. THE LIGHTS ON SUBLEVEL 4 STAY RED. LANG IS NOT LANG AFTER 02:40. DO NOT LOOK AT HER HANDS." I left it and called from the hall. When Security arrived, the safe was shut and showed no tamper. The note was on my pillow. No one had entered on camera. The timestamp jumped forty seconds, which Temporal logged and Psychology called an artifact. Lang visited with her hands in her lap. They looked like hands. I watched them anyway. The site split into two theories and argued them in memos I was no longer cleared to read. Copies still appeared on my tray, always on the same paper, always in my hand. Temporal called it a closed loop, localized to cellulose stock issued to Site-19. Future instances of me were laying down ink without moving mass. They isolated me from every pad they could find. Inscription never appeared on other media. Notes kept arriving on Foundation memo paper, including sheets locked in archival drawers below me, sheets whose serial numbers Logistics said had not been issued. Later Logistics corrected the ledger. They said the numbers had always been issued. I had seen the blank range. Psychology called it intrusion by a sapient in Humanoid Wing that had learned my script from old reports. They pointed at the contradictions. One note said the breach would vent halon. Another, found the same hour in a sealed sleeve, said halon had been gone since 2019 and that I was remembering a site that did not exist. A third insisted I had a sister named Mara. I do not. The file they showed me later listed a sibling, deceased, whose photograph was my face at twelve with the hair wrong. I stopped being sure which file I had seen first. The notes degraded. Verbs dropped out. Margins filled with tallies I could not read. One said only, "you already opened it." Another, "copper." A third looped until the letters stacked into a dark band: "i am still writing the paper is the only thing that crosses they will call it illness because illness is cheaper than a rewrite of thursday." Thursday came. I did not go near Sublevel 4. At 03:17 I sat on the observation floor and counted my breaths. No alarm. No copper. Lang entered at 03:40 with coffee and ordinary hands and said the night had been quiet. I wanted to believe her so badly that the wanting felt like a symptom. At 04:02 a note was under the cup. I had watched the cup the entire time. "Quiet is how it starts when you listen to them. I was wrong about the airlock. I am wrong about more every time I cross. Trust the fear, not the details. The details rot in transit. Do not let them file you." They filed me anyway. The report I was allowed to read offered three phrases at once: a possible temporal echo, a possible cognito-hazard vector, or an acute dissociative break. It recommended isolation from standard memo stock. They took the paper away. Notes arrived on paper they had taken away. A technician swore a sealed blank sheet developed letters on the evidence table. The video showed it already written. He recanted by evening. I did not know if he had been corrected or if the second memory was the true one. I stopped reading the notes. That did not stop me from knowing what they said. The knowledge arrived like a taste. Hot copper. In the mirror my mouth was clean, then bloody, then I could not say which look had come first. On the seventh night I wrote nothing. I held my hands as Lang did. A sheet of memo paper lay on the desk when I lifted my eyes. The safe was in another room. The words were almost gone, a pressure of graphite that resolved only if I refused to focus. "if you can still tell the difference you are earlier than i was. i am sorry. i keep making it worse by warning you. they were right that something is using the paper. they were wrong that it is not also me." I folded it and did not call anyone. Outside the glass, the corridor lights were white. I thought I remembered them red. I could not decide whether that memory was mine or belonged to the hand that kept finding the only paper the Foundation trusted enough to leave everywhere, locked or not. I sat with the fold in my palm and waited to learn which of us was lying.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of the SCP-adjacent premise, told in first person, past tense, with interspersed notes as requested. The researcher's voice is clipped, procedural, and quietly unraveling — well matched to Foundation documentation culture. The escalating desperation of the notes is handled well: from coherent warnings to degraded fragments ("you already opened it," "copper," the stacked dark band of text). The contradictions with known reality (the sister Mara, the halon discrepancy, the redacted designation, the ledger corrections) effectively blur temporal anomaly against psychological manipulation, and the Foundation's two competing theories are given institutional texture without over-explaining. Strengths: the prose is restrained and precise; the ambiguity is sustained rather than resolved; the ending ("waited to learn which of us was lying") lands with earned unease. The detail of the paper being the only medium that crosses is a nice unifying conceit. The mirror/blood moment and the technician's recantation deepen the epistemic horror. Weaknesses: the piece is somewhat compressed relative to the 1000-word seed (it runs near that, acceptable). Some beats are familiar to the genre — the "trust the fear, not the details" note is a bit on-the-nose; the Thursday non-breach followed by the note under the cup is effective but the pattern of note-arrival scenes grows slightly repetitive. Dialogue is minimal and functional; Lang is thin as a character, though this is partly the form. The "I am wrong about more every time I cross" line does good work explaining the contradictions. Occasional sentences verge on over-compression, but never purple. The ending's darkness is earned. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7841 **Object Class:** Keter **Special Containment Procedures:** All known instances of SCP-7841-A are to be sealed with welded steel plates and monitored by remote sensors. Discovery of a new instance requires immediate lockdown of the host structure. Exploration of SCP-7841-B is suspended pending O5 review. Personnel whose files appear in the archive are not to be informed. **Description:** SCP-7841-A designates a series of identical unmarked wooden doors that manifest in abandoned buildings worldwide. Each door is unpainted, lacks hardware branding, and bears the same cluster of fine scratches around the knob—four short arcs, always in the same order, as if made by the same hand. Doors do not correspond to any room on building plans. Opening one leads to SCP-7841-B, a single continuous archive whose interior dimensions exceed the exterior of every host structure combined. SCP-7841-B is lit by failing fluorescent fixtures. Aisles of steel shelving recede past line of sight. Floors change level without stairs. Corridors rejoin themselves at angles that survey teams cannot reconcile. Air is dry and smells of paper and solvent. No external exits have been found except the door used to enter, which remains fixed in place relative to the explorer and not to the building. Documents in SCP-7841-B are typewritten, stamped, and filed under an organization styled the **Continuance Office**. Language, formats, and classification marks closely resemble Foundation practice. Several files name current Foundation staff and list birth dates centuries before those individuals were born. Others describe a prior global civilization ended by “an unspecified containment failure.” The failure is never named. Margins are often blacked out by a later hand. Mobile teams have observed figures in yellow impermeable suits, full-face respirators, and unmarked harnesses (SCP-7841-C). They remove boxes, wipe shelves, and retreat when approached. They do not speak. Pursuit ends at a turn that was not present on the inbound map. Recovered access logs, visitor chits, and a partial camera still indicate that at least three sitting O5 Council members have entered SCP-7841-B without logged authorization. None have acknowledged the visits. **Exploration Log 7841-7** **Team:** MTF Zeta-9 (“Mole Rats”), four members **Entry:** Door instance, derelict textile mill, Łódź The team passed the threshold at 02:14. The scratches around the knob matched photographs from doors in Recife, Busan, and a collapsed school outside Flagstaff. Inside, the mill’s brick gave way at once to painted cinder block and a directory board whose plastic letters read CONTINUANCE — LEVEL ∅ — RETENTION. They moved in column. Radios carried, but range collapsed after ninety meters. At the first junction the floor dropped half a step that had not been there when the point man crossed it. Specialist Okonkwo marked the wall with chalk. Twenty meters later the same mark appeared on their left, fresher, the chalk still dusting the air. Shelving here held personnel jackets. Lt. Rahman opened one at random. The name on the tab was his own. The photograph showed him older, in a uniform he did not recognize, dated 1841. A duty roster beneath it listed his current squad leader as “seconded from the prior Office, retained.” Rahman replaced the file. No one spoke. At aisle 14-C they heard casters. Three SCP-7841-C instances were stripping a bay: boxes onto a cart, shelf labels peeled, a solvent wipe over the bare metal. Their suits were identical, down to a tear at the left elbow patched with the same gray tape. When Rahman called a halt, all three turned. The nearest raised a gloved hand—not a threat, a refusal—and they pushed the cart into a side passage that the team’s mapper insisted was a wall. By the time Zeta-9 reached the corner, the passage was shelving again, empty, smelling of solvent. Chalk on the endcap read, in a hand none of them claimed: DO NOT FOLLOW THE REMOVAL. They did not. On the return, Okonkwo’s first chalk mark was gone. In its place was a visitor chit, unstamped, bearing an O5 seal and a time two hours ahead of the team’s watches. **Recovered Document 7841-R-12** (excerpt, Continuance Office jacket, partially redacted by an unknown later hand) Retention Memorandum, Office of the Twelve Subject: Prior civilization — terminal event The prior civilization did not fall to war, climate, or plague in any sense our instruments can separate from the event itself. It fell when a contained thing was no longer contained. The failure is not to be specified in open jackets. Specification is how it travels. What remains of their cities is not ruin. It is absence filed under ruin. Their offices burned their own names. We kept the method and changed the letterhead. Personnel who appear in both registries are not duplicates. They are continuations who have not yet been told they continued. Do not brief them. Briefing is a form of specification. **Recovered Document 7841-R-19** (excerpt, access addendum, undated) Visitor: [O5-██] Declared purpose: none Escort: refused Sections requested: Retention, prior Office, own jacket Note in margin, different ink: He already knew which aisle. He did not open his jacket. He stood with his hand on the shelf as if counting what was missing. When Removal arrived he did not order them to stop. He stepped aside. Second note, same hand as the elbow-tape patch description in Log 7841-3: Removal does not delete. Removal returns. What they take is already gone in the building we think we left. The scratches on the knob are not wear. They are a signature, cut once, and copied onto every door so we will recognize the way back and mistake it for coincidence. **Exploration Log 7841-7, addendum** At the door, the team found the scratches bright, as if just made. On the interior face, where no one had looked on entry, a strip of archive tape held a single line, typewritten: You are not the first Foundation. You are the file that has not yet been pulled. Okonkwo photographed it. The image, once offloaded, showed only the tape. The words were gone. In the mill, the welded plate installed the next day bore, by morning, four short arcs around a knob that was no longer there. Word count: approximately 1000.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong SCP entry that hits every required element: identical doors worldwide, impossible archive, prior civilization destroyed by unspecified containment failure, Continuance Office as Foundation precursor, personnel files dated centuries ago, hazmat-like removal entities who flee, and O5 visits without authorization. The third-person exploration team perspective with recovered document excerpts is executed properly, and length is on target. The piece's greatest strength is its restraint and implication-driven horror. Details like the four scratch arcs as a "signature," the chalk mark reappearing fresher, Rahman finding his own file dated 1841, and the final typewritten line that vanishes from photographs all work through understatement. The recovered documents are genuinely chilling—"Specification is how it travels" is an excellent conceit, and "You are not the first Foundation. You are the file that has not yet been pulled" is a memorable closer. The prose is clean, clinical where it should be, and avoids purple excess. The non-Euclidean geometry is conveyed economically ("floors change level without stairs," "corridors rejoin themselves at angles"). The removal entities are handled well—the raised gloved hand as "not a threat, a refusal" is a nice touch. Weaknesses: the exploration team is functional rather than characterized; Rahman's reaction to his own file ("replaced the file. No one spoke.") is effective but the team members are otherwise thin. The O5 margin notes are slightly over-explanatory in places—the second note in R-19 spells out the door-scratch theory a bit too neatly, edging toward telling. The "word count" line at the end is a minor artifact. Some ideas (the elbow-tape matching hand) feel slightly contrived connective tissue. Dialogue is essentially absent, which is fine for the format. Overall this is a polished, professional-grade SCP entry with strong conceptual payoff and disciplined execution. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The market had no walls, only the shade of awnings and the cooler dark under the old stone arches. Hain walked there with her hands empty and her translator switched off, which was against the brief and therefore, she had decided, necessary. The brief had described the city as stratified: upper terraces for the long-limbed, pale-skinned branch; lower streets for the stockier, darker-skinned branch; and a third, thinner population of the coastal type who were said to keep to the docks. It had used the word subspecies with the careful distaste of people who wished not to have invented it. What she saw was a woman selling dried fish to a man whose wrists were twice as thick as her own, and both of them laughing at a price. A child with the wide chest of the lower streets ran between stalls carrying a string of copper bells for a woman whose fingers were long and jointed like a bird’s. No one looked twice. Or rather, they looked as people look at a stranger: at the cut of Hain’s coat, at the offworld pallor of her face, at the way she did not know which hand to offer when a seller held out a sample of salt. The salt was grey and smelled of iron. She bought a pinch of it because refusal would have been ruder than ignorance, and stood under an arch eating it from her palm while the city moved around her. The arch was carved. She had been told the carvings were decorative, pre-Contact, of no political significance. Up close they were not decorative. A figure with too many arms held a ship above a wave. Beside it, a woman turned her face away from a garden and became, in the next panel, a tree. Further along, two brothers—one light, one dark, though the stone had weathered so that the difference was mostly in the depth of the cut—stood on either side of a door and would not look at each other. Old Earth, then. Myths carried in the holds of the first ships and set into the walls so that the people who came after would not have to remember the stories, only the shapes. A man stopped beside her. He was of the coastal type, narrow through the shoulders, with the faint webbing still visible between thumb and forefinger that the brief had called a vestigial trait and the medical annex had called an adaptation to cold water. He looked at the brothers. “They say the door is shut,” he said, in the trade language, slowly, so she would understand. “But the stone is the same stone. You see? One block. They cut the figures apart and left the wall whole. Someone’s joke, maybe.” “Or someone’s hope,” Hain said. He considered this with the seriousness of a person who sold things for a living and therefore did not waste agreement. “Hope costs more,” he said, and went on. She walked until the light changed and the awnings came down, and then she walked back by the long stair that the brief had said was closed to mixed traffic after dusk. It was not closed. People climbed it in both directions, carrying baskets, arguing, holding children by the wrist. A pair of city watchers stood at the landing and did not stop anyone. One of them nodded to her, not unkindly, as if to say: we see you, offworlder, and we have decided you are not today’s problem. In her quarters the lamps were already lit. Command was waiting, which meant the reprimand had been composed in advance and her absence had only confirmed it. “You were not at the reception,” said the voice from the wall unit. It was a woman’s voice, tired, from the ship in orbit. “The Minister asked for you. We told him you were indisposed. Do not make us liars twice.” “The reception was a briefing with wine,” Hain said. “I have read the briefing.” “You have read our briefing. He has another. Go and hear it. And Hain—stay on the routes we gave you. The city is not a text for you to interpret on your own time. You are not an anthropologist. You are a mouth.” The unit clicked off. Hain washed the salt from her hands and put on the coat that meant she was official, and went down through corridors that smelled of polish and recycled air to the room where the Minister of Science kept his political posting. He was older than the file had suggested, and smaller, and he had the long hands of the upper terraces, though he sat as if he had learned not to display them. The room was stone, like the market arches, and the far wall carried the same carving of the woman becoming a tree. Someone had set a lamp so that the leaves threw shadows over his shoulder. “Envoy,” he said. “You missed the fish. It was very good fish. Caught by people your brief calls a subspecies and served by people your brief calls the other one. I find the distinctions difficult to taste.” “I walked in the market,” Hain said. “I saw the distinctions. I did not see them where I was told they would be.” “Ah.” He poured tea. He did not offer her the seat until she had taken it, which was a small cruelty and also a test. “So you have already begun to correct us. That is efficient. Most envoys wait until the second week.” “I was sent to address tensions. If the tensions are not where the brief places them, I need to know where they are.” “They are where they are useful,” he said. “To us, sometimes. To your Command, sometimes. To the people in the market, less often, which is why they ignore them when they can. You saw the watchers on the stair. Did they stop you?” “No.” “They stopped a fight last night between two cousins who both claim the lower streets and both have cousins in the upper. Blood, Envoy. Not lineage. A debt over a net. Your people will enter it in the log as sectarian violence and adjust the threat assessment, and I will spend a morning explaining that a net is not a constitution. This is my science. I minister to the gap between what is observed and what is needed.” He watched her over the cup. The lamp made his eyes difficult to read. “You want me to report the brief as wrong,” she said. “I want to know whether you can hear a thing and not immediately become its courier. Your Command believes divergence is the problem and reconciliation is the product. They have a timeline. I have a city that has been diverging and un-diverging for eleven generations, according to whether the fishing was good and whether anyone was fool enough to govern by myth. Look at the wall.” She looked. The woman, the garden, the tree. “On Earth that story was a punishment,” he said. “Here the masons carved it as a choice. She turns away. She becomes something that can feed others. Your people read it as evidence of cultural retention. My opponents read it as proof that the upper terraces think themselves the garden and the rest of us the wood. Both readings are available. Neither is the stone.” “And what do you read?” “I read a wall that has not fallen. I am asking whether you can be sent into a room and come out with fewer certainties than you carried in. If you cannot, you will be very successful here, and you will do harm, and you will be promoted. If you can, you will be difficult, and you may be of use, and your Command will eventually replace you with someone who missed fewer receptions.” Hain set her cup down. The tea was bitter and clear. Outside, beyond the thick stone, she could hear the last of the market bells and, under them, the sea, which did not sort its waves by lineage. “The man in the market said the brothers were cut apart and the wall was left whole,” she said. “He thought it might be a joke.” The Minister smiled for the first time, a small, exact thing, not offered for comfort. “Then you were listening,” he said. “Good. Tomorrow you will sit with me while I tell your Command that the tensions are contained. You will not contradict me in the room. Afterward you may walk wherever you like, and you may decide what contained means, and whether a mouth is also allowed to have been in a street. That is the test, Envoy. Not whether you are brave enough to disobey. Whether you are patient enough to know which disobedience still serves the people who did not ask for you.” He stood. The interview was over because he had ended it, not because she had answered. Hain rose, and for a moment they were both reflected in the polished stone beneath the carving: two figures, different in height and hand and history, standing on the same block, not yet cut apart, not yet reconciled, only present. “I will be there,” she said. “I know,” said the Minister of Science, who was not a scientist. “That is why I asked for you, and not for the one who would have stayed at the reception.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece that captures Le Guin's anthropological sensibility, measured prose, and thematic preoccupation with how observers distort what they observe. The market scene is the highlight: concrete, sensory (the grey iron-smelling salt, the copper bells, the webbed thumb), and it efficiently dramatizes the gap between briefing and reality without editorializing. The carved arch motif—brothers cut apart but the wall left whole—is a genuinely elegant central image, and it pays off structurally in the final reflection scene. The Minister's dialogue is mostly excellent: "I minister to the gap between what is observed and what is needed" is a fine line, and the net-versus-constitution exchange is sharp political texture. However, the dialogue occasionally tips into aphorism overload—"Hope costs more," "the sea, which did not sort its waves by lineage"—where every character speaks in polished epigrams. Le Guin's characters are more uneven than this; the uniform wit slightly flattens the voices and makes the market vendor implausibly poetic. The ending is a touch tidy and self-congratulatory ("That is why I asked for you"), and the final mirrored-image paragraph verges on over-neat symbolism. The reprimand scene is functional but the Command voice is thinner than the Minister's. Still, the piece is coherent, disciplined at roughly the requested length, follows every prompt beat (slipping away, market, reprimand, the political Minister, the test of wits), and resists the obvious reconciliation arc. The prose is restrained, showing rather than telling, with earned thematic weight. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 85.0
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The panel coughed light across the bench in uneven pulses, bright enough to silver the dust, then dim enough that Mara’s hands went gray. She didn’t look up. Voltage stories were for people who still had spare regulators. She had a contract, a thawing vial, and a settlement that had eaten the last of the true seed three weeks ago. The vial was labeled in a hand she didn’t trust: *Grainline, filial zero, cold-chain fiction.* Black-market shorthand for something that had once been a cultivar and was now a rumor with a half-life. Corporate seed had been built to forget itself. One generation of honest yield, then sterility, then the quiet arithmetic of repurchase. The collapse had not canceled the arithmetic. It had only removed the sales desk. Mara cracked the vial over a ceramic boat she’d fired from river clay and glazed with the last of a lab-grade slip. The slurry inside was the color of weak tea and already warming. Engineered genomes didn’t die like ordinary things. They frayed. Promoters silted up. Kill-switches that had been marketed as safety became weather. If she waited until the panel steadied, there would be nothing left worth amplifying. She fed the boat into the cycler, a pressure-cooker shell wound with salvaged heater wire and a thermistor stolen from a dead incubator. The lid sealed on a strip of bicycle inner tube. No clean room. No laminar hood. A sheet of builder’s plastic stapled to the ceiling did what it could with the drafts, which was not much. On the wall, a child’s thermometer and a kitchen timer stood in for the instrument her old lab would have called a protocol. She had stopped calling it that. Protocols assumed the world would hold still for thirty cycles. While the wire ticked, she checked the buyer’s terms again, scratched on the back of a nutrient invoice. *Viable grain. Enough to plant the lower field. Payment in antibiotics, lamp oil, and one course of marrow-patch.* The marrow-patch was the part that made her jaw tighten. Untested edits taken as medicine: a gray-market cassette meant to bully bone into making blood again after the rust-fever. She had used a cousin of it last winter, when her own counts crashed. It had worked, in the way a fire works. Three days of fever so high she dreamed in base pairs. Then a clarity she still didn’t like to name—nights when she could hear the panel’s flicker as a pitch, mornings when bruises mapped themselves before they surfaced. The settlement called it a blessing. She called it interest on a debt her cells were still paying. The cycler hiccuped. Voltage sagged; the heater wire dulled from orange to sullen red. Mara swore once, quietly, and thumbed the hand-crank generator until her shoulder burned. Jury-rigged science was mostly shoulders. The temperature climbed back into the band where copying was possible and damage was merely likely. She watched the clay boat through a warped inspection port and thought of the field below the ridge, already scratched open by people who trusted her more than they should. When the timer chirped—a sound like a trapped insect—she killed the heat and let the boat cool against a slab of roofing tin. Condensate beaded and ran into a groove she’d cut with a nail. The product, if it deserved the word, was a cloudy thread in a thumb’s width of buffer. She didn’t sequence it. She didn’t have a sequencer that still believed in bases. She had a strip of paper, a wick of antibody ink traded from a clinic that no longer admitted anyone, and the old gambler’s test: did the band appear where living grain used to announce itself? It did. Faint. Crooked. Alive enough to argue with. She aliquoted the thread into three glass capillaries stopped with wax, the way her teacher had done when the institute still had glass and teachers. Two capillaries went into a padded tin for the lower field’s starters—people who would nurse the copy through soil that remembered better crops. The third she held up to the stuttering panel. In that light it looked almost honest. The knock came as she was labeling the tin with a charcoal stub. Not the settlement knock, which was fists and hurry. This one was two taps, a pause, one tap: the market’s manners. “You’re early,” she said, without opening the inner curtain. “Voltage’s dying all down the ridge,” a voice answered. Woman’s, dry. “Figured your panel would lie to you before mine lied to me. You have it?” “I have a maybe that grows if nobody breathes on it wrong.” “That’s the vintage.” A soft laugh. “Obsolescence was the product. We’re just late customers.” Mara parted the curtain. The buyer wore a coat boiled down from a lab gown, pockets stiff with vials. One eye was milk-bright from an old edit gone decorative—night vision that had stuck halfway and now collected light like a wound. An upside, if you liked seeing in rooms that wanted you blind. A toll, if you liked sleeping. They traded on the bench between the cycler and the clay boats. Tin for a wrap of antibiotics, a flask of lamp oil that smelled faintly of oranges from some dead supply chain, and a sealed cassette no bigger than a finger joint: marrow-patch, batch unmarked. Mara didn’t open it. She knew the feel of the plastic, the way it warmed too fast in the hand, eager. “Your people,” the buyer said, nodding at the tin. “They’ll eat what comes up?” “They’ll eat,” Mara said. “If it breeds true, we eat next year without you. If it frays, we eat once and learn the shape of the mistake.” “Corporate would have called that a feature.” “Corporate isn’t here to invoice the feature.” The buyer’s milk eye tracked the flickering panel, then Mara’s hands, which had a tremor she no longer bothered to hide. Fever-echo. The patch she had taken still wrote small weather through her nerves when the voltage swung. Useful, sometimes: she felt a drop coming before the lights admitted it, and saved a run. Unuseful, always, at night, when her pulse tried to keep time with a machine that wasn’t in the room. “Next contract’s animal,” the buyer said, already turning. “Something that doesn’t forget how to calve. If your shoulders hold.” “Shoulders hold,” Mara said. “The genomes are the ones on a clock.” After the curtain fell, she sat with the cassette and did not take it. The lower field could wait until dawn to be seeded with a copy that might last a season or a lie. Outside, the ridge wind worried the plastic stapled over the vents. Inside, the panel found a few steady minutes and laid a clean bar of light across the bench, as if the world, briefly, intended to be reproduced. She labeled the tin in full, so no one would have to trust her memory: *Grainline. Copied under bad light. Plant anyway.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of biopunk flash fiction that hits nearly all prompt requirements: post-apocalyptic world with obsolescence-engineered seed, jury-rigged lab equipment (pressure-cooker PCR cycler, clay boats, bicycle inner tube gasket, hand-crank generator), physical toll and unexpected upsides of untested gene medicine (fever-echo tremor, premonitory sensitivity to voltage drops), and a black market contract as the plot's spine. Length is close to the 1000-word seed. Strengths: The prose is disciplined and evocative without tipping into purple. World-building is delivered through concrete objects and idiom ("cold-chain fiction," "a rumor with a half-life," "obsolescence was the product"). Mara is a nuanced character—competent, self-doubting, pragmatic, carrying ambivalence about her own body's edits. The buyer is efficiently characterized via the milk eye. Dialogue is terse and thematically loaded without being exposition-heavy. The ending resists false uplift: "Plant anyway" is a hard-earned, conditional hope. Weaknesses: The plot is thin—the contract resolves without real friction or stakes being tested; the buyer arrives, trades, leaves. Some metaphors crowd together ("worked, in the way a fire works" is good; "dreamed in base pairs" borders on cute). The thematic point about corporate obsolescence is stated a few too many times. The buyer's aphorisms ("We're just late customers") occasionally feel authorial. Minor contrivances: the antibody-ink test resolving neatly, the buyer's timing. But these are quibbles against a genuinely well-crafted piece. Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Arthur kept adjusting his collar. The fabric had been cut for a man who expected to be looked at, and Arthur Neegan had spent eleven years expecting only dust. The transfer vessel's lounge was a cylinder of pale metal and quieter engines, Mars falling away beneath a viewport no larger than a helmet plate. Someone had thought of everything except the habit of a miner's hands. "Leave it," said the woman across from him. She wore the Antares sunburst on a dark tunic, silver on charcoal, and had not given a name. "They will notice if you fidget. They notice everything else." "They," Arthur said. "You keep saying they. Your people took me off my own lease with three armed aides and a smile. I'd like a noun." "The Corps is a noun." She did not smile. "Diplomatic in the charter. Practical in the field. You were not arrested, Engineer Neegan. You were invited. The distinction matters to lawyers and to history, if either survives the decade." A soft chime moved through the hull. The stars outside did not so much appear as assert themselves when the glare of the planetary limb dropped away. Arthur had ridden ore lighters and pressure hops. He had never ridden anything that treated vacuum as a hallway. "Azra doesn't care about charters," he said. "It sits in the rock and does what it does. My assays are clean. The vein is real. If your Corps wants tonnage, the lease office on Chryse has forms." "The lease office," she said, "has already been informed that your plot is under review for strategic materials. Informing is not the same as deciding. That is why you are here." The ship shuddered once, a courteous docking. Beyond the lock a larger hull waited, windowless, lamplit in the old way: tubes behind frosted glass, the light slightly too warm, as if someone in a ministry still distrusted cold diodes. Arthur stepped through and smelled ozone and polished brass. The chamber was round. A table of dark stone occupied its center, bare except for a carafe and two cups. One man stood at the far curve, hands behind his back, watching the blank wall as if it were a window. He was older than the aides, younger than the corporations Arthur dealt with, and dressed as if a reception might begin at any moment and also never begin at all. "Mr. Neegan," he said, turning. "I am Consul Vey of the Antares Mission. Sit, if the collar allows it. Tea is from Earth. I am told that still means something to first-generation settlers." Arthur sat because his knees had opinions. "Consul of what, exactly? Antares is a star. Last I checked, stars don't issue invitations." "Antares is also a compact," Vey said. "Three systems, one fleet, and a shared dislike of watching the inner worlds turn a mineral into a monopoly. Your Azra accelerates decay. That sentence is already in every intelligence summary from Mercury to the Jovian yards. What is not in those summaries is the grade of your vein, the depth, and whether the effect scales when the metal is alloyed rather than merely adjacent to a pile. You have the rock. We have the laboratories that are not yet on fire." "On fire," Arthur repeated. "Metaphor, for the moment." Vey poured. The liquid smelled of leaves Arthur had only read about. "There was an accident at a corporate test cradle over Deimos. Officially, a containment irregularity. Unofficially, someone attempted to spike a drive core with a few grams of poorly refined Azra and discovered that 'poorly' and 'refined' are not casual words. The cradle is gone. So are forty-three technicians and a section of orbital traffic law. The corporations will say it was sabotage. The Fleet will say it was greed. Both will be partly right, which is the most dangerous kind of right." Arthur's cup was warm. He did not drink. "And you want me to hand over the vein before the next accident has my name on it." "I want you to choose the accident you can live beside." Vey's voice stayed level, the way a good engineer described a pressure drop. "The Chryse combines will offer you a buyout that looks like wealth until you read the indenture clauses written in the margin. They will speak of partnership and mean ownership. The weapons bureaus of at least two inner powers will offer you protection, which is a word that means guards at your door and no door of your own. We offer a third path. Lease the extraction rights to the Mission under a civil compact. You remain operator. Ore moves through our transports, assayed in the open, alloyed under published protocols. No private stockpiles. No quiet grams in a courier's pocket. In return, the Corps guarantees your title against forcible seizure and places your name on the research board. Not as a mascot. As the man who knows where the vein pinches." "Guarantees," Arthur said. "With what? Your aides had sidearms that weren't diplomatic." "With the fact that seizing you in public would start a quarrel the corporations are not yet ready to finish, and that hiding you would start one they cannot control." Vey set his cup down without having tasted it. "You are already in the center, Mr. Neegan. The invitation merely moved the center into a room with better light. If you refuse us, you will not return to a quiet plot. You will return to visitors who do not pour tea. Some of them will be polite for nearly as long as we were." Arthur looked at the blank wall and imagined Mars under it, red and indifferent, his claim staked with a beacon no larger than a fist. He thought of the core sample in his locker: a dull thread in ordinary basalt, warm to the touch in a way ordinary metal was not, as if time itself had been asked to hurry. "If I say yes," he said, "what do you need first?" "Your maps," Vey said. "And your silence, until the compact is filed where everyone who matters must pretend to have read it. After that, you may talk as loudly as you like. Loud men are harder to disappear." "And if the metal does what the drive people hope?" "Then the stars get closer," Vey said, "and the guns get ruder. We would prefer the first to arrive without the second already loaded. That is the entire policy. It is not noble. It is arithmetic." The woman with the sunburst had remained by the lock, a still figure in a room that suddenly felt smaller than the ship. Arthur touched his collar once more, then left it alone. "Arithmetic I understand," he said. "Show me the compact. And Consul—if your laboratories are not yet on fire, keep them that way. I've seen what a little Azra does to a Geiger counter. I don't want to see what a lot of it does to a treaty." Vey inclined his head, as if a door had opened somewhere behind the courteous light. "Then we are already in agreement about the danger," he said. "The rest is only politics, which is danger that has learned to speak."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter opens exactly as instructed, with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, and delivers a dialogue-heavy negotiation scene with an unnamed Antares agent and Consul Vey. The prose is clean and controlled, with a dry, cerebral Asimovian flavor: policy discussed over tea, danger framed as arithmetic. Vey's dialogue is the highlight—epigrammatic, sinister under courtesy ("Loud men are harder to disappear"). World-building is efficiently woven in (the Deimos cradle accident, the compact of three systems, indenture clauses in margins), hitting the big-picture/small-picture balance well. The retrofuturistic touches (frosted tubes, distrust of cold diodes, Earth tea) are apt. Weaknesses: the plot beats are somewhat predictable—mysterious invitation, veiled threats, offer of a "third path." Vey is a familiar type (urbane spymaster-diplomat), and Arthur's capitulation is quick, though his engineering skepticism ("what a little Azra does to a Geiger counter") keeps him credible. Some metaphors strain slightly ("knees had opinions"), and the ending line flirts with aphorism overload. Still, the piece is coherent, well-paced at ~1000 words, and engaging throughout.
