+ Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 60.2
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The hourglass did not measure time so much as patience. Sand fell in a thin, glittering thread, and every grain seemed to land on Lord Dream’s composure. He sat as he always sat: still, pale, and arranged like a verdict that had not yet been spoken. Today the stillness had a seam in it. A finger tapped once against the arm of the throne and did not tap again, which, in that court, was nearly a shout. “The dream in question,” said the clerk, a moth in a wig, “belongs, by long custom, to the office of First Love. Recurring. Pastoral. Wildflowers. A schoolboy named Max. A girl. An almost-kiss. Emotional weather: warm, confused, harmless.” First Love stood with her hands folded so tightly the roses in her cheeks had gone judicial. “It was calibrated,” she said. “Three summers of almost. The muddle was the point. He was learning how to want something without being destroyed by it.” From the dock, Mora swung one bare foot. She was beautiful in the way a shut door is beautiful when something breathes behind it. “And I improved it.” A murmur moved through the gallery of half-remembered jurors: a forgotten exam, a naked-in-church dream, a staircase that never ended. Dream’s eyes did not leave her. “You entered a crafted dreamscape without writ.” “I entered a chest,” Mora said pleasantly. “The dreamscape came with it. When she climbed on him—playful, your worship, all daisies and bad decisions—I finished the gesture. Sat where sitting does the work. Took a little breath. Left the confusion. I even kept the wildflowers. Some of them screamed, but aesthetically.” First Love made a small, offended sound. “He woke unable to move. He thought the girl he likes was eating him.” “A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” The moth-clerk’s wig slipped. Somewhere in the back, a nightmare laughed and tried to turn it into a cough. Dream regarded the hourglass. The sand had opinions. He had heard this defense before, in other mouths: hunger as jurisdiction, terror as improvement, the sleeper as pantry. Mora was not wrong that the Dreaming fed. She was wrong in the way a wolf is wrong when it files a claim on a lamb’s first pasture. “The boy’s terror,” he said, “is not in dispute. Your artistry is not in dispute. Your right is.” Mora shrugged, and the shrug had weight. “First Love gets the flutter. I get the paralysis. Between us he learns the whole curriculum. Romance and the thing under it. Call it a joint tenancy.” “I do not share,” First Love said, with the terrible dignity of someone who had once made a whole adolescence out of a brushed hand. Dream was tempted. The temptation arrived dressed as fairness and smelled faintly of mischief. He could split the dream down the middle: flowers on the left, suffocation on the right, the almost-kiss stranded on the property line like a lost shoe. He could assign Mora Tuesdays. He could rule that she might feed only on dreams already rotten, and watch her argue that puppy-love was a kind of rot. He could give the boy to neither of them and let the dream go feral, which was sometimes kinder. He did none of those things aloud. He let the silence work, which was his oldest trick and, today, also his irritation cooling into shape. “Ownership,” he said at last, “is a clumsy word for what happens in sleep. Craft is not. The field, the girl, the almost-kiss: those are First Love’s making. You may not wear them to dinner.” Mora’s smile thinned. “And if he dreams of me anyway?” “Then you may come as yourself,” Dream said. “Not as her. Not in her dress, not in her weight, not in the moment she leans down. You will not poach a first love to season a meal. If you must sit on his chest, you will do it in a dream that knows your name.” “That’s just branding,” Mora muttered. “It is a border.” He turned his head a fraction toward First Love. “And you will stop pretending innocence is a locked room. He is a boy. The world will sit on him eventually. Teach him the muddle. Do not teach him that every sweetness is owed your copyright until the nightmare files an appeal.” First Love opened her mouth, reconsidered the throne, and closed it. The roses returned, bashful and furious. Dream lifted one hand. The hourglass hesitated, as if embarrassed to have been watched. “Petition granted in part. The dreamscape returns to First Love. Mora is enjoined from substitution, impersonation, and picnic-based predation. She may hunt in her own weather. Costs: one evening of honest fright, paid by the boy to no one in particular, because the court does not itemize childhood.” Mora stood, already bored, already hungry. “A girl’s gotta eat.” “Eat elsewhere,” Dream said. She went. The gallery exhaled a collection of bad nights. First Love curtsied too deeply and fled toward a meadow that was already repairing itself, daisy by daisy, the scream leaking out of the pollen. Dream remained. The sand resumed its fall. For a moment—only a moment—the corner of his mouth considered treason. He imagined Mora opening the wrong dream and finding not a boy but a clerk-moth with a writ, sitting cheerfully on her chest, feeding on her certainty. He did not smile. The hourglass, which had seen worse, glittered as if it had.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece that hits nearly every prompt requirement: the courtroom setting, Dream's irritation, Mora's "a girl's gotta eat" defense, First Love's characterization, dark understated comedy, and Dream's temptation toward mischief (which lands in the final image of the moth-clerk fantasy). The prose is elegant and controlled, with memorable lines ("beautiful in the way a shut door is beautiful when something breathes behind it"). Dialogue is sharp and character-revealing. The resolution is clever — the "branding/border" ruling and the costs line ("the court does not itemize childhood") are highlights. Minor criticisms: the piece occasionally leans on aphorism-density that borders on preciousness ("arranged like a verdict that had not yet been spoken"), and a few metaphors strain. The ending's "considered treason" mischief is well-earned but slightly mild relative to the prompt's "tempted to mischief." Some of Dream's ruling dialogue is a touch speechy. Overall, however, the piece is coherent, tonally consistent, darkly funny, and engaging throughout, with no meandering or amateurish habits. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The broken cart wheel lies on its side by the village gates, one spoke snapped clean, the iron rim still warm where a hand must have seized it and failed. Mud around the axle holds the print of a boot that slid, then ran. No voices rise from the houses. Smoke hangs thin and sour over the thatch, and the gates themselves stand open, as if the village decided, all at once, that walls were a story it no longer believed. Alucard steps through them without touching the wood. The red of his coat is the only clean color in the lane. He tips his hat at the empty square, orange glass catching the late light, and smiles at nothing in particular. “Left in a hurry,” he says. “How rude. I do enjoy an audience.” A woman stands in the shadow of the chapel, where the sun has already given up. Violet eyes. Black hair pinned as if the wind has been warned. The air around her smells of lilac and gooseberries, absurd in a place that smells of fear and cooling ash. “They left because something walked the road last night,” Yennefer says. “It did not bother with the gates.” He looks at her the way a man looks at a locked door he has already decided to open. “And you stayed. How flattering.” “I stayed because the something is still here.” She does not step back when he closes the distance. Her hands remain loose at her sides. Magic gathers anyway, a pressure behind the teeth, the taste of ozone and old stone. “Take off the glasses.” Alucard laughs, low and delighted. He does not obey. “Orders. From a woman who smells like a garden and stands like a blade. Tell me your name before I decide whether you’re worth the trouble.” “Yennefer of Vengerberg. And you are not a man.” “No.” The smile widens, showing nothing a villager would want to see. “Alucard. Hellsing’s dog, when I feel like wearing the collar. Tonight I feel like walking.” He circles her, boots silent on the packed earth. She turns with him, never offering her back. The broken wheel sits between them for a moment, a small wrecked sun. “Your power is pretty. Structured. All those careful little laws. I could tear the stitching out and watch what spills.” “You could try.” Her voice is cool. Inside, something older than pride answers him—not fear, exactly. Recognition. She has spent centuries making herself into a weapon that does not flinch. He is a weapon that enjoys the flinch. “You’re leaking. The dead in the ditch past the mill are yours. Sloppy. A monster who needs an audience is still performing for someone.” His head tilts. For the first time the amusement thins. “Careful.” “I’m not sweet,” she says, “and I’m not a maiden in distress in need of saving. If you came for screams, the village already spent them. If you came for me, say so and stop pacing like a dog that wants the chain and hates it.” He stops. The air changes. Shadows under the eaves thicken, not with dusk but with something that has too many limbs and not enough patience. Guns hang at his hips, absurd and enormous, silver waiting in the cylinders. He does not draw them. Drawing them would be an admission that steel matters. “You hide a crooked spine under all that sorcery,” he says, soft. “I can hear the old bone. You paid for the face. You paid with the rest. Infertile little queen of a body you don’t trust. And you call me the monster.” The words land where he meant them to. Yennefer’s mouth does not move. A portal sparks at her fingertips—black, star-flecked, hungry—and dies again because she will not spend it on a flinch. She steps into his reach instead. Close enough that the lilac cuts through the grave-rot on his coat. Close enough that if he wanted her throat, the geometry is already kind. “And you,” she says, “wear a man’s coat and a man’s grin because eternity bored you into costume. You want a death you haven’t earned. You toy with the weak so you can pretend the strong are coming. I’m not your ending, vampire. I’m not your mirror either.” His hand rises. Not to her neck. To the brim of his hat, a mockery of courtesy that stops a finger’s width from her hair. The restraint is worse than a blow. She sees it, and he sees that she sees it, and the balance tips—toward her, for a breath, because he chose not to take. Then it tips back. The chapel bell tolls once with no hand on the rope. Every shutter in the lane slams. Yennefer’s wards flare, invisible until they are not: a cage of sigils around her body, old Aretuzan work, precise as spite. Something vast presses against them from his shadow and finds the geometry insulting. “Pretty,” he murmurs again, but the word has teeth now. “Hold that. I want to see how long your pride lasts when the cage learns my name.” “The bird of Hermes is my name,” he adds, almost fond, almost quoting a grave, “eating my wings to make me tame. They never manage it. Will you?” She laughs once, short, unlovely. “Taming is for people who want a pet. I want to know what you are when the performance ends. Stand still.” He does not. He moves, and she moves, and the lane becomes a circle neither of them will break first. A spark of her magic kisses his wrist; the flesh blackens and knits in the same instant, and his delight at the pain is so naked she almost looks away. Almost. His shadow brushes her ankle like a tongue of cold water. Her ward answers with fire that is not fire. Neither strike is meant to finish. Both are tests. Both fail to find a flinch. Beyond the gates the abandoned wheel creaks as the wind shifts it. The village does not return. Whatever hunted the road last night has found, in the square, something that will not run and something that will not kneel, and the space between them hums like a drawn string. Alucard’s glasses slide down his nose. Red eyes, endless, amused and starving. Yennefer meets them. “After you,” she says. “Ladies first,” he answers. Neither moves. The light goes out of the square, and the game, whatever it is, does not end.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of fanfiction that largely fulfills the brief: third person, present tense, roughly 1000 words, medieval European setting, and a sustained power dynamic between Alucard and Yennefer that shifts without either breaking. The prose is confident and controlled, with an atmospheric opening (the abandoned village, the broken wheel) that shows rather than tells. Character work is the standout. Alucard's sadism, theatricality, and death-wish subtext are captured accurately ("You want a death you haven't earned"), and the piece smartly uses his perception of Yennefer's hidden hunchback and infertility as a weapon — a choice consistent with his cruelty and her deepest vulnerability. Yennefer is given agency, wit, and refusal to flinch; the detail of the portal sparking and dying because "she will not spend it on a flinch" is excellent. The famous quotes are integrated naturally rather than pasted in — Yennefer's line lands as genuine dialogue, and Alucard's Hermes quote is framed self-referentially, which is a clever touch. Weaknesses: some imagery strains toward the overwrought ("a small wrecked sun," "hum like a drawn string," "black, star-flecked, hungry" portal), though it never collapses into true purple prose. The ending's stalemate is thematically right but slightly static — the piece resolves into an elegant tableau rather than escalation, which risks feeling like the story declines to commit. The external threat (whatever emptied the village) is raised and dropped, functioning only as set dressing. A few lines ("the geometry is already kind," "finds the geometry insulting") repeat a word-pattern noticeably. Dialogue is generally sharp, though a couple of Alucard's lines edge toward wind-up villainy. No unearned transformations, no tonal inconsistency, no meandering — the piece is tight and purposeful. Emotionally, it delivers the required repulsion/fascination tension with genuine complexity. It's very good, but a notch below masterpiece due to the decorative prose tendencies and the unresolved external hook. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The chain-link fences within the yard rattle whenever an inmate passes by, a thin metallic shiver that never quite settles. Jolyne Cujoh walks the inner path with her hands in her pockets and her eyes on the wire. The prison is wrong in ways the guards will not name. Shadows lean the wrong direction. A woman two cells down has not blinked since breakfast. Jolyne’s butterfly tattoo itches under the sleeve of her jumpsuit, and Stone Free coils just under her skin, ready if the air decides to bite. Makima is already at the fence when Jolyne reaches the corner. Auburn hair, yellow rings in her eyes, a smile that looks borrowed from a kinder room. She does not rattle the links. The fence goes quiet around her, as if the metal has been told to behave. “You walk like someone who expects a fight,” Makima says, soft. “That’s exhausting. You could rest.” Jolyne stops a pace away. “And you talk like a brochure. Who the hell are you supposed to be?” “A visitor.” Makima’s hands stay folded. “They let me speak with people who interest me. You interest me, Jolyne.” The use of her name lands wrong. No introduction, no file, no guard calling it out. Jolyne’s mouth tightens. “Cute. Try that on someone who likes being read.” Makima tilts her head, pleasant as a closed door. “Your ability. The string. It comes from you, doesn’t it? Not a tool. Not a contract you signed and forgot. You unmake your own body and still remain yourself. That is rare.” Stone Free stirs. Jolyne feels the pull at her wrist, the temptation to peel a thread free and test the space between them. She does not. Not yet. “You staring at my Stand like it’s a dog you want to leash. Back off.” “I don’t need to stare.” Makima’s voice never rises. “I only need to understand what you want. Freedom. Your father. The people you refuse to abandon even when abandonment would be safer. Those are clean desires. Easy to hold. Easy to offer back.” A guard passes on the far side of the yard. The fence rattles for him, then stills again near Makima. Jolyne watches that stillness and hates it. Sweetness that does not pay the same price as everyone else is not sweetness. It is a trick with better manners. “You don’t know my father,” Jolyne says. “You don’t know my people. You know a list.” “Lists are honest.” Makima steps closer to the wire. Not through it. She does not have to. “Tell me what you would trade to walk out of here today. One name. One promise. I can make the doors agree.” Jolyne laughs once, sharp. “If there’s no Mickey, this shit ain’t Disney. You don’t get to sell me a parade.” For the first time, something in Makima’s eyes goes flat, then returns to warmth so quickly it might have been a blink. “You think I’m selling. I’m offering structure. You fight everything because you were taught that resistance is love. It isn’t. Resistance is noise. Control is care, when the person holding it is competent.” “Competent,” Jolyne repeats. The word tastes like iron. She lets a single strand of Stone Free slip from her fingertip, invisible against the gray light, and lays it along the fence between them. The string does not cut. It listens. Through it she feels the wire’s ordinary cold, and then a pressure that is not metal at all: attention, dense and patient, pressing back as if the fence has grown a spine. Makima notices. Of course she does. Her smile deepens by a degree no camera would catch. “There. You reached for me without being asked. That’s the beginning of trust.” “That’s me checking if you’re real,” Jolyne says. “You’re not. Not the way you pretend. You want my Stand because you can’t stand a power that doesn’t kneel when you look at it. You want my friends because loyalty is a handle. You want me calm because calm people sign things.” Makima does not deny it. Denial would be inefficient. “And if I do? Would that make the offer false? The doors would still open. Your father would still be safer if you stopped thrashing. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners. People are supposed to be useful to what is stronger than they are. I am only saying the quiet part with a gentle voice.” The yard seems to narrow. Somewhere a siren fails to sound. Jolyne’s pulse kicks, hot and stupid and alive. She has met liars. She has met monsters with badges. This is worse: a woman who will use Jolyne’s love as a collar and call the fit a kindness. “You think I’m beneath you,” Jolyne says. “That’s the tell. Sweet voice, dead math. I’m not signing, I’m not kneeling, and I’m not handing you Stone Free so you can walk it like a pet.” She yanks the string back into her hand. The fence rattles at last, a violent shiver that runs the length of the yard as if every link has remembered it is allowed to shake. Inmates look up. A guard shouts. Makima does not flinch, but the quiet she wore like a coat tears at the edges. “You will exhaust yourself,” Makima says, still soft, and the softness is the threat. “Everyone does. When you are tired enough, you will ask me what I can take off your shoulders. I will still be here. I do not leave things I have decided to keep.” Jolyne steps back, shoulders squared, foul-mouthed heart hammering clean. “Then decide slower. Next time you come at me with that fake honey, I’m not checking. I’m cutting.” Makima’s ringed eyes hold her a moment longer, intrigued, already revising the leash. Then she turns, and the fence goes silent in her wake, obedient, wrong, waiting. Jolyne stays until the rattle returns with the next passing inmate, ordinary and ugly and hers. She breathes. She does not look away from the wire. Suspicion, she understands now, is not enough. Makima does not persuade. She rearranges the room until refusal feels like cruelty. Jolyne cracks her knuckles and lets Stone Free hum under her skin, a promise with no bow on it. If the prison wants a pet, it can rattle for someone else. She will not be useful. She will not be owned. And when the sweet voice comes back, she will meet it with string, teeth, and the refusal to call a chain a gift.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong crossover piece that captures both characters well. The prose is controlled, present-tense third person as instructed, and approximately the requested length. Jolyne's suspicion and Makima's soft menace are rendered convincingly; the fence imagery (rattling for everyone but going silent around Makima) is an effective recurring motif that shows rather than tells Makima's control. Dialogue is sharp and in-voice: Jolyne's "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney" is deployed naturally, and Makima's "Dogs are supposed to die for their owners" is repurposed as a chilling escalation. The battle of wits escalates appropriately without tipping into a physical fight, which suits the prompt. Jolyne's read of Makima ("sweet voice, dead math") lands as earned insight rather than sudden revelation. Minor weaknesses: some lines flirt with over-polish ("foul-mouthed heart hammering clean" is a slightly awkward construction; "a promise with no bow on it" strains). The ending is a touch tidy and declarative, with Jolyne's final resolve summarized somewhat. Makima's menace occasionally tips into explicit statement of her own methods ("I am only saying the quiet part with a gentle voice"), which is a bit on-the-nose for a manipulator. But overall the piece is coherent, atmospheric, and engaging with few amateurish traits. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 78.7
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
I found the first note on a Tuesday that, according to every clock I trusted, had not yet decided to become dangerous. It lay inside my locked desk drawer, folded once, written in my hand. The paper smelled faintly of the bleach we used after Site-19’s last decontamination drill. I had not written it. I was certain of that for nearly four minutes. *Don’t open the secondary hatch on Sublevel 3 after 02:17. You think you’re sealing the breach. You’re feeding it. —You, Thursday.* I took it to Records. They logged it as an unsolicited internal communication and asked whether I wanted counseling. I said I wanted ink analysis. Dr. Lang from Materials returned the results that evening with the careful face she used when a result refused to be boring. “Graphite and iron gall,” she said. “Trace vanadium and a polymer we don’t stock. Nothing in the site supply cabinets matches. Nothing in the regional catalogs either.” “So not my pen.” “Not any pen we can name.” I slept badly and woke to a second note on the bathroom mirror, the letters smeared where steam had touched them and then, impossibly, dried into place. *Lang is going to tell you the polymer is industrial. She’s wrong. It’s residue from the foam they used on your coat after you came back through. You don’t remember coming back because you haven’t left. Stop trusting sequence.* I had not left the site in eleven days. My coat hung where I had left it, clean. By Wednesday the notes arrived faster than I could file them. One in my lunch. One inside a sealed evidence sleeve I had signed out myself an hour earlier, the seal unbroken until I broke it. One on the back of a printout of my own prior interview with SCP-████, the entity we had begun, privately, to call the Editor because it preferred other people’s sentences to its own. The notes grew worse. *They will say it’s the Editor. It isn’t. The Editor only rearranges what already happened. I am writing from a Thursday that keeps being deleted. If you read this, do not correct the timestamp on the breach report. The correction is how it gets in.* Another, the handwriting looser, letters climbing: *You already died in the stairwell. Ignore that. That version didn’t take. The one where you trust Hale does. Hale is—* The rest was a blot. Under ultraviolet the blot resolved into my employee number written thirty times, then a time, 02:17, then a sentence in a hand that was still mine and no longer careful: *reality is a draft with too many authors.* Hale from Temporal called me in with two observers from Memetics and a psychiatrist who did not introduce himself. They had me read the notes aloud while instruments watched my pulse do ordinary things. Hale’s questions were gentle and exact. “Have you had unlogged contact with SCP-████?” “Interview, Monday. Standard. It asked me to finish a sentence I hadn’t started.” “Did you?” “No.” “Any missing time?” I wanted to say no. The honest answer was that missing time would look, from inside, like time that had never been missing. “Not that I can locate.” They ran the paper again. Same vanadium. Same unnamed polymer. A technician from Archives swore the sheets matched a lot destroyed in a fire six years ago. The lot numbers were correct. The fire was correct. The sheets existed anyway. Memetics proposed manipulation: the Editor seeding anticipatory text, training me to enact a breach by fearing it. Temporal proposed a closed loop, a message arriving from a branch that our instruments had not yet consented to record. Neither proposal survived contact with the next note, which I found in my own pocket during the meeting, though my hands had not left the table. *Stop letting them sort me into categories. Categories are how the hatch opens. Hale will recommend amnestics at 19:40. If you take them, you walk into Sublevel 3 smiling. If you don’t, you walk in afraid. Both versions breach. I have tried fourteen. I am not your future. I am the remainder.* Hale did recommend amnestics. At 19:40. I watched the recommendation appear on the screen and felt the room tilt, not physically, only in the place where sequence was supposed to live. I refused the amnestics. That refusal is in the log. Later someone annotated the log with a time stamp I did not write: *subject already refused in draft 9.* I went to Sublevel 3 because not going had begun to feel like another kind of obedience. The secondary hatch was sealed. The corridor was empty. At 02:16 the lights browned, the way they do when something large draws power two floors away. My radio hissed. A voice—mine, tired past the point of performance—said, “Don’t.” I did not open the hatch. I stood with my palm on the cold metal until 02:18, then 02:19, counting because counting was the only procedure left that belonged to me. Nothing breached. No alarm. When I lifted my hand, a note was stuck to the hatch by nothing I could see. *Good. This is the version where you don’t. I think. Check your left sleeve.* There was ink on the cuff. Not wet. Vanadium-dark under the corridor light. I had not written on my sleeve. I could not remember writing, which was no longer evidence of anything. Upstairs, Hale waited with the psychiatrist and a containment proposal that used both theories at once, the way the Foundation does when it cannot afford to be wrong in only one direction. Temporal isolation of my quarters. Memetic screening of every surface I touched. No amnestics unless I requested them. The Editor’s chamber under raised observation, not because they had proof, but because proof had started arriving before the events it proved. I agreed to all of it. Agreement felt like a third door, and I had not yet been warned about thirds. In my quarters I found the last note of that night, centered on the pillow, letters shaking so badly I had to read them twice. Some words contradicted the site map. One sentence named a colleague who had transferred out in 2014 and, according to the database I checked with shaking hands, had never worked here at all. Another insisted the breach had already finished and that we were living in the report written afterward. *If the ink isn’t ours, neither is the hand. If the hand is yours, the future is already in the room. I can’t tell which sentence is the trap anymore. Burn this. Don’t burn this. I’m sorry. You were right not to open it. You opened it. Both are in the file.* I did not burn it. I bagged it, labeled it, and sat with my back to the wall until morning, counting my breaths and losing count, trying to decide whether the person I was failing to trust was a future self, a contained thing wearing my sentences, or the present mind that kept accepting paper from nowhere. At 06:00 the ink analysis on the hatch note came back. Trace elements unmatched. Polymer unmatched. My handwriting, to every expert who would sign the form. I wrote nothing down for an hour. Then I wrote this, slowly, in a pen from the cabinet Lang had cleared. I do not know whether I am documenting an anomaly or completing one. If another note appears in the margin before I submit this, I will not read it until someone else is in the room. There is already a mark in the margin. I have not looked. I am trying, with what remains of sequence, to keep that true.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of the prompt. It delivers a first-person, past-tense SCP-adjacent narrative about a researcher receiving notes from a possible future self, with escalating desperation, contradictory information, institutional attempts to classify the anomaly (temporal loop vs. memetic manipulation by "the Editor"), and a genuine erosion of the narrator's trust in their own perception. Strengths: The prose is controlled and precise, with a dry, clinical Foundation register that occasionally cracks into genuine dread ("I was certain of that for nearly four minutes"). The notes themselves are the highlight—each one destabilizes more than the last, and the contradictions (the colleague who never worked there, "You already died in the stairwell. Ignore that.") are well-judged. The institutional texture is convincing: ink analysis, the fire-destroyed paper lot that exists anyway, Hale's dual-theory containment proposal. The ending resists resolution—the mark in the margin, unread—is an excellent final beat that honors the prompt's ambiguity requirement. The Foundation's "cannot afford to be wrong in only one direction" is a sharp line. Weaknesses: The piece is not formatted as an actual SCP report—it's a personal narrative, which the prompt arguably requested ("SCP report about a researcher") but the deviation is notable; there are no SCP document conventions (object class, containment procedures headers). Some aphoristic lines strain slightly ("reality is a draft with too many authors," "I am the remainder")—the Editor conceit flirts with cleverness over authenticity. The dialogue is functional but thin; Hale's lines are serviceable rather than distinctive. The word count is roughly on target. A few images ("the place where sequence was supposed to live") are effective; a couple ("a Tuesday that had not yet decided to become dangerous") tip toward preciosity. The middle section's note-quoting rhythm becomes slightly repetitive before the Sublevel 3 sequence arrives. The narrator's character is deliberately thin—appropriate for the genre, but limits emotional depth; the fear is intellectualized more than felt at times. Overall: a confident, disciplined piece with a strong ending, minor stylistic self-indulgence and a loose interpretation of "SCP report" format. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7194 **Object Class:** Keter **Special Containment Procedures:** Doors matching SCP-7194’s profile are to be sealed with welded plate and a false wall. MTF Epsilon-6 (“Village Idiots”) surveys condemned structures in cities with documented disappearances. Entry requires Level-4 approval and a three-person team with redundant beacons. No document is to leave the threshold. Personnel named in recovered files are barred from assignment. **Description:** SCP-7194 is a series of unmarked steel doors appearing in abandoned buildings on every inhabited continent. Each door is flush, unnumbered, and lacks a handle on the exterior; it opens only when pressed at the seam. Many doors are more weathered than the masonry around them—pitted, salt-stained, edges rounded as if centuries of traffic had worn a building that is itself only decades old. Beyond each door is the same place: a stack of concrete corridors, filing halls, and spiral stairs that do not close. Survey lasers lose lock after roughly four hundred meters. Floors repeat without matching. Skylights show a gray sky that does not correspond to local weather. The air smells of paper dust and a faint chemical sweetness. The archive holds bound ledgers, microfilm, clay tablets in modern cabinets, and loose folios in languages that predate their scripts’ attested use. Recurring subject: a global administrative body that maintained “holdings” until an unspecified containment failure ended it. Later folios use a circular seal nearly identical to the Foundation’s, captioned in several hands as the *Office of Standing Custody*, the *Keeper’s Bureau*, and once, in English cursive, *the Foundation*. **Exploration Log 7194-C** **Team:** Researcher Adeyemi, Agent Ruiz, Agent Pell **Foreword:** Entry via a door in a 1971 textile mill, Gary, Indiana. Door face showed oxidation inconsistent with the mill’s age. Adeyemi’s lamp found the first hall already lit by failing tubes. Shelving ran past the beam. Ruiz called distances; the numbers did not add. At the second landing they heard casters. Three figures in yellow impermeable suits, full hoods, no insignia, were loading folios into a wheeled bin. Their suits looked institutional and wrong at once—taped seams, scuffed visors, no tanks. When Pell hailed them, all three stopped. One turned. The visor was opaque. They abandoned the bin and withdrew down a side corridor at a run that did not echo correctly. Pursuit failed at a stair that ended in a wall the suits had apparently passed through. Boot prints in the dust stopped mid-stride. The bin held partial indexes. Several tabs had been cut away with a heated blade. Remaining headers included *Breach — littoral*, *Breach — grain*, and *Names retained*. Further in, a reading room contained a visitor log bound in cracked leather. Recent ink—weeks, not centuries—listed times without dates. Three entries used Foundation authentication phrases obsolete since 1998. The signatures matched on-file samples for O5-2, O5-7, and O5-11. None of those Council members had an authorized absence covering the relevant window. A margin note in O5-7’s hand read only: *Do not let them finish the redaction.* The team withdrew when beacons began reporting their own positions as already outside. **Recovered Document 7194-14** (excerpt, translation from a Romance dialect with anachronistic technical terms): > The Keepers write that the door is a mercy. We have learned it is a drawer. What fails is not put down. It is filed, and the filing is mistaken for an ending. When the littoral holding opened, the clerks did not run. They reclassified the sea. By morning the harbors were shelves, and the ships were entries that could not be checked out. > > If you are reading this in a building that has forgotten you, leave the names where they lie. Someone is already coming to take the page that proves you were warned. **Recovered Document 7194-31** (personnel jacket, paper stock consistent with late 19th-century rag; typescript dated “Year 214 of Custody”): > **Adeyemi, I.** — Archivist, provisional. Assigned to coastal redaction after the second grain failure. Noted for refusing to initial a destruction order concerning living indexes. Status: still in post. *Do not inform the subject that the post has not yet occurred.* A matching jacket exists for Agent Ruiz, listing a commendation for “pursuit of unsanctioned clerks” dated more than a century before her birth. Agent Pell’s file is a single sheet, blank except for the footer: *Removed by order of the visitors in yellow.* **Addendum 7194-O5:** When confronted with copies of the visitor log, O5-11 stated that the signature was forged and terminated the interview. Forensic analysis found the ink still wet relative to the page’s age, as if the signature and the paper had not shared a century. O5-7 has not responded to summons. A door matching SCP-7194 was subsequently found in a sub-basement of Site-01 that does not appear on any blueprint. It was older than the concrete. It has not been opened. The weld is holding. The dust on the interior side, visible through a hairline gap, shows fresh caster tracks leading away.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, disciplined SCP entry that hits every required element: identical unmarked doors in abandoned buildings worldwide, an architecturally impossible archive, references to a prior global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure, the Foundation under other names, personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago, hazmat-like entities removing documents who flee when approached, and evidence of unauthorized O5 visits. The third-person exploration team perspective and recovered document excerpts are both present. Length is close to the 1000-word target. The prose is controlled and clinical in the right way for the format, with occasional striking images ("the ships were entries that could not be checked out," "a run that did not echo correctly," "the door is a mercy. We have learned it is a drawer"). The central conceit—that containment is filing, and the Foundation is a recurrence of a prior Custody—is genuinely unsettling and well-executed. The personnel jacket for Adeyemi ("Do not inform the subject that the post has not yet occurred") is an excellent temporal-loop implication, and Pell's blank file "Removed by order of the visitors in yellow" gives a chilling personal stake. Weaknesses: the exploration log is somewhat compressed and reads more like summary than scene; the team members have little individual voice, so the character stakes are conceptual rather than felt. The dialogue is minimal (a single hail), so that criterion barely applies. Some ideas—the wet ink, the Site-01 door—are excellent, but the ending's "the weld is holding" line is a bit tidy. The recovered documents occasionally strain under the weight of their own cleverness, and the piece leans on aphoristic mystery rather than earned revelation, which is genre-appropriate but limits emotional depth. Still, this is a confident, coherent, atmospheric piece with almost no amateurish tells. Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Maret left the reception by the service stair, the cloak still on because the ship’s manual said the air of Kedth would chill an unadapted body. It did not. The street was warm as breath, and the cloth, cut for another gravity, swung and caught at the knees. People looked. Not long. A glance was courtesy here, she had already learned that much, and then the eyes went elsewhere, as if a stare might stick. They wore little: a band at the hip, a film of pale fiber over the chest, sometimes nothing but the skin the sun had made. Two lineages shared the market lane. The night-born were narrow through the shoulder, their eyes large and lidless-seeming in the glare, the skin a deep dusk that drank light. The day-born were broader, hairless at the scalp, the hide thick and faintly scaled along the forearm where the briefings had said “armor.” Children of both kinds ran the same errand between stalls, and nobody sorted them. The briefing had said segregation. It had said markets were fronts, kinship a weapon, touch a claim of dominance. Maret bought a cup of the sour seed-drink with the ship’s scrip and was given, without ceremony, a second cup “for the heat in the cloth.” The vendor was night-born. The hand that passed the cup was day-born, resting a moment on the vendor’s wrist in the ordinary way of people who have stood together all morning. A board behind them listed prices in two scripts and a third that was only notches. No one explained it. Explanation, Maret thought, was what the Embassy mistook for knowledge. She walked until the cloak was a foolishness she could feel in the set of her shoulders. A woman with the heavy day-born jaw stopped her, not unkindly, and said, “You will faint in that. We have pegs.” There were pegs, a row of them under an awning, holding other people’s excess: a rain-cape, a sling, a child’s mask for the dust. Maret did not leave the cloak. Protocol was a small god, but it was the one she had sworn to. She thanked the woman in the trade-speech and went on, sweating, observed, and for the first time since landfall not interpreted. When she returned, Command was already in the anteroom, which meant the anteroom had ceased to be hers. “You were not cleared for the lower ward.” “I was cleared for the city.” “The city is a diagram until we draw it. You do not draw it by vanishing.” Command’s voice had the flatness of people who believe flatness is fairness. “The Minister of Science has asked for you. Personally. You will go as you are. Do not apologize for the excursion. Do not mention it unless it is used against you. The posting is political. Remember that the title is not the work.” The Minister kept no instruments in the room. There was a window, and a table with nothing on it, and a chair that had been set a little too far from the window, so that whoever sat there would have the light in their eyes. Maret remained standing. The Minister was day-born, older, the scalp mapped with pale scars that might have been ornament or weather. The smile was exact. “The cloak,” the Minister said. “They will have offered you a peg.” “They did.” “And you refused a kindness in order to remain a document. That is one school of diplomacy. It has a high casualty rate among the young.” A pause, measured. “Your bureau’s paper says the night-born cannot sustain cooperative labor past a single task. Your bureau’s paper says the day-born hoard water rights and breed for mass. You drank in the lane. What did you see that the paper did not?” “A price board in three hands,” Maret said. “A touch that was not a claim. Children unsorted. I saw that your ministry’s title is not your work, and that mine may not be mine either.” The Minister’s smile did not widen. “Good. Then we can begin without the insult of pretending you are only a courier. They will ask you, soon, to certify that we are one species in law and two in fact, so that the charter can be split and the mines leased under separate seals. If you certify what you have not lived, you will be useful. If you insist on living it, you will be late, and lateness here is read as allegiance.” The scarred hands opened on the empty table. “So. Offworlder. Will you be useful, or will you be late?” Maret felt the cloak, heavy, wrong, still hers. Outside, the market would be closing its awnings against a sun that both peoples had learned, differently, to survive. She did not answer at once. The Minister, who had made a life of other people’s haste, waited as if waiting were a tool, and Maret understood that the test was not the question but whether she would let the silence be filled for her. “I will be accurate,” she said. “If that makes me late, your charter was never waiting on me.” The Minister inclined the head, a small, unsentimental acknowledgment, the kind given to a piece that has finally been seen to have a move of its own.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of Le Guin-inflected science fiction that hits nearly every beat of the prompt: the envoy slips away, encounters a market contradicting the briefings, is reprimanded, and faces a testing conversation with the political Minister of Science. The prose is spare, aphoristic, and controlled — very much in Le Guin's anthropological register. The worldbuilding is delivered through observation rather than exposition: the price board in three scripts, the pegs for excess clothing, the touch on the wrist. The dialogue is sharp and functional, particularly the Minister's "useful or late" gambit, and the ending's refusal to fill the silence is a genuinely earned character beat. Weaknesses: the piece is compressed to the point of sketchiness in places. The Minister's revelation about the charter and mines arrives abruptly and is explained rather than dramatized — a mild tell-don't-show lapse in an otherwise showing piece. Maret's characterization is thin; her "protocol is a small god" loyalty is asserted more than tested across time. The night-born/day-born divergence is evocative but generic — large eyes, scaled forearms — and the colony's politics (water rights, mines, charter-splitting) are gestured at rather than inhabited. The aphoristic density ("Explanation was what the Embassy mistook for knowledge") occasionally tips toward preciosity, though it never becomes purple. The word count is somewhat under the 1000-word seed (roughly 850), a minor adherence issue. The reprimand scene is efficient but slightly mechanical; Command is a voice, not a presence. Still, the piece is coherent, tonally consistent, and quietly engaging, with a satisfying, unsentimental close. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 86.6
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The contract was written on the back of a seed packet that had already gone blank. Mara held it under the hood lamp until the grease-pencil letters steadied: three kilos of viable grain, delivered before the river ice set, payment in insulin analog and a crate of unbroken glass. No signatures. The broker had pressed a thumb to the corner and left a print that fluoresced faintly green, the old corporate tell for a deal that would not be repeated. She worked in what had been a cold-storage bay behind the settlement kiln. The thermocycler was a rice cooker wired to a car battery and a scavenged thermostat; it clicked like a beetle and lied about its temperature by two degrees on the warm side. She had learned to trust the lie. Around it, empty canisters from Helix & Meridian—matte white, the logo half-scraped—stood in for reagent bottles. One still smelled of the citrus solvent the company had used to fake cleanliness. She had boiled it twice and still would not store anything that had to stay alive in that one. The others held her real inventory: salt she had baked out of a road cut, a thumb of polymerase hoarded from a clinic fridge that had died in the second winter, primers written in her own hand because the printed sheets had faded to the color of old bone. The obsolescence was not a rumor. Helix had built it in. Each licensed cultivar carried a tail that frayed after a single reproductive cycle, a profit clock disguised as a safety feature. When the towers went dark, the fields went sterile in a season. What Mara had was worse than sterile: it was almost. She tipped a few grains of last year’s barley into a cracked watch glass. Under the hand lens the embryos looked intact. Under the stain they showed the familiar unraveling, threads of sequence sloughing off like smoke. If she waited another month there would be nothing left to copy. She loaded the cycler anyway, because the contract did not care about almost. The splice was crude. She was not chasing a patent. She was chasing a winter. A fragment from a feral oat that had reseeded itself along the ditch—ugly, low-yield, stubborn—cut against the corporate barley’s remaining starch genes before those genes finished dying. She worked with a blade honed on a roofing nail and tape that had already been used on someone’s splint. When the cycler beeped she did not celebrate. She labeled the tube with a scratch on the canister lid and set it in the one corner of the bay that still held a pocket of cold. Her hands shook. Not from the cold. The shakes were the price of the patch she wore under her ribs, a gray disc of unlicensed tissue grown in a jar that had once held paint. The settlement’s medic had called it a bridge: something to keep her marrow producing until a real course of the analog could be found. It itched in weather. It made her dreams loud. It also, unexpectedly, made her night vision almost indecently good, which was why she could read grease pencil by a hood lamp that would have blinded her two years ago, and why she had stopped carrying a second lantern on the path back from the ditch. She did not mention the upside in the log. Upsides made people want the patch. The patch was not a kindness. Three of the first volunteers had fevered out; one had grown a ridge of cartilage along the jaw that the medic still would not name. Mara’s own blood, drawn monthly into a chipped vial, showed a marker the old assays did not have a column for. She kept drawing it. Data was the only thing the dead companies had left that still behaved. At dusk the broker’s runner came to the fence and did not cross it. Young, hood up, a Helix canister under one arm as if it were a lunch pail. Mara met them at the wire with the tube in a sock. “Three kilos,” the runner said. “You don’t have three kilos.” “I have a start,” Mara said. “It has to finish in soil that isn’t ours. Your buyer has a glasshouse. I don’t.” The runner looked at the sock, then at Mara’s hands. The tremor was visible. People in this trade learned to price tremors. “The analog is short a vial,” the runner said. “Glasshouse had a crack. They lost a rack.” “Then the grain is short a kilo, and they can explain it to whoever eats in March.” Wind moved through the kiln yard and brought the smell of wet ash. Somewhere inside the bay the cycler ticked, already cooling, already useless until she fed it again. The runner shifted the empty canister from arm to arm. Mara recognized the lot number. She had three of that lot on her bench, labels burned off, holding salt and a hope she would not say aloud. “They’ll take the start,” the runner said at last. “Payment at the culvert. Half now if the tube survives the walk.” “It survives if you don’t put it in your pocket against your skin.” The runner nodded, almost a flinch, and took the sock with both hands as if it were hotter than it was. Mara watched them go until the green of that old thumbprint—no, that was gone; this one left no light—until the figure was only a darker seam in the dark. She went back inside and set a clean canister under the lamp, the citrus ghost still faint in the plastic, and wrote the next day’s work on the seed packet’s blank face: ditch oats, second cut, do not trust the warm side. Her ribs itched. She did not scratch. Outside, the river was beginning to think about ice, and the grain that might outlast its makers was already walking away from her in a sock, toward a glasshouse she would never see, carrying one more generation than the company had ever meant to sell.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of post-apocalyptic biopunk fiction that hits nearly all the prompt requirements with precision and craft. The prose is controlled, evocative, and economical—each detail (the rice-cooker thermocycler, the citrus-scented canister, the grease-pencil contract on a blank seed packet) does double duty as world-building and characterization. The obsolescence mechanic is woven in naturally rather than explained in an info-dump. The physical toll and unexpected upside of the untested medical patch (tremors, itching, loud dreams, but enhanced night vision) is handled with exactly the ambivalence the prompt requested. The black market contract drives the chapter's plot, and the negotiation scene has genuine tension. Strengths: the voice is consistent and confident; the imagery is specific and tactile; the dialogue is terse and believable, with subtext (pricing tremors, the runner's near-flinch). The ending line—"carrying one more generation than the company had ever meant to sell"—is a well-earned thematic capstone. The moment where Mara almost sees the green thumbprint again ("no, that was gone") is a subtle, effective touch of her altered perception. Minor weaknesses: the plot is somewhat low-stakes and the runner's capitulation is a bit quick; the broker/buyer remains abstract, so the contract never fully ignites into real danger. A few phrases ("a hope she would not say aloud") flirt with sentimentality but stay on the right side of it. The piece is more vignette than chapter with a full arc, though it satisfies the brief. Length is close to the 1000-word target. + Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 59.5
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The transfer vessel had no name that Arthur Neegan could find, only a registry string that the bulkhead display kept rewriting in patient green: hull pressure nominal, spin within tolerance, coolant loop two a half-degree warm. He watched the characters crawl and reset. Somewhere aft, a pump knocked once, the way a knuckle knocks a door that does not intend to wait. They had come at dust-fall, four of them in the grey of the Antares Diplomatic Corps, which was diplomatic in the sense that a lock is courteous to the key. The insignia on the shoulder was a star cupped in a hand. No one raised a voice. The tall one had said, “Mr. Neegan, your presence is requested,” and the short one had already been looking at the assay cabinet as if the cabinet had volunteered. Now the red of Mars was a coin behind them, and the green text said TRANSIT WINDOW OPEN. “You may sit,” said the woman across the narrow cabin. She had not given a name on the surface. Here, with the spin-gravity settling into his boots, she seemed willing to spend one. “I am Consul Vey. The others are my retinue. You are not under arrest.” “That’s a comfort,” Arthur said. “People who aren’t under arrest usually get to finish their coffee.” A man by the hatch almost smiled. The carbines were slung, not aimed. Politeness, Arthur was learning, could be machined to a tolerance. Vey folded her hands. “Your leasehold sits on a vein the Survey numbered only last month. Azra. You know what it does.” “I know what the broadsheets say. It hurries decay. A spoon of it in the right lattice and a drive that should take a century takes a year. Or a warhead that should merely frighten a city learns ambition.” He glanced at the screen. Green still. LIFE SUPPORT REDUNDANT. “I also know my plot was supposed to be iron and regret.” “Regret is a mineral every colony exports,” Vey said. “Azra is not. The Corporations of the Tharsis leases believe the vein is theirs by the fine print of your indenture. The Compact believes the vein is a strategic reserve. Antares believes neither of those beliefs should be allowed to harden into fact before a conversation.” “And I’m the conversation.” “You are the man whose name is on the stake.” She leaned forward. The cabin light was the old kind, a bar of white that made faces honest and tired. “Off-world, in three hours, you will meet someone who can alter that name’s weight. I am to deliver you intact and uncoached. I dislike both conditions. Intact, because intact men make their own trouble. Uncoached, because coaching is my profession.” The display flickered: COMM LASER LOCKED — DESTINATION WITHHELD. Arthur felt the small animal fear that comes when a machine refuses to name the dark it is speaking to. “If I refuse the meeting?” “Then the Corporations arrive with lawyers, and the Compact arrives with auditors, and someone less polite than I arrives with a cutting charge. Your neighbors are already receiving offers for their silence. Indenture is a chain with many links, Mr. Neegan. Yours happens to be the one that glitters.” He thought of the shaft, the black glitter in the core sample, the way the counter on his wrist had chattered as if the rock were impatient to become something else. He had capped the hole and sat on the tailings until the sun was a rusted rivet. A first-generation settler learned early that discovery was a kind of debt. “Who is this someone?” Vey’s mouth tightened, which on her was nearly a confession. “A principal. Not a consul. Not a colonel. The sort of person whose memos become borders. They will make you an offer. I am permitted to say that the offer will sound like mercy and spend like a mortgage.” The hatch man spoke for the first time. “Antares doesn’t want the metal for a flag, engineer. We want the schedule. Whoever refines Azra first sets the clock for every hull between here and the Coal Sack. Drives. And the other thing.” He did not say weapons. The green text seemed to say it for him, cycling through harmless words: GYRO, GYRO, GYRO. Arthur said, “You’re asking me to pick a master.” “I am asking you to notice that you already have several.” Vey’s voice softened by a degree, no more. “The vein will be taken. That is not a threat. It is geology plus politics, which is a faster geology. What remains negotiable is whether you are paid, protected, disappeared, or made into an example for the next man who drills where he was told the ground was only tired.” A soft bell. The display cleared its diagnostics and held one line, brighter than the rest: DOCKING RADAR — ANTARES STATION / DIPLOMATIC RING. Through the port the station swelled, a wheel of old steel and new pride, lit in the amber that shipwrights still favored because their grandfathers had. Retrofit gantries clung to it like barnacles that had learned geometry. Arthur saw a courier blaze away sunward, and another hang in the traffic lane with the patient stillness of a thing that could become a weapon if asked twice. Vey rose. “When we board, do not volunteer the depth of the vein. Do not volunteer your mother’s name, your debts, or your opinion of the Compact. Answer what is asked. If you must lie, lie about small matters. They already own the large ones.” “And if their offer is a collar?” “Then you will at least have seen the hand that fastens it.” She paused at the hatch. The retinue made a corridor of grey shoulders and courteous muzzles. “There is a story the Corps tells its juniors. A man finds a star in his field. He thinks the star is his because the field is his. The star was falling before his grandfather was born. The field is only where it landed.” The lock sighed open onto warmer air, spiced with ozone and the dry perfume of recycled water. Somewhere a public address voice announced, in three languages, that diplomatic immunity was not a suggestion. Arthur stepped through, the green afterimage of the diagnostics still printed on his sight, and understood that the meeting had already begun — not in a room, but in the fact that he had been allowed to keep his boots on. At the end of the ring corridor a door dilated. Beyond it a single chair waited under a lamp, and opposite the chair a figure whose face the light had been instructed not to flatter. No guards showed. That, Arthur thought, was the most armed thing he had seen all day. “Mr. Neegan,” the figure said. “Sit. Let us discuss what your ground has decided to become, and what we might pay you to pretend you decided it.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong pastiche of Asimov-style classic SF: dialogue-driven intrigue, big-picture politics (Antares, the Compact, Tharsis Corporations) filtered through one small leaseholder's predicament, and a retrofuturistic aesthetic (spin gravity, comm lasers, amber-lit stations). The prose is polished, with several memorable lines ("politeness... machined to a tolerance," "geology plus politics, which is a faster geology"). The dialogue carries exposition efficiently while hinting at larger stakes. Vey is a nicely drawn secondary character; Arthur's voice is wry and consistent. The chapter fulfills the prompt: armed retinue, Antares insignia, off-world meeting, offer teased. Minor flaws: the meeting with the "principal" is only reached at the very end, so the actual offer is deferred; some aphorisms verge on cleverness-overload; the ending line is strong but the chapter ends just as the central scene begins. Length is appropriate. No purple prose or amateurish habits; coherent and engaging throughout.
