+ Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 62.5
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
Before the sun cleared the tiles of the ludus, I did what I always did on a fighting day and never on any other. I took the iron nail from the crack beneath my pallet—the one I had worked loose from a corpse-cart’s wheel the winter I was sold—and held it in my fist until the metal went warm. Then I touched it once to my tongue. The old Samnite who had trained me, dead now of a fever that cared nothing for skill, had said iron that had carried the dead kept Nemesis from misreading a man’s name. I believed him because I was still alive, which is a poor kind of proof and the only kind I had. Three drops of oil on the clay feet of her figurine. I spoke her name three times, no more. The oil smelled of the cheap press behind the fish market, rancid at the edges, and it beaded on the cracked paint of her wings. Outside, someone was already cursing a mule. The city answered with its usual choir: cartwheels on stone, a woman’s laugh cut short, the far clang of a smith, doves fouling the eaves. Barley and water for the morning. Lentils I would not touch. The same Samnite had sworn they weighted a dead man’s feet in the crossing, and I was not inclined to argue with the habits that had kept my throat uncut. The cook slapped the bowl down and did not meet my eyes. On ordinary days he joked. On these days he treated us as if we had already gone thin at the edges, half-ghosts borrowing bowls. I sat in the yard while the others stretched and oiled themselves. The sand was still night-cold under my heels. From beyond the wall came Rome in full throat: hawkers crying figs and sausages, the wet slap of fish on a board, a priest’s pipe somewhere toward the Forum, thin and sour. When the wind turned, the Tiber arrived with it—mud, tannery, the sweet rot of garum vats—and under that, charcoal and hot bread and the animal stink of the streets, horses and men and the lime they threw when the gutters failed. I breathed it in because it was not the hypogeum. Down there the air tasted of lamp smoke, wet stone, and fear that had soaked into the mortar. A boy from the kitchens said the emperor had ordered beasts enough to empty a province, and that the grain ships had been late again. He said it the way boys say anything, proud of the news and ignorant of its weight. I listened anyway. In the Dacian wars men had died for a line on a map and a triumph that would smell of perfume and slaughtered oxen. Here, if the ships were late, the same crowds who would scream my name by afternoon might scream for a magistrate’s blood by evening. The games were the lid on that pot. I had heard a senator’s freedman say as much in the portico last month, laughing, wine on his breath: keep their bellies soft and their eyes on the sand, and they will not count the taxes. He had looked through me as if I were a post. I was not Roman. I had been taken in a quarrel that was not mine, on a coast that still had my mother’s voice in it if I let myself listen, which I did not. The brand on my shoulder had faded to a pale hook. The law called what I did infamia—a stain that would not wash off if I lived to be freed, that barred me from the honors free men spent their lives angling for. Yet there were citizens in the cells upstairs who had sold themselves for debt or for the chance of a purse, and they slept no easier. Freedom, I had learned, was a word with many prices and few doors. I thought of Lucia, who sold ribbons near the cattle market and who had twice left bread where I could find it, wrapped in cloth that still held the scent of her hands—wool, dye, a little myrrh she must have touched in some other woman’s purchase. She could not stand in the open with me. A gladiator’s shadow was bad for trade and worse for reputation. If I won today there would be coin, and the lanista would take his share, and what remained might buy her a bolt of better cloth or nothing at all. If I lost, the nail and the oil would have been a story I told myself. I did not let the thought finish. Thoughts like that loosen the wrist. The doctore crossed the yard, scarred and precise, and nodded once. No speech. He knew which of us were marked for the afternoon and which were only sweating for the crowd’s idea of readiness. A whip cracked at the far gate—not on flesh, only in the air, to move a line of new men who still flinched at everything. The sound jumped along my spine anyway. I hated that it did. By midmorning the heat had climbed the walls. Oil on skin, leather, dust. A fly drank at the corner of my eye and I let it, because sudden motion felt like spending something I would need later. Over the wall I could see a slice of street: a woman in a saffron mantle, a boy with a cage of hens, two soldiers in red whose armor flashed and went dull again as a cloud passed. One of them laughed. They would have seats if they wanted them, or at least the right to stand where the smell of the arena rose sweet and rotten through the vomitoria—blood and perfume and the sawdust they threw down to keep the sand from going to paste. I would be under it, in the dark, listening to the crowd become one animal. Politics, the doctore liked to say, was just another arena with softer sand. He was wrong. In the other arena the men who lost kept their houses. A grain shortage, a whisper against the palace, a governor skimming the African shipments—these were stones thrown high, and they landed on people who had never held a sword. I was both stone and target. The editor of the games wanted a long afternoon and a short memory. The crowd wanted to feel, for an hour, that death could be arranged to please them. I wanted the nail to stay warm in my memory and the gate, when it opened, to open onto sand I already knew. Near noon they brought water that tasted of the pipe. I drank slowly. Somewhere a hydraulic organ was being tested in the amphitheatre; the notes wandered, broke, found themselves again, absurdly merry. Vendors would be staking claims on the approaches. Priests would be checking the small shrines. Nemesis had her place there too, cooler and better painted than mine. I preferred the cracked one. She had heard my name often enough to be tired of it, and tired gods, I hoped, were less inventive. I retied the strip of red wool at my left wrist, another bargain with luck, and stood. My legs were steady. My mouth still held the ghost of iron. In the street a crier was shouting the program, my arena name among others, already a story for men who would eat while they watched. I touched the figurine once more, not a fourth naming—only the oil, to be sure it had not run off—and listened to Rome breathe: smoke, dung, bread, river, incense from a procession I could not see, the bright senseless music, the restless human roar building toward a pleasure that was not mine. The gate to the street would open soon. I was not afraid in the way the kitchen boy would have understood fear. I was narrowed, the way a flame narrows in a draft. Whatever the sand decided, the city would go on selling figs and lying about grain and raising statues to men who never had to taste a dead cart’s nail. I waited with the others, smelling oil and dust and the faint rancid sweetness of the offering, and I did not look at the sky.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of historical fiction that fulfills nearly all prompt requirements: first person, past tense, non-combat slice of a gladiator's day, rich sensory detail, interiority, and political/social context (grain shortages, infamia, bread and circuses, provincial extraction). The word count is roughly on target. Strengths: The voice is consistent, restrained, and world-weary without becoming monotonous. The opening ritual with the iron nail is an excellent, specific detail that characterizes through action. Sensory work is layered and precise—the Tiber's "mud, tannery, the sweet rot of garum vats," the hypogeum's "fear that had soaked into the mortar." The political material is mostly integrated through the narrator's perspective rather than lectured, though a few passages (the freedman's speech, the "lid on that pot" reflection) edge toward essayistic exposition. The Lucia thread gives emotional stakes without sentimentality. The closing image—"I did not look at the sky"—lands well. Weaknesses: The piece occasionally over-annotates its own themes ("Politics, the doctore liked to say, was just another arena with softer sand. He was wrong."—this is a bit on-the-nose). Some aphoristic sentences ("Freedom... was a word with many prices and few doors") are polished but slightly writerly, showing the author's hand. The middle section on politics is the weakest stretch, drifting toward commentary. There is no dialogue, which is fine given the prompt, but the piece is entirely interior and observational, which limits dramatic momentum—appropriate for a "slice" but it means the piece risks stasis. A few metaphors ("half-ghosts borrowing bowls," "the crowd become one animal") are effective; others ("tired gods... were less inventive") are clever to the point of preciosity. The piece is very good but not a masterpiece: it doesn't quite achieve a moment of genuine surprise or emotional rupture. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 87.5
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
14 October Mam, The tender put me off at half-three and would not wait for the sea to lie down. I had the box with the blankets and the tin of tea, and that was the lot of it. The stair up from the landing is cut into the rock and greasy with weed. I went up it twice, once with the box and once because I had left the tea on a step like a fool. The light itself is sound. I wound the weights before dark and the optic turned clean, a full turn every minute as the book says. The dwelling is two rooms and a scullery, all of it smelling of paraffin and damp wool. There is a stove. The coal store is half what they told me in Oban. I will send the wage as soon as the agent pays it. Do not put any of it aside for me. Your son, Callum — 22 October Callum, The ten shillings came. I paid Mrs Kerr the two months we were behind and bought oats and a bit of bacon. I am not putting any aside. You said not to, and I have not got the habit of arguing with a man who is not in the room. Eat. You were always the one to miss a meal and call it discipline. It is not discipline if your hands shake on a stair. Write when you can. The street is the same. The MacLeods have taken in a lodger who sings. I shut the window. Your mother — 9 January Mam, I have not written because the weather has been at us and the tender has missed both calls. That is the plain of it, and also I did not want to put this down. On the third the drive that turns the optic seized. Not the weights. The weights drop fine. It is the collar above the pedestal, salt worked into it until the metal dragged. I had oil and I had a rag and neither of it mattered. From dusk to near five in the morning I turned the lens by hand so the character would hold. One turn a minute. You count it or the ships get a fixed light and a fixed light is a lie. My shoulder is bad on the right side. I sleep an hour in the forenoon and then I am at the collar with a file and a kettle of fresh water, trying to wash the salt out of a thing that was never meant to come apart. The coal is down to a scrape. I burn the stove only to heat water for the metal. At night I stay in the lantern room where the lamp keeps the air off freezing. My breath still rimes the glass on the landward panes. The light has not failed. I need you to know that before anything else. It has not failed. If the tender comes I will send what I can. Do not write back asking me to leave it dark an hour. I will not. Callum — 28 January Callum, I was not going to ask you to leave it dark. You think I do not know what a light is for. Your father ran for the mail boat in worse than this and came home with his hands split, and I never told him to tie up short of the harbour. I am angry that they left you one man on a station with a seized collar and no coal. That is the Commissioners’ doing, not the sea’s. When you are back on a mainland pier you will tell them so, and you will not make it small to spare a clerk. Mrs Kerr asked after you. I said you were well. I will not say it twice. There is a tin of ham in the press from Christmas that I was keeping for no good reason. It will do neither of us any good in a press. I have spoke to the agent. If they will take a parcel on the next tender it will be on it, and a pair of your father’s thick gloves that I should have sent in October. The right one has a darn across the palm. It will still turn a handle. Eat the ham when it comes. All of it. Not half for later. Your mother — 17 March Mam, The tender got in on the eleventh, first time since the new year. The ham is gone. I am not proud of the speed of that. The gloves fit. The darn sits where the handle bites, which is either luck or you remembering which hand I favour. I think it is the latter. You always watched closer than you let on. I got the collar free on the fourth of February. Not with the file. The file only polished the seizure. I drew the pin out of the scullery door hinge, heated it in the stove until it ran a colour I trusted, and set it through the collar as a shear where the old pin had worn oval. It is an ugly mend. It has turned every night since. I check it at each hour and again if the wind backs. Some nights I still stand with my hand on the frame, not turning, only ready. The shoulder wakes me before the clock does. A coaster passed on the ninth, close enough that I saw her deck cargo shift in the troughs. She held her course by the flashes. I counted them against my own count and they matched. I sat on the gallery after and was ill over the rail, from the standing still, I think, or from having a use for the ugly pin. I have written to the Commissioners. Not small. I said the station wants two men through the winter and a spare collar in the store, and that a keeper turning an optic by hand is not a romantic thing, it is a fault in their maintenance. I do not expect a reply that pleases me. I expect the light to keep its character until my relief. The wage note is in with this. Pay the rent through May. After that I will be on the Oban road with my own box, tea included this time. I am not signing again. I thought I would be ashamed to tell you that. I am not. The quiet here is not peace. It is a weight, and I have carried enough weights for them. Callum — 2 April Callum, May, then. I will have the bed aired and the window shut if the lodger is at his song. You tell me you are not ashamed. Good. Shame is a poor wage and you have already earned the other kind. The pin in the collar, the nights you counted, the letter you sent them without making yourself small: that is the work. Coming home is not the undoing of it. I paid through May. There is a little over. It will stay in the tin until you are here to argue with me about it in the room, which is the arrangement I prefer. The stair at this house is steep enough. Mind your shoulder on it. Your mother
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an accomplished epistolary piece that fulfills the brief with notable discipline. The two voices are genuinely distinct: Callum is terse, technical, and self-effacing, while his mother is dry, wry, and quietly fierce ("I have not got the habit of arguing with a man who is not in the room"). The Scottish working-class register is convincing without lapsing into phonetic caricature — diction like "half-three," "the plain of it," "rimed," and "I have spoke to the agent" does the work instead of apostrophized dialect. The plot unfolds gradually and well: the arrival, the wage, the seized collar crisis, the hand-turned optic, the improvised pin mend, the letter of complaint to the Commissioners, and the resignation. The crisis letter is the emotional core, and its restraint is its strength — "The light has not failed. I need you to know that before anything else" lands hard precisely because it is not elaborated. The mother's reply, refusing to ask him to leave it dark and invoking the father, deepens both characters economically. Show-don't-tell is largely exemplary: the ham eaten too fast, the darn placed where the handle bites, the vomiting over the rail after the coaster passes, the pin drawn from the scullery door hinge. These details carry personality and motivation without editorializing. The ending — resignation framed not as defeat but as refusal to carry more weight for them, and the mother's affirmation that "Coming home is not the undoing of it" — is earned and avoids both sentimentality and incongruent brightness. Minor criticisms: the mother's final letter edges toward aphorism ("Shame is a poor wage"), slightly more polished than her established voice. The emotional arc resolves perhaps a touch neatly; the Commissioners' negligence is never answered, though that ambiguity is arguably realistic. The piece is short of the 1000-word seed but not drastically. Some might find the mother's wisdom slightly too consistently on-target, flattening her into a moral anchor. But these are small flaws in a piece that is otherwise controlled, unsentimental, and moving. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I told myself I would look at her eyes. I have been looking at the reflection in the wineglass instead, because reflections are honest and eyes are a protocol I keep misreading. The restaurant is loud in the way places get when they want you to lean in. She leaned in. I did. That part worked. She said she played Magic, and something in my chest unclenched like a lock I had forgotten was set. Not the competitive circuit. Kitchen-table, sleeves in a shoebox, the kind of player who still says "the blue one" and means a whole philosophy. She is talking about a deck she built around tokens. I file it without meaning to. Parallel Lives. Anointed Procession. She likes multiplication more than removal. She would rather the board get crowded than clean. Generous, or greedy. Both, probably. She laughs when she admits she still runs Swords to Plowshares "for the mean friends," which means she understands mercy as a resource you spend on other people and keep a little of for yourself. I am supposed to be having a date. I am having a date. The bread is good. Her hands are careful with the glass. I notice the carefulness and then I notice that I noticed, and I hate the second noticing more than the first. Her phone lights up face-down beside the candle. She flips it, thumb already moving, and the pattern is three dots in a corner and a lazy diagonal, the kind of shape a person draws when they have decided the world is mostly kind. I see it the way you see a door left open. Not because I reached. Because my eyes still do the inventory before my mouth gets a vote. I should let it go. Reformed is a verb I practice. White hat is a costume that only counts if you keep it on when nobody is scoring you. "That's a pretty guessable pattern," I say. The sentence leaves before I can put it back. Her thumb stops. The phone goes dark. She looks at me the way people look at a smoke alarm that went off for toast. "Sorry," I say, which is true and also insufficient. "Occupational hazard. I used to get paid to find the lazy diagonals. I don't do that work on people I'm trying to like." She sets the phone face-down again, slower. "Trying to." "Am. Liking. Present tense. The hazard is past tense. Mostly." She takes a piece of bread and does not offer me the basket, which is fair. I catalog that too, and then I make myself stop cataloging the basket. She talks about a game she lost because she tapped out for a huge Doubling Season and ate a counterspell. I hear the preference under the anecdote: she overextends when the math gets pretty. She believes in the turn where everything becomes more of itself. I want to tell her that belief is a vulnerability and also the only reason any of this is worth sitting through. I do not say vulnerability. I have used up my quota. "I play control," I say, because silence is starting to look like reconnaissance. "Or I did. Counterspells, board wipes, the long game. People hated playing me. I was very proud of that, which should have been a clue." "So you don't build the huge turn." "I stop other people's huge turns and then apologize with my face." She almost smiles. It is not the smile from before the phone. It is smaller and more expensive. "You apologized with your mouth just now. Face is still doing the thing." "What thing?" "Like you're reading the menu for exploits." The waiter arrives with plates and saves me from an honest answer. Her pasta. My fish. I focus on salt, heat, the ordinary miracle of food that is only food. She mentions a commander, Atraxa, and I feel the old grid light up: proliferate, counters, inevitability, a strategy that wins by becoming slightly more true every turn. She likes engines. She likes time on her side. She would lose to someone patient enough to let her build and rude enough to knock the engine over once. I used to be that someone. I am trying to be the person who asks what the deck feels like instead. "Does it feel fun," I ask, "or does it feel like you're solving them?" She chews. Considers. "Both. That's the problem with the game. And with you, maybe." "Maybe." She unlocks the phone again, turned toward herself this time, angle closed. Good. I am relieved and also ashamed of the relief, because relief means I was still watching the angle. She shows me a photo of a beat-up playmat, not the screen underneath. Goblin Rabblemaster in the corner, half under a coffee ring. Aggression, tokens again, pressure that does not ask permission. She is not only the proliferate player. She has a red deck for the nights she does not want to wait. "I keep meaning to get a screen thing," she says. "Privacy whatever. My brother yells at me about it." "Your brother is right, and I should not have been the one to say it like that." "Like a party trick." "Like I couldn't help it. Which is worse, because it means the help is still optional and I didn't choose it fast enough." She nods, once. The date is not saved. It is also not dead. Those are different states. I have spent years confusing them. She talks about a mirror match that went to time because neither of them would attack into a board of saprolings. I add it to the list I promised myself I would not keep: she fears the counterattack more than the stalled game. She would rather draw than lose. That is a strategy preference and also a dating preference, and I am not allowed to weaponize either. I can only hear it. "If I order dessert," she says, "are you going to audit the spoon?" "I'll try to taste it." "Try is doing a lot of work." "I know." She orders the chocolate thing. I do not mention that the receipt printer at the host stand is facing the room, or that the waiter reused a password-shaped shrug when the card reader hiccuped, or that her bag is open under the chair with a house key glinting like a bad joke. I put my hands on the table where she can see them. I ask which card she would never cut, even if it was wrong. "Parallel Lives," she says. "Objectively cuttable. I refuse." I laugh, and it is not a performance. She likes the card that makes more of what she already chose. She would rather be inconsistent than small. I write that down in the only place I am still allowed to write things: not a report, not a vector, just the part of the evening I hope she lets me keep. The chocolate arrives. She breaks the crust and does not hand me the first bite, which is correct. She watches me not watching her phone. "Still noticing?" she asks. "Yes," I say. "I'm not going to do anything with it. That's the whole reform. Not the not-noticing. The not-using." She considers that the way she considered tapping out for Doubling Season. Then she slides the plate an inch toward the center. "Okay," she says. "Tell me a card you refuse to cut." I pick up the spoon. For three full seconds I only taste the dessert. Then I answer, and I leave the rest of the room unopened.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece that executes the prompt with precision and genuine craft. The internal monologue voice is consistent and distinctive: clipped, analytical, self-surveilling, with the hacker's habit of "cataloging" rendered as both comedy and pathology. The Magic: The Gathering material is used exceptionally well—not as decoration but as a parallel language for the characters' emotional strategies (she overextends into hope; he plays control and counters; the "huge turn" as vulnerability). The MTG references are accurate and thematically load-bearing (Parallel Lives, Doubling Season, Atraxa, Swords to Plowshares, Goblin Rabblemaster). The phone-pattern faux pas lands naturally, and the fallout is negotiated with believable small stakes: the withheld bread basket, the angled phone, the "smaller and more expensive" smile. The dialogue is sharp and characterful—"Try is doing a lot of work," "You apologized with your mouth just now"—though occasionally the banter tilts toward overly polished quippiness ("I stop other people's huge turns and then apologize with my face"). Weaknesses: the prose occasionally overreaches for aphorism ("Reformed is a verb I practice," "inevitability... a strategy that wins by becoming slightly more true every turn," "the ordinary miracle of food that is only food"). Some of these land; a few feel like the writer admiring their own cleverness, a mild purple/overwrought tendency. The ending is good but slightly neat—the plate sliding an inch toward center is a touch on-the-nose as a reconciliation gesture. The final line is strong. The transformation is appropriately modest (not saved, not dead), avoiding unearned resolution. The piece stays within the word target and is almost entirely internal monologue as instructed. + First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 86.3
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I have already said the word “okay” four times, and none of them counted, because none of them left my mouth. They lined up behind my teeth like kids who know the answer and still won’t raise their hands. Okay if I take the data sheet. Okay, your handwriting is better. Okay, I brought extra graph paper, which is not a confession, which is not I thought about you while I was at the store and put two packs in the basket and then put one back because two would look like a plan. Ms. Keller said partners, and the word landed in my chest before it landed in the room. He slid his chair over. The leg caught on the tile and squeaked, and I smiled at the squeak like it had told a joke, which is worse than not smiling. Now my face is doing the wrong thing and I can feel it from the inside, the muscles pulled too high, and if I fix it too fast he’ll see the correction, so I have to let the smile die of natural causes. That takes forever. Forever is the length of him uncapping a pen. Say something normal. Normal is: the independent variable is light. I have said this in my head with three different stresses. Light, like I’m reminding him. Light, like I’m discovering it. Light, like it’s funny that plants care. None of those are funny. If I make it funny I will sound like I’m performing, and performing is one wrong turn from weird, and weird is the hallway version of me that people quote later with the wrong eyebrows. He says we should do the one with the lamp. His voice is ordinary. I hate that I have filed it. I hate that ordinary can still rearrange the air. I nod. Nodding is safe if it is one nod. Two nods is eager. I do one and then my head betrays me with a smaller second one, a comma, and I pretend I was looking at the lamp cord. The group is four. Maya is measuring the beaker like the beaker insulted her. Jordan is already writing the hypothesis in handwriting that leans forward, impatient. He—I keep not using his name even in here, as if the name is louder—is drawing the setup, boxes for pots, arrows for light. I am supposed to record observations. I open the lab notebook to a clean page and the page looks like a test I didn’t study for. Tiny sketches. That part I can do without permission from my throat. A circle for Maya, eyebrows two short lines, because she concentrates with her whole forehead. Jordan as a rectangle with a pen taller than his head. Ms. Keller in the corner of the margin, hair a cloud, because she orbits. And him: not a face. If I draw his face and he leans over, the drawing becomes evidence. I do his sleeve instead. The cuff. A hand on a ruler. Hands are facts. Faces are accusations. “You good with notes?” he asks. Yes. I am good with notes. I am good with notes the way I am good with entire paragraphs I will never spend. Out loud I manage, “Yeah.” The yeah comes out smaller than the room. I watch it go and want to edit it. Add I’m fine, or I like this part, or something with a shape. Too late. Yeah is already a stone in the middle of the table. He doesn’t look disappointed. That is worse. Disappointment would be data. This is nothing, and nothing can mean he didn’t notice, which is what I want, or that he noticed and filed me under quiet, which is the folder people don’t open twice. Rehearse the next line while Jordan argues about soil. Option one: I think we should control for water, same amount each day. Intelligent. Useful. Proves I read the sheet. Risk: I interrupt Jordan, and interrupting makes me visible, and visible is where mistakes live. Option two: wait until Jordan finishes, then say it softer, like I’m offering, not correcting. Risk: by then Maya will have said it, and I’ll be the echo, and echoes sound like they were afraid to be first. Option three: write it in the notes and turn the notebook so he can see, a silent contribution, no voice required. Risk: he reads my handwriting, which gets worse when I know it’s being read, and also the margin already has his sleeve in it. I close the notebook one inch. Open it again. The inch was suspicious. My knee is bouncing. I stop it. Stopping it is also a movement, and movements can be read. I put both feet flat and then I am so aware of both feet that I forget the hypothesis. The hypothesis was about light and height. Height of the plant, not height of the silence, though the silence has a height. It stacks each time I almost speak. He laughs at something Jordan says. The laugh is short. I smile again because not smiling at a group laugh is a sign, a sign that says I am elsewhere, and elsewhere is where weird people live, the ones who watch too carefully. So I smile at the right time and hate that I timed it. Monitoring is a second job. Word, face, hands, feet, the angle of my shoulders, whether I am turned toward him too many degrees. Desperate is an angle. I don’t know the number. I keep adjusting by half degrees until I am facing the lamp like the lamp is the interesting one. “You want to do the measuring?” he asks me. Direct. Kind, maybe, or just practical. Practical can wear kind’s jacket and I will not be able to tell them apart, which is the exhausting part, the part nobody claps for: I will go home and replay practical until it changes shape. “Sure,” I say. Better than yeah. Two syllables. I almost add if you want, and kill it, because if you want is a door I would be holding open with my whole arm. Sure is a closed door that still lets him through. Good. Leave it. He slides the ruler over. Our fingers don’t touch. I notice the not-touch so precisely that it becomes a kind of touch, which is insane, which is exactly the thought I cannot have on my face. I look at the ruler. Centimeters. Safe. I can be a person who cares about centimeters. That person has a voice. She says, in my head, We’ll mark the stem at the soil line so we don’t count the pot. Clean. Correct. I open my mouth and what comes out is, “Soil line.” Just the noun. A fragment. He nods like a fragment is a sentence. Mercy or indifference. I take the mercy because indifference has better posture and I am tired. Maya says the lamp is too close. She is right. I knew she was right four seconds before she spoke and still didn’t say it, and now the four seconds sit in me like a mint I can’t swallow. I write Lamp distance: 30 cm in the notes so the knowing has somewhere to go. Under it, without deciding to, I add the smallest sketch yet: four dots in a row, the group as seen from the ceiling, and one dot a little nearer the center than it meant to be. I scribble the nearness into a smudge. Evidence removed. The smudge looks like a mistake. Mistakes are allowed in lab notes. Wanting is not. He leans in to check the number I wrote. I smell pencil and the cafeteria’s leftover orange. I do not inhale on purpose. I think about inhaling on purpose and then I am monitoring my breath, which is so stupid I could laugh, and laughing would be unexplained, so I don’t. I hold still. Stillness, if you work at it, starts to shake. “Thirty’s good,” he says. I want to say I can do the next one, or we should label the pots before we forget which is which, or your drawing of the arrows is clearer than the diagram on the board. All of those are true. All of them can be said by a person who is not desperate. I know this. My inside voice is already writing the lab report, topic sentences and all, calm as a teacher. My outside voice is a stalled engine. The gap between them is where I live. It is not dramatic. It is a hallway with too many doors and a girl standing in it, hand on none of them, rehearsing the knock until the bell rings. “Cool,” I say. Cool. I will hear it tonight. I will try to sand it into something smoother and it will still be the only word I managed while he was close enough to read my notes. He sits back. The air returns to its normal size. Jordan starts a timer. Maya sighs at the soil. I draw one more tiny thing in the corner, a lamp with too many rays, and tell myself the rays are data, not a feeling, and almost believe it, which is as close to brave as I get before the next measurement, when I will have to speak again, and the rehearsals will already be lining up, bright and useless, behind my teeth.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally strong piece of internal monologue writing that fulfills nearly every requirement of the prompt with precision and craft. The narrator's voice is articulate, self-aware, and consistently anxious without becoming repetitive or whiny. The gap between her rich internal voice and her fragmentary spoken output ("Yeah," "Sure," "Cool," "Soil line") is dramatized rather than merely stated, which is the prompt's central demand and the piece's greatest success. The metaphorical texture is impressive and mostly controlled: rehearsed words "lined up behind my teeth like kids who know the answer and still won't raise their hands," the smile that must "die of natural causes," "Desperate is an angle," "Wanting is not" allowed in lab notes. These are fresh, age-appropriate, and character-revealing. The science-project setting is used structurally—the language of variables, data, evidence, and observation becomes the lens through which she processes social interaction, which is both clever and thematically unified. The character is nuanced: intelligent, self-monitoring, wry about her own absurdity ("I do not inhale on purpose"), and capable of small acts of agency (the sketches, the smudged dot). The crush is never named, a deliberate and effective choice the narrator herself flags. The minor characters (Maya, Jordan, Ms. Keller) are sketched economically but vividly. Weaknesses are minor. The piece occasionally risks over-cleverness—nearly every sentence carries a metaphor or inversion, and a few ("the silence has a height," "indifference has better posture") tip toward the overwrought, though the narrator's self-awareness mostly licenses this. The dialogue is intentionally minimal and appropriately stunted; it serves the piece. The ending is honest rather than transformative—no false breakthrough—which is the right call, though the final paragraph slightly over-explains the "gap" theme the whole piece has already shown. The word count is close to the 1000-word seed. + First-person unique perspective: Rehearsing Rejection — Score: 64.1
Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The shirt is wrong. I already know it is wrong because I chose it to look like I did not choose it, and they will see that, the trying, the soft cotton pretending to be accident. If I change it I will be late, and late is a sentence. Late means I do not respect their time. On time means I was waiting, which is worse, which is need with its face washed. Through the wall the television is saying something about weather. A woman’s voice, then a man’s, then laughter that does not belong to either of them. I cannot make out the words. I keep trying anyway, as if the forecast might tell me whether to go. They have been quiet. Not gone. Quiet. Three days of short answers, a heart on a photo and nothing under it, a call that ended because they were “in something.” In something. I have built the something. I have furnished it. They are sitting across from someone easier, someone who does not check the read receipt like a pulse. They are rehearsing how to say it kindly. They are tired. Of course they are tired. I would be tired of me. I practice it in the mirror so my mouth will not do it later. You don’t have to explain, I say to the glass. I’m not going to make this a thing. That sounds like a thing. That sounds like a trap with the teeth filed down. Fine. Then: I noticed you’ve been distant. I just want to know where I stand. Where I stand. As if there is a floor and not a drop. They will say, I’ve been busy. They will say it gently, which is how people leave while still in the room. I will nod. I will be reasonable. Later I will hate them for the gentleness, for making me the one who heard a door in a draft. The neighbor’s laugh track swells and cuts. Someone on the other side of the plaster is having a night that arrives on schedule. If I cancel, I am punishing them for a crime they might not have committed. If I go, I am handing them the knife and calling it trust. Both are true. Both cannot be true. My chest does not care about cannot. I text: On my way. A period, not an exclamation. Exclamation points are begging. Their reply comes before I have put the phone down. Can’t wait. Missed you. Missed you. The words land in my body before they land in my mind, a heat under the ribs, stupid and total. I read them again. Can’t wait. As if the three days were weather and not a verdict. I almost smile at the screen. Then the smile curdles, because of course they would say that if they were about to do it in person. Kindness first. The soft open. I have used it myself. I am not going to do this, I tell myself, and the sentence has no weight. I know the shape of it. I have named it in other rooms, to other ceilings. It does not stop the next frame: their face when they see the shirt, the small recalculation, the way love looks when it is already packing. The hallway smells like someone else’s dinner. On the stairs I invent the conversation we will not survive. I didn’t mean to pull away, they say. You didn’t pull away. You vanished. There’s a difference. I needed a minute. A minute is three days when you’re the one counting. You always count. There. There it is. The criticism I can answer, because I have answered it in cars and bathrooms and the blue dark before sleep. I am too much. I make a thermometer out of ordinary silence. I hear abandonment in a delayed text the way other people hear a smoke alarm. And the defense rises on cue, hot and ready: if you didn’t disappear, I wouldn’t have to measure the distance. If you stayed where I could see you, I could be a person and not a vigil. It feels like logic. It feels like a locked door that proves the house is safe. Outside, the air is ordinary. That offends me. A bus sighs at the corner. I walk faster so I will not be the one who arrives already wounded, and slower so I will not be the one who arrives starving. I fail at both. They are already at the table by the window. They stand when they see me. Not the half-rise of obligation. They stand, and their face does the unguarded thing, the one I have screenshotted in my head and then accused of being performance. Their hand finds my wrist, not my elbow, not the safe public inch. Wrist. Pulse. They say my name like it is not a problem to solve. “Hey,” they say. “God, hi. You look—” They stop, almost laugh at themselves. “I had a sentence. It left. Come here.” I come here. The hug is too long for a café and not long enough for the three days. I feel them breathe. I feel chosen, which is a physical event, embarrassing, a flood behind my eyes that I blink back because if I cry at hello they will know what the quiet did to me, and knowing will make them careful, and careful is the hallway before the exit. “I missed you,” they say into my hair. “Work ate the week. I kept meaning to call and then it was midnight and I didn’t want to be the person who only calls when they’re useless. That’s a bad reason. I’m saying it anyway.” Work. Midnight. A reason with furniture, not a metaphor. I should let it be a reason. For a second I do. The second is so relieving I almost resent it, the way thirst resents the glass for ending. Then the other voice, quick, professional: They prepared that. They knew you would audit the gap, so they brought a receipt. Useful. Midnight. Listen to how clean it is. I sit. My hands find the menu so they have a job. “You don’t have to explain.” “I want to,” they say. “You went quiet on your end too, and I did the thing where I assume you’re fine because assuming you’re not feels like I’m making it about me. Which is also making it about me. I’m not good at this yet. I want to be.” Yet. Want. The words are so close to what I needed that I distrust them on principle. Need is a tell. If I show them the size of it, they will measure the door. The neighbor’s television is not here, but I hear it anyway, muffled dialogue, a life continuing on the other side of a wall I carried with me. I look at their mouth. They are talking about a deadline, a coworker, a stupid email, offering me the ordinary as proof. Their knee rests against mine under the table and does not retreat when the server comes. I press back. The contact goes through me like a current and I think, don’t move, don’t be the first to move, if you move first it means you were keeping score. They notice. Of course they notice. “You okay?” “Yes.” Too fast. I try again, because some small part of me is still in the room and not in the rehearsal. “I got in my head. About the quiet. I do that. I know I do that.” There. The recognition, thin as a receipt. I can see the pattern from here: the trial I held without them, the defense I polished, the resentment I put on like a coat so the cold would be my idea. I know the coat. I am still wearing it. Knowing is not the same as taking it off. The coat has pockets. The pockets have their voice in it, saying the things they have not said. They don’t flinch at the admission. They look relieved, which I immediately translate as relief that I am the problem, so they don’t have to be. Then they reach across and turn my hand over, thumb in the center of my palm, a small stupid anchor. “I wasn’t leaving,” they say. “I was bad at saying I was still here. Those aren’t the same. I’m going to get better at the second one. You can tell me when the first story starts. You don’t have to win it alone before I arrive.” I want to believe them so badly it feels like a fall. I do believe them. I don’t. Both at once, the dissonance sitting in my teeth. Their thumb moves once, a fact, not a speech. I hold still inside it. The imagined confrontation keeps talking in the back room, indignant that it was not invited to the table. I let it talk. I also order the thing I actually want, and when they laugh at something small I said without auditing it, the laugh is not a laugh track through plaster. It is here. It is for me. I feel it. I need it. I start, already, to ask what it will cost, and for one breath I do not ask out loud.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece executes the prompt with considerable skill. The internal monologue dominates, cycling convincingly through anticipatory rejection, rehearsed confrontation, preemptive resentment ("the coat"), and the desperate intake of validation followed immediately by suspicion. The friend-lover is warm, explains their distance plausibly, and the narrator's distorted translations ("relief that I am the problem") capture cognitive dissonance exactly as requested. The limited self-awareness is handled well: "Knowing is not the same as taking it off. The coat has pockets." The recurring neighbor's television motif gives structure and atmosphere. Strengths: sharp, aphoristic imagery ("need with its face washed," "a trap with the teeth filed down," "a thermometer out of ordinary silence"); the imagined dialogue feels both rehearsed and defensive; the actual interactions are warmly mundane and believable; the ending resists a full cure—doubt persists "in the back room," which earns the lightness. Weaknesses: the aphoristic density occasionally tips toward over-cleverness, with nearly every paragraph reaching for an epigram; the lover's dialogue, while plausible, is somewhat idealized—articulate, perfectly attuned, almost therapeutic in phrasing ("You don't have to win it alone before I arrive"), which softens believability slightly. Some metaphors (the receipt, the audit) feel like authorial showing. Word count is near target. Overall, a strong, controlled performance with minor over-polish. + Physical-spatial: Blood Debt — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The temple had lost its god and kept its echo. Moonlight fell through a split in the roof and laid a pale bar across the stone, and through that bar a thread of water crept from a cracked flagstone, running north to south like a vein. It was no wider than a hand, but it polished the floor to glass. Men and women pressed along the broken walls, coins clenched, voices low. No master was here to forbid what their masters had forbidden. Takeshi stood on the west side, three paces from the water, bare feet set wide. The old arrogance sat in his shoulders: Jigen-ryū did not circle. It arrived. Opposite him, Bao waited east of the trickle, jacket sleeves rolled, weight on the balls of his feet. Between them the wet line shone. Eight paces of air. The crowd’s breath made a single animal sound. Takeshi moved first. Two dry steps ate the distance; the third planted on the slick. His right foot shot a finger’s width outward. He dropped his hips to save the line and fired the right cross anyway, a straight bolt meant for Bao’s center. The slip stole a hand’s width from the punch. It arrived short and hot, knuckles grazing cloth. Bao had already gone north, off the line, left foot clear of the water’s eastern lip. His right arm whipped in a long downward arc—not a block so much as a scythe—and met Takeshi’s forearm, shedding it toward the south. The same motion carried on. The heel of Bao’s palm cracked into the point of Takeshi’s right shoulder. The sound was dull, like a melon set down too hard. Takeshi’s charge did not stop. He blew past Bao’s hip and fetched up against the broken altar on the east side, stone biting his ribs. He spun. Now the altar was at his back. Bao stood north of him, between him and the water, facing southeast. The crowd on the north ledge roared; coins changed hands in the dark. Takeshi did not reset. He exploded off the altar, left foot leading, cutting the angle to Bao’s right. A short left jab probed, then a right elbow driven on the same track, meant to collapse the space Bao liked to live in. Bao gave the elbow the circle it hated. He pivoted on his left foot, hips turning west, and the elbow found only the sweep of his left forearm. Cloth whispered. Bao’s right hand came back the other way, a whipping backfist that clipped Takeshi’s ear and set a bright ring in his skull. They were tight now, north of the altar, the water a pace to Bao’s left and behind Takeshi’s right heel if he retreated. Takeshi felt that. Retreat was not in him. He stamped, feinted high, and drove a low right kick at Bao’s lead thigh. Bao lifted the leg. The kick met shin, not muscle, and Takeshi’s planted left foot—set too near the wet thread—skidded. For a heartbeat his stance was a rumor. Bao took it. He stepped in on the wet stone as if he had been born to it, knees soft, and lashed a circular left palm into Takeshi’s floating ribs. The strike did not crash; it wrapped and snapped, the force arriving late, after the arm had already passed. Air left Takeshi in a grunt. He answered on instinct, the school’s whole creed in one motion: he crashed forward, forehead dropping, right hand spearing for the throat while his left forearm chopped down at Bao’s wrist to pin the circle still. He caught cloth. Not throat. Bao had already folded away to the south, along the water’s edge, and the chop met empty air. Takeshi’s right foot chased and found the slick full on. The sole went out from under him. He did not fall so much as ride the skid, turning it into a lunging knee aimed at Bao’s hip as Bao crossed back toward the center. The knee landed. Bao’s breath broke. He staggered east, one hand slapping the altar for truth, the other still moving in that loose whip the street had taught him. Takeshi came after, both feet finally on dry stone east of the thread, pride burning hotter than the ribs. Three strikes, he told himself. One to break the guard, one to break the body, one to end the name. He threw them. Left hook to the head—Bao slipped inside it, south shoulder brushing Takeshi’s chest. Right straight to the body—Bao’s left forearm rolled it down and away, the deflection feeding his own turn. Takeshi’s third strike, an elbow meant to finish on the jaw, never found its mark. Bao’s right foot had planted on the dry lip just east of the water; his hips coiled; his right arm came up from the low outside in a long rising arc, palm open, and met Takeshi at the hinge of the jaw as Takeshi’s own momentum carried him onto it. The crack was small. The effect was not. Takeshi’s head snapped west. His lead foot, chasing balance, stepped back onto the thread of water and went. He sat down hard on the wet stone, one hand in the trickle, the other still half-raised in a strike that had nowhere left to go. Blood threaded from his split lip into the water and ran south, toward the drain. Bao stood over him, chest heaving, palm stinging, the north crowd already screaming his school’s name and the south crowd cursing the slick as if the stone had taken a side. He did not offer a hand. Takeshi did not ask for one. For a moment the only clean sound was the water, patient, carrying a thin red line between them across the floor their masters would never see.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a tightly controlled, well-choreographed fight scene that fulfills nearly all of the prompt's demands. The physical coherence is excellent: the writer establishes a spatial anchor (the thread of water running north-south, the altar on the east side) and consistently tracks both fighters relative to it. Slips, skids, and momentum shifts are all causally motivated—the wet stone is introduced early and pays off repeatedly, culminating in Takeshi's final fall. The choreography is legible and specific: strikes, deflections, and counters are described with directional and anatomical precision without becoming a dry blow-by-blow list. The stylistic contrast between the two arts is well rendered. Jigen-ryū's explosive linear aggression ("It arrived") is set against Piguaquan's circular, whipping evasiveness, and the class animus is conveyed economically through posture and instinct rather than exposition. The crowd, wagering, and setting are sketched with restraint. Prose quality is high: sentences are rhythmic, concrete, and largely free of cliché. A few lines flirt with over-polish ("his stance was a rumor," "the temple had lost its god and kept its echo"), but these are effective rather than purple. The ending is appropriately unsentimental—no handshake, no reconciliation—which suits the rivalry and the "blood debt" title. Weaknesses: characterization is thin beyond archetype; the fighters are defined by style and pride but have little interiority beyond Takeshi's brief "three strikes" thought. The piece is almost entirely action with minimal emotional arc beyond the fight's ebb and flow. There is no dialogue, which is fine given the prompt. The word count is slightly under 1000 but acceptable. Some might find the outcome (the slick deciding the finish) slightly convenient, though it is well-seeded. Overall this is a strong, professional-grade piece of fight writing with minor limitations in depth. Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The white X under my left heel is the only honest thing in the room. Everything else is a lie I am supposed to learn by heart. Mirrors take the north wall from corner to corner. Eight of us face them in two rows of four, shoulders squared to the glass, a meter between bodies. I am back row, second from the left. Front-left is Minjae, already perfect, his reflection a clean vertical line. To my right, Hana holds her arms like they have been measured. Instructor Park stands at the northeast edge of the mirror, just off the glass, black fan closed in her right hand, left foot pointed toward the formation so she can see our angles and our faces at once. Speakers sit on the south wall behind us. The downbeat will come from over my left shoulder and hit the mirror a fraction later. I have already decided I hate that delay. “Five, six, seven, eight.” The track is bright and merciless, sixteen counts of a chorus we have been killing since dawn. On one I am meant to isolate the chest—pop forward, freeze, no bounce in the knees. My ribs do it. My knees do not. A street groove drops into them, the old pocket from the corner by the bus stop, weight rocking through the balls of my feet before I can kill it. The mirror shows the mistake as a smear: everyone else is a still photograph; I am a half-second of weather. Two: right arm shoots to a forty-five, elbow locked, wrist flat, fingers a blade. I get the angle. I do not get the death in it. The arm arrives and wants to keep traveling, a liquid wave looking for a wrist circle that does not exist in this choreography. Muscle memory finishes the circle anyway, small, shameful, a coin-flip of the hand. In the glass, Hana’s arm is a stopped clock. Mine is still negotiating. Three and four: pivot on the left foot, quarter-turn to camera-right—east—right knee lifts to hip height, toe pointed, standing leg straight. I turn. The room swings. Park slides from the corner of my eye to dead ahead, fan still open a crack. My right knee comes up late and soft, the way I would chamber a top-rock step, not a picture. The lift has flavor. Flavor is the crime. Five and six: drop. Both rows collapse on the same count into a low crouch, spines long, palms flat on the floor beside the tape marks, heads level. I go down through the bounce instead of through the hinge. My left palm finds the X. My right palm lands a hand’s width too far east because the turn left my weight on the wrong edge of the foot. The formation’s shoulders make a clean horizontal in the mirror. Mine breaks it by a thumb. Seven and eight: the change. Front row steps straight back on the right foot, passing between us; back row steps forward on a diagonal—left foot first for me, cutting toward the mark Minjae is abandoning, so that I arrive center-front, facing north again, arms snapping down to the sides on eight. I know the map. I have walked it twenty times marking. Full out, my body files it as a cypher entry. I cross in front of Hana instead of slipping the diagonal inside her path. Our shoulders clip. She corrects without looking at me, a small reset of her right foot back onto her new X. I am now where Minjae was, a meter from the mirror, too close, breath fogging a coin of glass. He is behind me on my old mark. The geometry is almost right and therefore worse. The fan shuts. One crack, dry as a bone. The track dies under it. We hold the end picture because no one has been told to release it. My arms are down. My chest is still trying to pop a count that already ended. Sweat runs the line of my spine and stops at the waistband like it, too, has been given a mark. Park walks the north edge, not into the formation, along it. The fan taps her opposite palm once for each body she passes. She stops in front of my reflection, which means she is slightly to my left in the real room, close enough that I can see the stitching on the fan’s guard. “Again, the arm,” she says. Her English is precise and tired of me. “You give it a tail. This choreography has no tail. Hit. Dead. The knee is a count, not a mood. And you crossed Hana. Her lane is not your freestyle.” I look at the glass because looking at her feels like looking at a locked door. Behind my reflection the others are still as coat racks. Back home, if you stood this still in a circle, somebody would shove you and laugh. Here stillness is the skill. Here the people who grew up with winter lessons and private mirrors already know how to make a body into a product shot. I arrived with bus-stop concrete in my ankles and a scholarship letter soft from being folded too many times. Every clean hit they throw is a receipt I cannot match. “From the top,” Park says. “If the wave comes, you cut it. Potential is not permission.” The fan opens. The track restarts. Five, six, seven, eight. One: chest. I lock the knees this time. The pop is uglier and righter. Two: the arm blades out. At the end of the line the wave rises in the forearm, faithful as a dog. I feel the choice in the wrist—let it finish, keep the voice that got me off my block, or kill it and become a picture they can sell. I kill it. The hand dies flat at forty-five. The mirror accepts me for half a count. Three, four: pivot east, knee up, toe pointed, no mood. Park is in front of me again, fan narrowing. Five, six: hinge, not bounce. Both palms find the floor on the marks. Seven: left foot cuts the true diagonal, inside Hana’s lane, not across it. Eight: I land center-front, arms snapped down, a meter from the glass, breath held so it will not fog the lie. The fan stays open. The chorus keeps going into a phrase I do not trust yet. My dead wrist hums where the wave was cut. I do not know if I passed or if I only proved I can disappear on command. The X I left behind is empty. The one under me now does not know my name.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a tightly controlled, disciplined piece of writing that fulfills nearly every instruction with precision. The spatial choreography is tracked with almost obsessive clarity: the narrator's position (back row, second from left), the mirror geometry, the diagonal path that clips Hana's lane, the corrected second run. The count-by-count structure (one through eight, twice) gives the prose a metrical spine that mirrors the militaristic discipline being demanded—form enacting theme. The strongest element is the contrast between movement languages. "Hana's arm is a stopped clock. Mine is still negotiating" is an excellent line, as is "everyone else is a still photograph; I am a half-second of weather." The muscle-memory betrayals are specific and kinetic: the knee groove from the bus-stop corner, the wrist circle that "finishes anyway, small, shameful." The second run, where the narrator kills the wave, dramatizes the conform-or-rebel decision point without resolving it sentimentally—the ending is appropriately ambivalent ("I do not know if I passed or if I only proved I can disappear on command"). Instructor Park is efficiently characterized through the fan, the dry crack, and clipped dialogue ("Potential is not permission"). The class anxiety is rendered concretely: "winter lessons and private mirrors," "a scholarship letter soft from being folded too many times," "every clean hit they throw is a receipt I cannot match." Weaknesses: the piece is so controlled it risks feeling airless. The metaphors occasionally crowd each other ("a coin-flip of the hand," "coat racks," "a product shot")—a few are strained or slightly overwrought, and the relentless precision of the prose sometimes performs the same rigidity it critiques, which is arguably intentional but can flatten emotional range. The supporting trainees (Minjae, Hana) are functional sketches rather than people. The dialogue is minimal and serviceable rather than memorable. The ending's ambivalence is earned, but the piece never quite breaks its own formation to surprise us—the structure is predictable (fail run, correction, corrected run), though executed at a high level. Minor incoherence: Park's fan is "closed" at the start, then "shuts" with a crack, then "opens"—this is actually tracked correctly, but "fan still open a crack" mid-piece reads ambiguously against the later "The fan shuts." A small blemish in an otherwise coherent physical world. Overall: an accomplished, vivid, disciplined piece with a few over-polished edges. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bailiff’s voice arrived before he did, a weather system in a throat. “The Court of the Dreaming is in session. All rise for the Lord of this place, who is already standing, and has been, and will be.” Dream did not move. Irritation sat on him like a well-cut coat. He had kingdoms to unmake before luncheon. Instead he had this. “Call the matter,” he said. “Ownership of Recurring Dreamscape, designation—” the bailiff squinted at a slip of starlight, “—Field of Reasonably Wild Flowers, Almost. Plaintiff: First Love. Defendant: Mora, also known as—” he drew breath, disastrously, “—MORA THE CHEST-SITTER, NIGHT-MARE, BREATH-THIEF, and—forgive me—‘that one.’” Somewhere in the gallery, a minor anxiety giggled and was hushed. First Love stood at the plaintiff’s rail, rosy to the ears, hands worrying a stem that had not decided whether it was a flower. “My lord. The dream was mine. I built it carefully. A schoolboy. A field. His crush. The light doing that thing light does when it is trying not to be obvious. Each recurrence ended in an almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion. Formative. Gentle. Mine.” “And now?” Dream asked. “Now,” First Love said, wounded, “when she leans over him, she becomes her.” Mora lounged in the dock as if furniture were a suggestion. Pale, heavy-lidded, faintly pleased. When she smiled, several sleeping minds three realms away rolled over and decided against it. “Defendant,” Dream said. “You infiltrated a crafted dream.” “I improved it,” Mora said. “The girl gets on him—playfully, I’m not a monster about choreography—and then the truth arrives. Weight. Paralysis. The interesting face. I sit. I feed. He wakes certain that love is a door with something behind it. Educational.” “You fed on his breath.” “A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” The bailiff, helpful, boomed: “The witness will refrain from cuisine.” “I wasn’t addressing you, pronunciation.” Dream’s mouth did not smile. Something behind his eyes considered it and declined. “Plaintiff. Describe the original culmination.” First Love flushed, which was most of his professional equipment. “He almost kisses her. He doesn’t. He lies there full of weather. No one is harmed. No one is eaten. The confusion is the sweet kind. I measured it.” “Measured,” Mora said. “With what, a blush?” “Call the dreamer,” Dream said, already regretting it. “MAXIMILIAN—no—MAX, THE BOY, THE ONE WITH THE—” the bailiff faltered, then committed, “—FEELINGS.” A thin figure was led in, still half-asleep at the edges, grass in his hair that was not grass. He looked at the court as if it might also turn into a girl and then into a problem. “You are the dreamer,” Dream said. “I think so. Sorry. Is this detention?” “It is worse. Recount the dream.” Max scratched his neck. “There’s a field. She’s there. We almost—um. Then she’s on me, which is—confusing, in a good way? And then her face does a thing, and she’s still—I don’t know—looking like someone I’d notice in a hallway, except she’s sitting on my chest and I can’t move and the air is leaving like it owes her money. I wake up embarrassed and terrified. Sometimes in that order. Sometimes at once.” First Love made a small, devastated sound. Mora spread her hands. “See? Range. I gave him two genres.” “You poached a jurisdiction,” First Love said. “First love is not a feeding ground. If every nightmare may squat in a tenderness because it is tender, then nothing gentle will survive the week.” “If every rosy clerk may fence off a sleeper’s chest because he got there first with wildflowers,” Mora said, “then I starve, and the night becomes a pamphlet. He was ripe. The almost-kiss is a door left open. I walk through doors.” Dream regarded them both. The case was small. The principle was not. He disliked both facts. “The dreamscape,” he said, “was crafted. Craft is a claim. Hunger is not a title.” Mora’s eyes cooled. He continued, because irritation enjoys company. “Nor is a crafted sweetness a lock against the night. The boy did not commission a pastoral. He slept. Sleep is a country with more than one law.” He was tempted—truly, pettily tempted—to give the field to Mora until the flowers learned fear, or to give it to First Love and let the boy almost-kiss forever, a fly in amber. Either would be a ruling. Neither would be justice. Mischief, though, could wear justice’s coat if the stitching was mean enough. “Judgment,” he said. The bailiff rose, booming on instinct. “ALL RISE FOR THE—” “Sit,” Dream said, and the word had weight. “The dream remains the plaintiff’s in its first movement. Field, girl, almost-kiss, pleasant confusion. Mora will not unmake that craft, nor feed before the culmination.” A pause, exquisite and unkind. “After the almost-kiss, the dream will fork. One path returns the boy to morning, muddled and whole. The other—” he looked at Mora, “—is yours, if he lingers. If he turns back for the second look. You may sit. You may take the breath you are owed by his curiosity, and no more. You will not wear the girl’s face longer than the moment of turning. Terror may be attractive. It may not counterfeit the plaintiff.” Mora’s smile thinned. “That’s a diet.” “It is a border.” First Love blinked. “And if he always lingers?” “Then you have built a door,” Dream said, “and doors are not cages. Teach him a sweeter hesitation, or accept that hesitation has teeth.” Max, forgotten, raised a hand. “Do I get a vote?” “No,” said Dream, Mora, and First Love, together. “Figures,” Max said, and yawned a yawn that tried to become a field and thought better of it. Dream stood. The court, which had never properly sat, pretended to conclude. “Next matter,” he said. The bailiff inhaled, doomed. “Boundary dispute between the DREAM OF TEETH FALLING OUT and the DREAM OF TEETH FALLING UP, petitioners respectively DENTAL ANXIETY and—” he squinted, gave up, and boomed the rest as if volume could invent the syllable, “—WHATEVER THAT IS.” Dream closed his eyes. In the dark behind them, a schoolboy almost kissed a girl, stopped, and—just for a moment—looked back. Somewhere, very softly, something sat down to wait.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece that hits nearly every requirement of the prompt: the courtroom farce, Dream's irritation, Mora's "a girl's gotta eat" defense, the dark understated humor, and the mischievous resolution. The bailiff's booming titles are a consistent comic engine, and the closing image (something sitting down to wait) lands the dark-comic tone perfectly. The judgment Dream renders is genuinely clever — a forked dream that satisfies both parties while being "exquisitely unkind" — and the temptation to mischief is explicitly dramatized. Max's "Do I get a vote?" / "No" in triplicate is a highlight. Weaknesses are minor. The prose occasionally strains for cleverness ("irritation sat on him like a well-cut coat" is good; "a weather system in a throat" is borderline). A few lines flirt with over-cuteness ("the light doing that thing light does when it is trying not to be obvious"). The teeth-falling-up gag at the end is a slightly predictable "next case" beat, though it works. Character depth is functional rather than deep — appropriate for a comic sketch, but Mora and First Love are one-note beyond their roles. The piece is coherent, well-paced, and the dialogue is consistently sharp and voice-differentiated.
